title: New Buy Now Pay Later rules - don't get caught out
text:
Don't get caught out by new Buy Now Pay Later rules
If you've bought something via Buy Now Pay Later (BNPL) since the summer, then you'll have been tested to see if you can afford it.
BNPL has always been a type of loan, usually paid back in instalments, but it's only been officially regulated since July.
This means stricter background checks on your ability to repay.
If you fail, then your purchase via BNPL will be blocked. If there's a chance of this happening to you, here are some ways to approach the situation.
What are the new rules?
BNPL lenders - such as Klarna, Clearpay and others - must now have regulator approval to operate, giving shoppers more access to refunds and independent rulings on complaints if things go wrong.
But new affordability checks on each BNPL transaction could also leave you blocked from services for the first time.
There are different affordability checks for different purchases, partially based on how much is borrowed.
But, with the expensive festive season approaching, here's how to avoid being blocked when time and finances are tight.
How do I avoid being blocked?
Here are four things to consider if you find your account is closed or your borrowing limit has been massively reduced, from Sara Williams, a former volunteer debt adviser at Citizens Advice who posts tips as Debt Camel on social media.
- Slow down your purchases: is what you are buying essential or can you postpone it?
- Be more careful about what you buy to avoid needing a high credit limit to, for example, buy lots of clothes in different sizes
- Cancel subscriptions to escape the trap of having to use BNPL to make up for the cost of previous payments
- Talk to debt charities for help and access to food bank vouchers if you are using BNPL for essentials
Avoid getting into debt
If you are struggling to make repayments on any type of loan - BNPL or otherwise - you should seek help before things spiral out of control.
The government-backed, independent, MoneyHelper website has a guide to finding free debt advice near you.
It also suggests writing down exactly what you owe, to help plan how you will repay the money.
There are also tools to work out if you are receiving all the benefits and grants you are entitled to, and a bill prioritiser to show which payments to make first and what to do if you miss a payment.
You should also be sceptical of supposed debt solutions you might see on your social feeds.

description: New affordability checks mean you could be blocked from using Buy Now Pay Later but here are ways to avoid it.

title: Judge dismisses Trump lawsuit over two Dan Sullivans in Alaska election
text:
Judge dismisses Trump administration's lawsuit over two Dan Sullivans in Alaska election
A judge has dismissed a lawsuit by the Trump administration that sought to delay certifying results in Alaska's crucial Senate race if the Republican incumbent loses.
The suit by the US Department of Justice argued that having two candidates named Dan Sullivan on the ballot could cause "voter confusion" and take support from incumbent Republican Dan S Sullivan.
The judge ruled that the federal government doesn't have authority to force Alaska to segregate and investigate any ballots in the three-way race between Sullivan, Daniel J Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola.
The Alaska Senate contest is considered one the closest in the Tuesday midterms, where control of Congress will be up for grabs.
"The United States provides no workable plan as to how it proposes to segregate ballots cast for Daniel J. Sullivan on Election Day and then conduct a court-ordered unspecified 'investigation' of those ballots in a manner that would preserve voter secrecy," US District Judge Sharon Gleason wrote in the ruling.
Alaska voters have the right to a secret ballot, she wrote, adding that regardless, such a move by the justice department would be too late as it is only days before the midterm election. Many voters have already cast their ballots in early voting and postal voting.
After the ruling, the justice department said it would file to appeal. It said in a statement that the court dismissed the federal case on "procedural grounds but did not dispute the argument of the United States that Daniel J. Sullivan (a/k/a Decoy Dan) entered the race as a frivolous candidate to confuse voters".
"Alaskan voters deserve a fair election, not to be misled in an attempt to rig outcomes," the statement continued.
Asked about the lawsuit last month, President Donald Trump said he had directed the justice department to file it.
"All of a sudden he decides to run for the Senate, and his name is Dan Sullivan. One is Daniel S., one is Daniel J. The Daniel J. is the fake," Trump told reporters.
Daniel J Sullivan, the little-known candidate running with no party affiliation, had previously told The New York Times he has voted both Democrat and Republican in the past.
Senator Dan S Sullivan, the incumbent Republican, and his allies have accused the Democrats of trying to confuse voters.
Then last week, controversy erupted when The New York Times reported that Democrats on Peltola's team worked with people who tried to recruit spoiler candidates in the Senate race.
Peltola has denied she knowing anything about an alleged "scheme" that led to the two Dan Sullivans standing in the race.
The Alaska race is considered by analysts to be one of the tightest in the upcoming US midterm elections, which will decide which party controls Congress for the last two years of Trump's presidency.
description: The Department of Justice had sought to delay certifying results in Alaska's crucial Senate race if the Republican incumbent loses.

title: Fake nuclear warnings issued after Ukrainian and Russian air alert apps hacked
text:
Fake nuclear warnings issued after Ukrainian and Russian air alert apps hacked
Ukraine and Russia have both said air alert apps were hacked on Sunday night after fake messages warning of attacks, including nuclear, were sent to users.
Ukraine's widely used app sent red-level air raid warnings across the country, with additional warnings of radiation, chemical attacks, and street fighting sent to some residents in areas including Kyiv.
A few hours later, Russian authorities said a similar app was hacked after fake alerts, some of which contained foul language, were triggered.
It was unclear who was behind the cyberattacks or whether the two incidents were connected.
Many Ukrainian citizens are used to receiving almost nightly alerts warning of incoming Russian missile and drone attacks. Some told the BBC that, four and a half years into the war, they have disabled the app altogether.
After Sunday night's hack, the country's air force urged people to consult other official channels.
In a post on Telegram, the air force said: "The Air Alarm application has probably been subjected to hostile interference. There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our [Telegram] channel."
The government said it had temporarily disabled the app for maintenance, saying it had "apparently been compromised".
Some of the fake warnings were written in Russian, which would have alerted many users to the fact they were not legitimate.
But Olena, a Kyiv resident, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme she had been alarmed, saying: "The first thought was 'oh my god, I'm not prepared for this'.
"I'm prepared for blackouts, for a cut in central heating and water supply, but not for nuclear attack."
Olena says her husband then received alerts for "street fighting attacks in Kyiv" and another alert, written in Russian.
"After that I understood that somebody had attacked the app, because all notifications we get in Ukrainian."
In Russia, the government said one of its air raid alert apps had also been targeted by "a massive cyberattack", which sent "fake information to the public".
A purported screenshot of a fake alert was shared on Telegram by Atesh, a partisan Ukrainian group operating inside Russian-held territory.
It warned some users that "nuclear warheads mounted on P1-Suns [a Ukrainian attack drone] had been launched at all regions of Russia".
The alert, which included profanities, opened with a message telling residents there was a "risk of [things] getting lively" and told them to "stock up urgently on food for three weeks and hide".
On Monday morning there was no sense the messages had caused widespread panic in Russia and the incident did not feature prominently on media outlets.
Asked about the breach, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov did not address it specifically but said all Russian government internet resources were "one way or another... under constant cyberattacks", including the presidential site, which is targeted "round the clock".
He said the proliferation of AI technology was contributing to an increase in cyberattacks.
Russia's emergencies ministry said on Monday that the app's "full functionality will be restored by the end of the day" and the hack had not impacted the wider alert system.
While both Russia and Ukraine are widely believed to carry out cyberattacks against one another, the informal language used in the hoax alerts on Sunday pointed to so-called hacktivist groups, which could be aligned to Moscow or Kyiv but are not formally directed by either government.
Those responsible for the hack on Russia's system have likely had the capability to launch such an attack for some time but decided to hold off until Ukraine's alert app was compromised, cyber experts told the BBC.
Oleksander Merezhko, chair of the foreign affairs committee in the Ukrainian parliament, said the attack did not cause panic or extreme reactions.
Merezhko told the BBC that Ukrainians, especially in Kyiv, were used to "practically non-stop alerts", adding "this message was in Russian language which immediately aroused suspicions".
He continued: "It's a very unpleasant fact but it is part of cyber war and people in Ukraine understand that. It is possible and we are quite prepared for such possibilities."
Herbert Lin, a senior research scholar for cyber policy and security at Stanford University, told BBC World Service's Newsday programme: "I think it's the first time [a hack of this kind] happened to an official Ukrainian information app, but I suspect it won't be the last."
The alerts in Ukraine were sent minutes before the end of a localised ceasefire in Ukraine's frontline Kherson region, which was implemented last Tuesday. It had been brokered in part by US First Lady Melania Trump to allow civilians to evacuate the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky.
Fighting continued elsewhere while the Kherson ceasefire was in place. In the city of Dnipro alone, 15 people were killed in an attack on a train platform on Thursday.
Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Additional reporting by Jamie Whitehead and Helen Davidson
description: Neither government has confirmed who was responsible for the cyberattacks on Sunday evening.

title: Women with cleft lip scarring praise advance in aesthetics
text:
Cleft lip filler 'boosts confidence' - but expert warns of exploitation risk
Two young women who have turned to dermal fillers after having cleft lip surgery say it has given them confidence after they were both left with scarring.
"Now I feel like I can just go out and talk to anyone, be more social and just be confident," Amber Dorgan, 20, from Neath, said of the treatment, which is offered by the NHS as well as by aesthetic clinics.
But experts and clinics have called for regulations to be introduced for aesthetic practitioners providing the service.
It comes as one psychology academic warned people with a cleft lip were being "deliberately targeted" by the aesthetics industry and "left vulnerable to potential harm and exploitation".
Aesthetics treatment for people with scars involves using filler to reduce their appearance, restore symmetry, and add volume after cleft lip surgery.
Dorgan was born with a cleft lip and has faced hearing difficulties, speech difficulties and bullying at school because of her scars.
She had five operations as a child, as well as regular hospital appointments for speech and language therapy.
Now she receives free dermal filler for life through The Welsh Centre for Cleft Lip and Palate based in Morriston Hospital in Swansea, something she feels extremely fortunate to have.
Dorgan said: "I've always been insecure about how I look, going out and about, I've always had anxiety and I just get nervous.
"Now the lip fillers have made me feel confident in myself a little bit more. It's helped a lot," she said.
Dorgan believes the treatment should be available to everyone with a cleft lip "because it makes you much more confident and happy".
"Before [filler] I was really shy, I wouldn't talk to anyone, I didn't want to leave the house."
What is a cleft lip and palate?
A cleft lip and palate is a condition which is present from birth when the upper lip, roof of the mouth, or both, fail to fuse properly during pregnancy.
It affects one in every 700 babies born in the UK and surgery to close the cleft is typically given when a baby is three to six months old.
A cleft lip and cleft palate can cause a number of issues, particularly in the first few months after birth before surgery is carried out.
This can include difficulty feeding, hearing problems, dental problems and speech problems.
The NHS offers lifelong care to those with the condition.
Emily Evans, 21, from Kidwelly in Carmarthenshire, is a stay-at-home mum to her two young children.
She was born with a cleft lip and underwent two surgeries, one as a baby to close her cleft, and one when she was 10 to smooth out her lips.
Growing up she always felt different, as her peers would ask questions about her scar.
"Nobody hates anything more than being different," she said.
"I would often joke I was bitten by a shark."
Evans was discharged from cleft services when she was 17. She was never offered filler treatment for her scars, but was told to keep in contact.
"When I was younger, I was seeing these people who all look perfect and the same, and I didn't," she said.
"So it sort of felt like I needed to sort of get something done."
Evans said she thought aesthetics treatments might help boost her confidence.
"I understand why people might not choose to have filler, it makes people unique, it's nice to have something that makes people different," she said.
But she added: "I think more people would choose to have it if it was a more well-known option."
Both women agree that seeing more people with a cleft lip in the public eye would help young people with the condition.
Evans discovered through social media that treatments were available and found aesthetic practitioners in England offering it to those with scars.
But she said she found a lack of practitioners in Wales.
That was until Evans discovered Summer Rose-Dorland, who runs a clinic in her hometown in Somerset and sometimes runs pop-up clinics in Wales.
After completing extra training she now works with non-profit organisation CleftInject, which help adults with scarring from cleft lip surgery find aesthetic practitioners who understand the condition.
According to Rose-Dorland, some practitioners associated with CleftInject "offer a majority of treatments free of charge", especially for people's first treatments.
She said: "A lot of my clients struggle with their scar, I have messages from people that say that they had to stand side on in photos or when they're talking to someone because they feel like they obviously have to stand a different way."
Some people may choose an aesthetic practitioner over the NHS, she said, as they believe they will have more choice about how their lips will look after.
There are currently no regulations in the aesthetics industry, and some people believe that practitioners like Rose-Dorland should not be allowed to offer and administer these treatments.
Rose-Dorland, who qualified four years ago and said she had since done 20 training courses, said: "I'm a non-medic and I stand for having regulation, I generally think we need it in the aesthetics industry.
"There are some people out there that just do things that are actually quite scary, but I don't think it should be that a non-medic can't practise.
"The person I trained with trains medics, so it's not just non-medic doing these trainings. There's doctors, nurses, midwives, they are all actually doing the same training as well."
Dr Neil Brierley is a consultant cleft and plastic surgeon in the West Midlands Cleft Service.
He said it was important for people who have had a cleft lip or have loved ones with a cleft to engage with NHS teams that provide lifelong support and care.
The surgeon said they could offer an "unbiased" opinion to come to "an appropriate decision between the individual that's seeking assistance and what we feel is their best and worst options".
"What we don't want is to have people who are potentially vulnerable who are looking for maybe a quick fix or a solution to feel that they don't have an option to come back to the NHS," he said.
"And they certainly do not have to, but we are here if they need us."
Brierley said everyone was entitled to their own choice about using aesthetic practitioners, but that it was important to be aware of how to deal with any complications.
"I think it's important to inform your cleft team because it may impact any further treatment that you might need," he said.
"For example if you were wanting revisional surgery, placement of filler in certain areas would prevent certain operations from being possible afterwards."
Brierley said the lack of regulations around injectables and cleft dermal fillers was also concerning.
"I know that there are a number of organisations, various world colleges and specialist societies [which] are trying to bring in regulation in line with government but at the moment the entire field is unregulated, he said.
"There will be many excellent practitioners out there, but it will be impossible to know in advance if there is someone who isn't following best practice."
Dr Nicola Stock is an associate professor whose work focuses on the psychological impact of appearance-altering conditions such as a cleft lip.
Alongside others, she has worked on a project at the University of the West of England's Centre for Appearance Research. They have looked into the use of dermal fillers for people with a cleft, the people who provide them, what experiences and qualifications they have, and how these fillers are being marketed to the community.
Stock said research suggested adults born with a cleft still had concerns with their appearance after surgery.
The research also suggested that more people born with a cleft lip were interested in aesthetics treatments like dermal filler.
She believes the way filler is being marketed on social media is fuelling this steady increase of people seeking out treatment.
"Within the general population, dermal filler has exploded in popularity in recent years, and it's now one of the most common non-surgical cosmetic procedures used worldwide," she said.
"And we believe that this is being fuelled predominately by the aesthetics industry and predominately on social media."
Stock said she was worried that adults with a cleft lip, who have a complex medical history, were being "deliberately targeted" and "left vulnerable to potential harm and exploitation at the hands of the aesthetics industry".
Until there are more guidelines in the sector, Stock recommended that anyone considering dermal filler should research their options and get in touch with their local NHS cleft team or contact the Cleft Lip and Palate Action charity.
If you have been affected by the issues raised in this story, information about available help and support can be found via BBC Action Line.
Additional Reporting by Lucy Vladev.
description: Two women from Wales are among the growing number of people having lip filler after cleft lip and palate surgery.

title: Drugs, cash and weapons found in South Wales Police e-bike raids
text:
Drugs, cash and weapons found in raids as e-bikes 'blight' communities
Amphetamines, cannabis, suspected cocaine, cash and weapons have been found in early morning raids across south Wales as part of a clampdown on illegal e-bikes.
Police are growing increasingly concerned about the link between e-bikes, serious organised crime and child exploitation - with many suspected offences being committed by children.
One senior officer said people were "fed up" of e-bikes "blighting" areas across the UK, while an expert said they could "grease the wheels" of organised crime.
The BBC has been given access to an operation by South Wales Police to combat e-bike related crime, from illegal riding to drug dealing - a local response to a national problem.
It is six o'clock in the morning and the BBC has been invited to a police briefing involving undercover officers in Merthyr Tydfil.
Operation Grebe is a response to escalating concerns about illegal e-bike use across the UK.
An organised crime officer, who cannot be identified, leads the briefing.
"The aim is to disrupt criminal networks operating across the south Wales area, identify and safeguard vulnerable adults, children affected by criminal exploitation [and] seize criminal assets and disrupt criminal finances," he said.
This operation is about seizing vehicles, but also disrupting the darker side of e-bikes.
Officers have received intelligence that e-bikes and e-motorbikes may be linked to drug dealing in the area.
On a dark, wet, misty morning, police vans make their way to homes across south Wales.
"These e-bikes are blighting communities, they're making it unsafe for people to live - so we're taking action," said Supt Emma Fox, who oversees the raids.
As the head of specialist operations within the force, she knows how potent a criminal tool e-bikes and e-motorbikes have become.
"It's prevalent across the UK," she said, adding e-bikes were "often linked to drug use, drug supply and organised criminality".
And she was particularly concerned about children on e-bikes being "exploited" by hardened criminals.
Frankly, she said, "it's easier to avoid the police", on the bikes.
But police forces are fighting back, and are employing increasingly sophisticated ways to tackle e-bike related crime including drones and their own fleets of e-motorbikes.
Surrey Police launched Operation Scramble in response to e-bikes being linked to criminal activity - this year, the force seized 136 e-bikes, up from 127 in 2025.
Dr Timothy Holmes, senior lecturer in criminology and policing at Bangor University, said e-bikes could "grease the wheels" of organised crime.
"From a criminal activity point of view, it's a very versatile vehicle - it's easily manoeuvrable and goes at a high speed," he said.
"They are becoming an emerging issue because they are so visible."
He compared the supply and availability of illegally held and adapted e-bikes and e-motorbikes to the illegal arms industry, where there is "a big legal industry" and an illegal industry "bleeding off from it".
He said, for police, it was a "balance" of "how much do you stop this escalating into a problem, in lieu of going after the more serious areas of organised crime, like drug trafficking like county lines".
In Merthyr Tydfil, the police van pulls up near a redbrick, semi-detached home.
Officers pour out and stand ready with a battering ram, but the front door is already open.
There are also raids in Cardiff, Pontypridd and Swansea.
Across the 14 raids, 12 bikes were seized. Some will be destroyed, and 11 people were arrested, including for suspected drugs offences.
Four people in the Swansea raid were charged with suspected drugs offences, including supply of crack cocaine and heroin.
And in Merthyr Tydfil, Fox said there was a "significant seizure".
"We have seized a quantity of drugs and cash - suspected cannabis and cocaine," she said.
"The drugs have been found upstairs in the house."
The suspected drugs will now be tested.
Alongside the suspected drugs and £1,300 in cash was an electric bike, electric motorbike and a quad bike.
Two people were arrested and taken away from the house in handcuffs.
"It shows the link between the use of electric illegal bikes and criminality," Fox said.
"Air weapons" had been found in the address, Fox said, which she added officers were "surprised" to find.
"We wouldn't have known about them, but it is something that has been recovered from the address," she said.
Senior officers say they are investing in technology to combat e-bikes, but said this was not just a policing problem, and would need a broader effort to tackle the issue.
description: A senior police officer says e-bikes and associated crimes are "blighting" communities across the UK.

title: Holyhead murder arrest after police attend 'medical emergency'
text:
Murder arrest after police called to 'medical emergency' on residential street
A 61-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of murder following a "medical emergency" in the early hours of Sunday morning.
North Wales Police said officers were called at 03:49 GMT to a residential property on Morawelon Road in Holyhead, on Anglesey, by the Welsh Ambulance Service.
Det Insp Rob Mahoney said the force was treating it as an "isolated incident" and there was no ongoing threat to the wider community.
He added there would be increased police presence in the area while detectives continued to "investigate the circumstances of this incident".
The arrested man remains in custody and police asked anyone with information to contact them.

title: Plane may have broken apart ahead of deadly Florida jet crash, say investigators
text:
Plane may have broken apart ahead of deadly Florida jet crash, say investigators
The US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) says it will investigate whether parts of a jet that crashed in Florida broke off before it nose-dived and exploded, killing all nine people on board.
The Learjet 60, which was travelling from Austin, Texas to the Bahamas on Sunday, crashed on a street nine miles (14 km) from President Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago resort.
A tech entrepreneur and his young family, as well as the 20-year-old copilot, were among those who died.
The NTSB said on Monday that it would also investigate to what extent ice and turbulence may have been contributing factors.
It confirmed that, after the jet took off from Austin, the crew transmitted to air traffic control that they were encountering ice and moderate turbulence.
"We are picking up precipitation, requesting to climb to 37,000 feet if able," the crew said.
NTSB member Tom Chapman said that less than 30 seconds later, the plane began to descend and the crew issued a mayday call.
The transmission then became "unintelligible", he said, adding that: "Sadly, all aboard were lost."
The NTSB said that ice and turbulence were factors in the crash but that determining its probable cause will be a "lengthy investigatory process".
Thunderstorms had been reported in the area at the time.
Officials are also trying to find out whether a cockpit voice recorder was on board at the time of the crash and if it can be recovered.
As part of the investigation, the NTSB is working with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), representatives from Learjet as well as meteorologists and air traffic control experts.
Recovering the wreckage from the crater on the roadway will be a "daunting challenge", said Timothy Monville, an air safety investigator with the safety board.
Flight analysis indicates the jet was plummeting hundreds of feet per second before crashing.
In air traffic control audio, a crew member can be heard declaring an emergency, shouting "we are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000ft per minute", before saying, "we are going to crash into the ground".
About 35 seconds after the initial mayday announcement, the last remark from the cockpit appears to be "we're out of time".
The seven people killed who were travelling as passengers were identified in a joint statement from their families as tech entrepreneur Adam Robinson, his wife Helen Sharp, and their two children - Emma and Charlie - as well as Rachael Reed, Charmi Fehr and Anita Maria Cetina.
The pilot was named in media reports as Jeffery Gregory, while Nathalia Filgueiras, who earned her pilot's licence when she was 17, was reported to be the copilot.
As well as those killed, one man on the ground sustained a leg injury when the plane nosedived onto the street.
The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said the crash happened on Military Trail, a six-lane road lined with businesses and restaurants.
Images from the crash scene show a large fiery crater in the middle of a residential suburban street.
The debris was scattered across sports fields, businesses and homes in the area, officials told a news conference on Monday, possible evidence that the plane broke up before it hit the ground.
Unverified footage posted on social media shows what appears to be a dash-camera recording of the moment of the crash.
Trump was at Mar-a-Lago on Sunday morning, and departed from an airport nearby on Air Force One about an hour before the crash.
description: The National Transportation Safety Board also believes weather could have been a factor in the crash, but warns it is too early to determine the cause.

title: Newcastle Fenwick Christmas window Gruffalo Child theme revealed
text:
Fenwick Christmas window's Gruffalo theme revealed
Thousands have tuned in to watch the unveiling of this year's Fenwick's Christmas window.
The theme at the Newcastle department store took its inspiration from Dame Julia Donaldson's The Gruffalo's Child.
Dame Julia said she was "delighted" her book would be part of creating special memories for families in the city this year. "It's wonderful to see The Gruffalo's Child brought to life in such a magical way," she said.
Meanwhile the store's head Mia Fenwick said bringing the Gruffalo to the Christmas window was a "long-held ambition" fulfilled.
The city centre department store's festive display has been a fixture for generations of families since 1971.
For 2026, Fenwick teamed up with Donaldson and German illustrator Axel Scheffler to recreate their 2004 book for the display.
Scheffler said it was a "real pleasure" to see the world of the book brought to life on such a "grand scale".
"It's wonderful to see my illustrations transformed into something so imaginative and full of life," he said.
For the fifth year running, a special score was composed in partnership with the Glasshouse International Centre for Music in Gateshead, and performed by the Royal Northern Sinfonia.
The music reimagined Edvard Grieg's In the Hall of the Mountain King with sleigh bells and animal sounds, according to the orchestra.

title: Russian strikes cut power to thousands in Ukraine as Kherson ceasefire ends
text:
Russian strikes cut power to thousands in Ukraine as Kherson ceasefire ends
A rare humanitarian ceasefire in Ukraine's front-line Kherson region that allowed civilians to evacuate the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky has ended.
The localised ceasefire was due to end at 22:59 Ukrainian time (21:00 GMT) on Sunday. While the truce had held since it was implemented last week, fighting had continued elsewhere.
On Sunday evening, Ukraine's air alert system was apparently hacked, the country's air force said, warning of radiation over Kyiv - a reference to a possible nuclear attack.
The Air Force message read: "The Air Alarm application has probably been subjected to hostile interference. There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia had struck energy infrastructure in four regions overnight on Saturday, leaving hundreds of thousands of homes without power. Some connections were restored on Sunday.
Another overnight strike killed two people, including a 13-year-old girl, in the Vinnytsia region, the State Emergency Service of Ukraine said.
Meanwhile, Ukraine hit a major missile fuel producer in Russia's Rostov region, which caused a fire and damaged four production facilities, Zelensky said.
In Ukraine, repair works to restore power continued throughout the day. Most customers in the Dnipropetrovsk region had their connections restored by early evening, but more than 60,000 were still without power, the governor said.
Because of regular attacks on energy infrastructure, emergency power cuts have been introduced across the country. Even in the capital Kyiv, electricity is cut off for most of the day, and water supplies are also disrupted.
Zelensky said in a social media post that the intensity of Russian strikes has been "extremely high" over the past week, adding that Russia was "trying to take maximum advantage of the shortage of ballistic missile interceptors".
He added that "every day" Ukraine communicated its need for Patriot missiles - the only effective weapon for downing Russia's deadly ballistic missiles - to the US, Europe and other partners. He thanked countries for their support so far and longer-term commitments, but called again for more immediate aid.
The limited pause in hostilities, which started on Tuesday, was brokered with the help of US First Lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo.
It was originally confined to the city of Oleshky, which has been occupied by Russia since the first days of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and was expanded across the wider region of Kherson.
Oleshky had been trapped on one side by the Dnipro river and the other by Russian forces, with routes out mined and subject to drone attack.
Residents trapped there were suffering severe shortages of food, water and electricity, with many resorting to cooking garden weeds to survive.
The truce allowed for Oleskhy residents to evacuate if they wanted, and there were emotional scenes on Saturday of reunions between loved ones who hadn't seen eachother for years.
There are Ukrainian military positions just 5km (3.1 miles) from Oleshky, but evacuees had to travel through Russian-occupied territory to southern Russia, where they flew to Belarus, before finally being driven across Ukraine's northern border.
The oldest evacuee was 94 years old, while the youngest was one, according to Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's human rights ombudsman.
description: A rare humanitarian ceasefire allowed civilians to evacuate the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky.

title: Waverley council launches grant funding for loneliness projects
text:
Grant fund aims to tackle loneliness and isolation
A council is offering grants of up to £35,000 to support community projects aimed at reducing loneliness and improving wellbeing.
Waverley Borough Council said funding of between £3,000 and £35,000 would be available for projects supporting vulnerable residents across the borough.
A council spokesperson said the funding will be available between April 2027 and March 2028.
Kika Mirylees, portfolio holder for community services, said: "Our voluntary and community sector plays a vital role in supporting residents and helping people access the services, advice and connections they need to thrive."
She added: "Local organisations provide invaluable support every day, often reaching people who may otherwise struggle to get the help they need.
"They help reduce isolation, improve wellbeing and strengthen communities across the borough."
To be eligible for the funding, not-for-profit organisations must provide a service in the borough which fits the initiative's goals.
The council said grants would be awarded for specific projects rather than for organisations' general running costs.
Applications must be submitted by 21 December.
The bids will be assessed in January before funding is allocated in February 2027.

title: Coventry fan, 14, hands himself in after Bradley Lowery taunt
text:
Boy hands himself in after Bradley Lowery taunt
A 14-year-old boy has handed himself into West Midlands Police after a video posted on social media appeared to show a Coventry City fan taunting opposition Sunderland fans with a photo of Bradley Lowery.
Sunderland fan Bradley, who died aged six in 2017 after being diagnosed with a rare childhood cancer, captured the hearts of the football world.
The Sky Blues said they were investigating the video footage from Saturday's Premier League match and Bradley's mother, Gemma, issued an emotional statement.
West Midlands Police said they had begun an investigation. "A 14-year-old boy has since handed himself in and will be spoken with in due course," a spokesperson said.
The police spokesperson added: "We understand the upset and outrage this video has caused in the community and to the victim's family, and our officers are keeping them up to date with the progress of our investigation and working closely alongside both football clubs."
Coventry City said in a statement earlier on Sunday: "Coventry City FC is aware of footage circulating on social media in connection with an incident during our Premier League fixture against Sunderland [on Saturday].
"The club does not tolerate offensive behaviour and will liaise with the relevant authorities to determine the appropriate course of action."
'A beautiful memory'
Gemma Lowery issued a statement through the Bradley Lowery Foundation, which raises funds and awareness to help and support children with cancer, saying her "beautiful boy deserves to be remembered with love, not hate".
She posted on Instagram: "As Bradley's mam, this is heartbreaking, especially as it's one of my favourite photographs of him. Just look at that smile.
"I remember that day like it was yesterday. He was so happy, having so much fun. Those moments were precious because they were few and far between.
"So much of Bradley's short life was spent battling cancer and enduring treatments no child should ever face.
"To see such a beautiful memory used in such a cruel way really does make my heart hurt."
She added: "I'm all for football banter, but surely mocking a child who died from cancer is not banter?"
The mother said she hoped the club took "appropriate action" and the individual's family helped him understand "how hurtful his actions were".
"I don't want hatred directed towards him, so please please don't, just for him to learn from this," she said.
"Thank you to everyone who has defended Bradley and shown us so much love. It means more than you know."

title: Democrat Haley Stevens endorses Republican in Michigan Senate race
text:
Democrat endorses Republican candidate in key Michigan Senate race as party spat erupts
A Democrat in Michigan has endorsed the Republican candidate in the state's crucial US Senate contest, as a spat with her own party's candidate Abdul El-Sayed escalated just days before the vote.
Haley Stevens, a sitting congresswoman who lost out on the Democratic Senate nomination to El-Sayed, made a surprise appearance alongside the Republican candidate Mike Rogers on Sunday.
"I don't belong in Abdul's campaign," she said in a video posted to X shortly after that appearance. "Who we are as Michiganders is not hate and is not what we are getting out from our Democratic nominee right now."
"That's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers," Stevens said.
The move stunned many of Stevens' fellow Democrats who condemned her decision to break from the party and switch her support just two days before the election, with one calling it a "despicable betrayal".
The public feud between Stevens, a centrist Democrat, and El-Sayed, who represents the party's left-wing, has boiled over in recent days.
Stevens called on El-Sayed to denounce a campaign advert from an outside liberal group that linked US support for Israel with high prices. El-Sayed criticised the advert and said he had nothing to do with its contents.
Stevens had been scheduled to appear at an event with El-Sayed on Sunday in an effort to display party unity, but he reportedly asked her not to come and she chose to attend a church service with his Republican opponent instead.
"This is a very close election, we all know that, but Abdul made clear that I was not welcome in his campaign, that he didn't need me there, that he didn't want me there," Stevens told reporters as she stood alongside Rogers outside the church.
When asked about Stevens' endorsement, El-Sayed told reporters he was focused on the problems Michiganders are facing.
"At the end of the day, I don't think about Haley Stevens," he said on Sunday. "None of this matters."
The Michigan Senate race is considered by analysts to be one of the tightest in Tuesday's midterm elections. It is one of a handful of battleground contests that will ultimately decide control of the Senate.
The seat is currently held by a retiring Democrat and the last time a Republican was elected to this Senate seat was in 1994. But in presidential elections, it is one of the crucial swing states - Michigan voted for Joe Biden in 2020 but Donald Trump in 2024.
Rogers welcomed Stevens' endorsement and said it showed "courage" during brief remarks with reporters.
President Donald Trump echoed that sentiment during a campaign rally in Iowa, calling her "very brave".
"I don't know Haley. I've never met Haley. But Haley said what few people were willing to say," Trump said. "I'd love her to join the Republican Party actually."
Many of Stevens' staff reportedly resigned immediately after her announcement, while the chair of the Democratic Party in Michigan said her decision "shows that she has abandoned everything she claims to care about".
"We reject the attempts by Stevens and bad-faith actors to divide our party and undermine our momentum," Curtis Hertel said in a statement.
Top Senate Democrat Chuck Schumer called Stevens' endorsement of Rogers "a despicable betrayal".
In downtown Detroit, several Democrats the BBC spoke to said they were disappointed by Stevens' endorsement of Rogers.
"I just genuinely don't understand it," said Summer Lawrence, a 21-year-old student. "I do think it's a betrayal of the party because the things she stands for are not the same things that he stands for as a Republican."
"Maybe she had frustrations with the party," Matthew Barera, another Michigan voter, said.
Others, including Republicans who support Rogers, said they doubted it would make a difference to the race.
"People can see right through her actions, you know? She's just angry," Marissa Lee, a Rogers supporter, told the BBC. "She is not going to make anybody change their mind."
Over the weekend, as Stevens' criticism of El-Sayed escalated, a number of Democratic politicians in Michigan publicly encouraged her to end the feud and back the party's candidates more directly.
The primary, and the conflict between the pair, has underlined divisions over the party's direction ahead of the 2028 presidential election.
Former public health official El-Sayed, who is the son of Egyptian immigrants, has channelled grassroots frustration with Washington politics as well as US ties to Israel.
Stevens is a more centrist Democrat - and had the support of party figures such as Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer during the primary race.
The party is hoping to regain control of the Senate in Tuesday's elections, but will need a net gain of four seats to do so. A loss in Michigan - which they currently hold - would represent a major blow and leave them needing to flip five seats.

title: Conwy Golf Club closes after fire causes "significant damage"
text:
'Great sadness' as fire damage forces golf club to close
A golf club has been forced to close after a fire caused "significant damage" to its clubhouse on Saturday evening.
North Wales Fire and Rescue Service said firefighters were called to a building fire at Conwy Golf Club at about 21:21 GMT.
Crews from several fire stations attended the scene and remained on site on Sunday, but the cause of the blaze has not yet been determined.
In a statement on social media, Conwy Golf Club said: "It is with great sadness that we must share that a serious fire occurred at the clubhouse last night."
It added "thankfully, no-one was hurt," and said it was "incredibly grateful to the emergency services and hard work throughout the night".
"For safety reasons, the golf course and all club facilities are currently closed," it said.
"We know this news will come as a huge shock to our members, visitors, and the local community."
The fire service said firefighters from Conwy, Colwyn Bay, Llandudno, Rhyl, Denbigh, St Asaph, Abergele, Betws-y-Coed and a high volume pump from Caernarfon were all in attendance.
Pictures showed the roof of the clubhouse was completely burned through.
The club said "emergency services have specifically requested that members, visitors, and the public do not attend the club premises under any circumstances until the site is declared safe", adding "access to the grounds and buildings is strictly prohibited".
Responding to the club's statement, one commenter said it was "incredibly sad news", while another wrote: "As members we will all have to pull together and play our part in the rebuild of this great club."
On its website, Conwy Golf Club describes its championship links course as located in a "stunning" coastal spot, and ranked number one in north Wales.

title: Sydney armed police start street patrols after Bondi Beach attack
text:
Armed police start patrols in Sydney after Bondi Beach attack
Heavily-armed police officers have started patrolling Sydney's streets, as part of heightened security measures following last year's deadly shooting at Bondi Beach.
The Armed Response Command (ARC) will see specially trained officers in busy tourist areas carrying long-arm rifles – an unfamiliar sight for most residents.
New South Wales police say the officers will also patrol major events like sports matches and places of worship "to prevent, deter and rapidly respond to serious threats, including active armed offender incidents".
Fifteen people - including a 10-year-old girl – were killed in December when two gunmen opened fire on an event marking the Jewish festival of Hanukkah at the popular beach.
The attack was Australia's worst mass shooting in almost three decades and prompted sweeping gun law reforms and a crackdown on hate speech.
One resident told ABC news that the sight of armed police was "unnerving".
"They are just everywhere. Those guns are huge."
But another woman told the broadcaster that seeing police with weapons made her feel safe.
ARC is specifically designed to be "highly visible across Sydney, driving specialist vehicles and carrying rifles," New South Wales police said in a statement.
Its role "is built on a simple principle - preserving life," Detective Superintendent Andrew Evans said.
The shooting on 14 December put huge pressure on Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's government, with calls for immediate action on antisemitism.
Jewish communities have welcomed the new police operation, which will eventually consist of 250 officers, but others have called for safeguards to protect human rights.
"No Australian wants to see officers with military weapons on our streets, but the sight of body bags is far worse," Alex Ryvchin, co-CEO of Executive Council of Australian Jewry, said.
But Amnesty International Australia said it was concerned about the "militarisation of policing", and asked for assurances from the state government that ARC will not be used to suppress peaceful protests.
"Any expansion of police powers and capabilities must be accompanied by clear, publicly accessible rules, robust independent oversight and accountability," said the organisation's Andrew Witheford.
The New South Wales administration defended the new measures.
"Our world changed forever. That's just the truth of it, right across this country. And I said it at the time, we will never be the same again," the state's Police Minister Yasmin Catley told the ABC.
One of the alleged gunmen, Naveed Akram, has been charged with 78 offences including 15 counts of murder, 40 counts of attempted murder, and one count of committing a terrorist act.
His father, Sajid Akram, 50 - who was also armed and shot at the crowd on Bondi Beach - was killed by police at the scene.

title: Holme Moss farm appeal as 30 sheep die after suspected dog attack
text:
Farm plea as 30 sheep die in suspected dog attack
Thirty sheep have died following a suspected dog attack on a family farm in West Yorkshire.
The incident happened on Field Head Farm in Holme Moss, south of Huddersfield, between Tuesday night and Wednesday morning.
Some of the sheep are thought to have been mauled to death, while others died from stress after being chased, according to James Brown, who works on the farm.
He asked for any witnesses to come forward with information and appealed to dog walkers to keep their pets on a lead.
Brown said he was "in shock" after finding the sheep's corpses on Wednesday.
He added that 28 animals, about 10% of the farm's livestock, initially lost their lives, while another two died later.
"It's the trauma of losing them, especially when they've been kept for such a long time and they were going to remain on the farm," Brown said. "They were not meat animals."
"From what we've pieced together it would appear to be a dog attack. It's the fifth we've had this year.
"This is the most severe one we've had, but it's not the first."
Robert Nobles, from the National Farmers Union, said dog attacks on livestock were "quite a problem".
He added: "Sheep are very sensitive animals and they don't stand a lot of stress.
"It's a stark reminder to people to be careful in the countryside.
"We want them to come out and bring their dogs with them, but they've got to be responsible. Where there's livestock, keep dogs on a lead and there's no risk of this happening."

title: Lindsay Clancy will reappear in court - but will her case be retried?
text:
Lindsay Clancy is back in court - where will her case go next?
Lindsay Clancy, the US woman accused of murdering her three children, will return to a Massachusetts court on Monday as lawyers debate retrying the case.
Her defence team and Massachusetts prosecutors are expected to discuss how to move forward, with both parties seeking different outcomes.
Last week, in response to a defence request to dismiss the trial, prosecutors offered their clearest hint yet that they are seeking a new trial before a different jury. "The Commonwealth [Massachusetts] should be permitted to continue to pursue justice for Cora, Dawson and Callan Clancy," her three children, prosecutors said.
Prosecutors could also reduce the charges in a potential second trial or dismiss them altogether.
Clancy's first trial ended in a mistrial after a 12-person jury failed to reach a consensus.
The 36-year-old has not denied killing her children in 2023, but her defence team argues she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis at the time. Prosecutors say the killings were intentional.
What happened when Clancy was last in court?
A jury first heard Clancy's case in August 2026, but failed to reach a unanimous agreement on whether the prosecution had proved Clancy was guilty "beyond a reasonable doubt" as required by US law.
A judge declared a mistrial in early September.
At a court appearance later that month, Clancy's lawyer, Kevin Reddington, argued the judge should dismiss her case. Meanwhile, prosecutors said the state had "met its burden" in proving her guilt.
But the hours-long back-and-forth ultimately didn't lead to a clearer answer about what might come next for Clancy - a dismissal of charges, retrial of the same charges, or retrial of lesser charges. These discussions will resume on Monday.
Judge William Sullivan seemed confident the case would be retried, saying in September he wanted to "get this thing moving".
He asked both sides to prepare to discuss possible trial dates at the November hearing.
Reddington said he would be unable to go to trial until at least June 2027 if the case was retried.
District Attorney Timothy Cruz said at the time that prosecutors had not yet decided whether to retry Clancy.
"We're doing our due diligence; we're going to continue doing that," he said. "We're going to do what we can for the children. That's what this case is about."
What do Clancy's legal team want?
Fundamentally, Clancy's legal team - with Reddington at the helm - is pushing for the charges to be dismissed or dropped. They've explored a variety of legal avenues.
In September, he asked for her to be found not guilty under Rule 25 - a Massachusetts provision that states a defendant should be found not guilty if prosecutors do not present enough evidence at trial.
That request was denied.
Judge Sullivan will hear arguments on several motions on Monday, but Heather Cucolo, a New York Law School professor and mental health law expert, told the BBC that the hearing will likely focus on a narrow point: was this an instance of a routine deadlocked-jury mistrial - in which the jury genuinely could not agree - or was this an improperly terminated trial?
She said Reddington may argue that a retrial could violate Clancy's Constitutional protection against double jeopardy - a legal standard that says a person cannot be tried for the same crime twice.
But legal experts agree that outcome is unlikely.
"The public attention that's been put on this trial and the need to have some conclusion in the near future, I think that the judge is going to say that this mistrial was appropriate, was legally accurate, and that they need to now look to set a date for a retrial," Cucolo said.
What do prosecutors want?
While the state's legal team has not explicitly said they will pursue a retrial, Cruz and the prosecutors who argued the case have consistently said they want justice for Clancy's children.
Last week, prosecutors asked Judge Sullivan to reject the motion to dismiss charges against Clancy on the grounds of double jeopardy.
They argue mistrial procedures were properly followed by the court, and thus they have a right to seek justice again on behalf of the children.
"Because a mistrial was properly declared due to the manifest necessity of a deadlocked jury, the defendant's motion to dismiss should be denied," prosecutors wrote in the motion.
What could happen on 2 November?
Judge Sullivan could make a determination over whether the case can proceed on Monday or he could rule later in writing, criminal defence lawyer Elyse Hershon told the BBC.
And how the District Attorney's office wants to proceed could be determined ahead of Monday's hearing, during it or even days after, she said.
"The three charges of first-degree murder are still pending; they are still hanging over Lindsay Clancy's head unless and until the DA announces otherwise," Hershon said.
Historically, Cruz, the district attorney, has made comments and announcements about the case at press conferences after court finishes. That could happen again this week, she predicted.
It is also likely, Hershon said, that Judge Sullivan pushes the lawyers on both sides to get a trial date on the calendar during Monday's hearing.
"It does not mean it's definitely going to be a jury trial, but [they will want to] put something in the books, hold those dates. It's a big chunk of time. It's four, five, six weeks of the court calendar; that's hard to fit in at the last minute," she said.
"I would anticipate they block off the time while they go through all these motions and the DA's office figures out what it wants to do."
description: The Massachusetts mother, accused of murdering her three children, is expected back in court as she awaits a decision on whether her case will be retried.

title: Hull adventurer Karl Bushby 'overwhelmed' at Humber Bridge crowds
text:
Karl Bushby 'overwhelmed' at Humber Bridge welcome
British adventurer Karl Bushby crossed the Humber Bridge through thick mist on the final leg of his 31,000-mile (49,890 km), 28-year trek from South America to Hull.
Bushby left Chile in 1998 to head home to the UK without breaking two self-imposed rules: not to return until he had fully completed his feat - and not to use transport to advance.
The adventurer said he was "absolutely overwhelmed" by the crowds who lined the bridge.
Bushby, a former paratrooper, is due to complete the challenge on Monday and will be met by his mother, his son and granddaughter when he arrives in Hull.
The adventurer has said the opportunity to embark on his walk came after the breakdown of his marriage, when his wife returned to Northern Ireland with their son.
"When I left home and I walked down south first of all to test the machine that I first had, I don't remember any of that journey except for the Humber Bridge," he said on Sunday.
"There's that mystic look to it where you can't see the other side of the river.
"It's kind of almost symbolic.
"The Humber Bridge has always been that iconic landmark in my mind."
Aged 29, Bushby said he walked out of Punta Arenas, Chile, with a few hundred dollars in his pocket and turned north for home.
By the time he swam back across the English Channel on 5 October, Bushby, now 57, had crossed four continents, a frozen sea, deserts, mountains and jungles.
"[I'm] just absolutely overwhelmed," he said on Sunday when he spoke to BBC Radio Humberside.
"And we're not even home yet."
By "we", Bushby may have meant the royal we, or The Beast, the cart he has spent 28 years pushing.
"This is my Wilson," he said, a reference to a volleyball that Tom Hanks's character talked to in the film Cast Away.
"I'm just a homeless guy pushing a shopping trolley, and the next thing you know is this," he said, nodding to the crowds lining the bridge.
"And I have to really kind of just stop and think about what this means to other people."
On Monday morning, Bushby will begin the final part of his walk back to his mother's home in north Hull.
He will set off from Hessle and walk to Queen Victoria Square, where a reception will be held for him outside the Civic Hall.

title: Gavin and Stacey's Neil the Baby hopes to be next Stereophonics
text:
Gavin and Stacey actor hopes his band will be 'the next Stereophonics'
Gavin and Stacey fans will likely remember Oscar Hartland, or Neil the Baby, for his heartwarming performance of The Beatles' Blackbird in the sitcom's 2024 finale.
The episode was watched by about 12.3m people on Christmas day and saw Hartland's character serenade the crowd at the wedding of his on-screen dad Smithy, played by James Cordon.
But that was just the start for Hartland, now 17, who says his band is aiming to be "the next 'Phonics, or something like that".
He has recently released a new single and he and his fellow band members are on a "mission to create a new modern sound for Wales".
Hartland, from Machen, Caerphilly county, said his latest release, Wild Bull, was rooted in "being a bit crazy" and the challenges of growing up in the south Wales valleys.
The actor and singer went on his first tour in 2025 and said the past few months had been about "figuring out the earth behind the sound" with his bandmates Cayden Hughes on bass, Aiden Williams on drums and Deacon Ball on electric guitar.
"We've had lots of people say it's rocky, but it's Welsh and it's got lots of stuff behind it," he told Lucy Owen on BBC Radio Wales.
"Growing up, I was just a wild bull, I was just mental, you know, in school, just out and about, playing rugby, being wild, being crazy. I know loads of my friends who are just the same.
"It's very hard as a young lad, especially Wales in the valleys, to keep yourself contained, because there is so much trouble to get up to."
Hartland said he surrounded himself with music growing up and described himself as a bit of a "black sheep".
"I was playing the piano while everyone else was watching rugby," he said.
But he added the new single was all about "letting go and saying, 'this is me I'm a wild bull'."
Hartland said the response to the song, which was released on Friday, had been brilliant.
"People are loving it, the interaction is nuts... it's really nice.
"The biggest thing is trying to create a movement, that people can feel a part of."
At 14 years old, Hartland took part in The Voice Kids in the hopes of kickstarting his rock career.
His performance of Foo Fighters' My Hero impressed the judges and was also seen by Gavin and Stacey writers James Cordon and Ruth Jones, who approached him with the idea of performing in the series finale.
The Christmas day finale episode became one of the most watched scripted TV shows of the century, seen by 19.11 million people after seven days of catch-up viewing and beating the show's previous record of 17.92m for the 2019 Christmas special.
Nearly two years on, Hartland said it "blows his mind" that people are still talking about it.
"It's ageing well to be fair," he said.
Hartland added support was "always there" from his fellow Gavin and Stacey cast members, which was "lush".
"A lot of people don't really know what it would be like to be in our boots, I suppose, sort of, with the size of it," he said.
He said it was nice to see cast members pursuing "other adventures" too, such as Melanie Walters, who played Gwen, recently taking part in Strictly Come Dancing.
Hartland has been recording at Rockfield studios in Monmouth, which has also played host to the likes of Oasis, Iggy Pop and Queen.
"I want to record there all the time, because I just love what the place is about and I want that to be behind me as well," said Hartland.
"It's spectaular, you feel all of the presence of the past bands there looking at you like 'is he going to make a good song?'"
Despite his developing music career, Hartland said he would not rule out more acting in the future, as he is "just trying things out".
While he has not yet had a chance to cover the iconic Gavin and Stacey theme song, Run by Stephen Fretwell, he said he would love to in the future.
"It's iconic," he said, adding "that would be brilliant".

title: Virgin Media O2 set to cut thousands of jobs to reduce costs
text:
Virgin Media O2 set to cut thousands of jobs to reduce costs
Thousands of Virgin Media O2 staff are facing redundancy as the telecoms firm attempts to save money in the face of billions of pounds of debt and tougher competition.
The broadband provider has not finalised the number of roles to be cut but it is likely be a sizeable chunk of its 16,000-strong workforce, the BBC understands.
Virgin Media O2 has billions in debt on its balance sheet and is tackling both smaller providers as well as giants like BT, which has agreed a deal to acquire rival TalkTalk, which Virgin Media O2 has firmly opposed.
The company declined to comment. Prospect, a union which represents Virgin Media O2 staff, said the cuts were "disappointing and very unsettling".
Noel McClean. deputy general secretary at Prospect, said the union was "committed to supporting our members through what is a difficult time, as well as also working with employers to explore ways to mitigate the number of redundancies and ensure retraining and redeployment of staff affected".
The majority of the affected staff are in roles that are not customer-facing and a number of senior leadership changes are already under way, the BBC has been told.
Virgin Media O2 is also expected to review its use of contractors and suppliers in conjunction with the job cuts.
As of 30 June, Virgin Media O2's total liabilities stands at £27.2bn while it holds assets worth £45.9bn, according to the firm's latest accounts.
Meanwhile, the company is dealing with fierce competition from cheaper "altnets" like Hyperoptic, Community Fibre, Gigaclear and YouFibre.
Virgin Media O2 had attempted to respond to this growing threat by buying altnet competitor Netomnia for £2bn via nexfibre, a joint venture owned by Virgin Media O2's owners.
However, the Competition Markets Authority (CMA) has provisionally found competition concerns in the deal, with a final decision to come in December, sparking anger from Virgin Media O2.
'Stitch-up'
In October, Virgin Media O2 called the BT's agreed takeover of TalkTalk a "stitch-up" that had allowed its rival to "tighten its grip" over the market.
BT said its deal provided "a safety net" for TalkTalk customers as their broadband provider faced collapse without the takeover.
On Friday, BT's share price jumped 7% after the Financial Times reported Virgin Media O2 was close to agreeing a deal to use its rival's fibre broadband network.
The BBC has been told the deal was very close and that Virgin Media O2 was highly likely to announce it will stop all investment in fibre in its results on Tuesday.

title: Bereaved families call for public inquiry into maternity care
text:
Bereaved families call for public inquiry into maternity care
Bereaved parents have come together in Glasgow to call for a public inquiry into the deaths of babies and mothers across Scotland.
A nine-month independent review of Scotland's maternity services started last month after families, staff and experts called for improvements to poor and sometimes deadly care in a BBC Disclosure investigation.
But families who have lost babies following failures claimed the current review would not go far enough, and have demanded "answers, accountability and justice for our babies".
Health Secretary Angela Constance said the voices and experiences of families "must be central" in informing the review.
Julie Keegan and Angus McLean were among campaigners in Glasgow city centre.
The couple's three-day old son Mason Scott McLean died after a series of errors in his care at the Queen Elizabeth University Hospital (QEUH) in Glasgow in 2023.
Failures in Mason's care included missing key tests that would have indicated he had a life-threatening infection.
An internal review by NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde (NHSGGC) found "several systematic issues" that may have caused his death.
But the couple said they were still trying to get answers to questions asked almost four years ago.
The health board apologised for "missed opportunities" for care and said it had taken action on the recommendations in the review.
"We want accountability and an independent public inquiry to find out how many of these babies could have been saved," Angus told BBC Scotland News.
"This is the only thing we can do now for Mason to honour him because he should still be here and we want to find out why he is not."
Julie, who works as an NHS intensive care nurse, said families should not have to fight for answers and claimed the review would not be enough.
"I want to know why my child was allowed to die from failure after failure after failure," she said.
"The review is only forward looking, it is not going to look at the past and does not dig deep on the hundreds of babies who have lost their lives."
Unannounced inspections of all 18 maternity units in Scotland have been ordered to be carried out by Healthcare Improvement Scotland, following a review into a number of spikes in new born baby deaths.
Common themes so far include staffing shortages, delays in care to pregnant women, and issues around investigations when things go wrong.
Lori Quate lost his wife and child within 24 hours in 2020.
A week before she was due to give birth, Jacqui was told her daughter had died in the womb and she would have to give birth to her stillborn daughter.
The 39-year-old was given medication to bring on the labour but suffered a cardiac arrest at Ninewells Hospital, Dundee.
Jacqui died two hours later from an amniotic fluid embolism - a rare and life-threatening emergency.
The next day, Lori found out his wife had been given eight times the recommended dose of the drug to bring on labour.
He said he was afraid the review would happen but the mistakes would continue.
"A lot of these end up with a placation of 'lessons will be learned' but nothing ever changes and it goes back to square one again," he said.
"It should be about making sure these avoidable deaths are unavoidable and talking to families which these mistakes have impacted."
He said the process could be exhausting and often took its toll, but he wanted to persevere and continue to give his voice.
Christine McCourt, a professor of maternal and child health at City St George's at the University of London, is chairing the review.
Her findings and recommendations will be submitted in July 2027.
Angela Constance said: "One of my first acts as health secretary was to establish the independent review of maternity services and I am fully committed to ensuring lasting improvements are made.
"I have been clear that the voices and experiences of families must be central in informing the review.
"A forward-looking and improvement-focused independent review will identify the systemic changes needed now to strengthen services and achieve better outcomes for women, babies and families," she added.

title: Israeli strikes in Gaza kill eight including child, hospitals say
text:
Israeli strikes in Gaza kill eight including child, hospitals say
Israeli strikes in Gaza have killed at least eight people, including a child, according to hospitals, despite a year-old ceasefire.
In Gaza City to the north, hospital officials said a missile attack hit a group of civilians next to Cairo School in the Al-Rimal neighbourhood, killing three people, including a four-year-old boy.
In the southern city of Khan Younis, the Hamas-run ministry of interior said a drone attack targeted a group of police officers in the Al-Mawasi area, killing five, as they were carrying out their routine duties.
The Israeli military said it had carried out two attacks on what it described as military operatives but has not yet provided evidence or further information.
Outside Gaza City's Shifa Hospital, video showed a crowd of men gathered to pray next to two body bags and the tiny body of the child, which was wrapped in a white towel.
"My son and his child were martyred. They were sitting in their tent, bothering no one, and nothing else was happening in the area when suddenly, a missile struck them, and they were martyred," Ali Oweis told AFP news agency. "There is no ceasefire; the war is ongoing, don't you see?"
At Nasser hospital in Khan Younis, women despaired as body bags lay on the floor, video showed. The interior ministry named the five police officers killed, who were between the ages of 23 and 53, and called the attack a "horrific massacre".
A ceasefire came into force in Gaza in October last year, but Israeli air strikes have continued almost every day.
Since then, 1,580 people have been killed, according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. Israel says it is targeting Hamas, but often civilians are also killed.
Meanwhile, a peace plan for Gaza, brokered by the Trump administration, has stalled.
The ceasefire saw thousands of Palestinians held by Israel released in return for all of the 48 remaining hostages held in Gaza, and an agreement to end the war.
The conflict was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage.
Since the war began, 74,594 people have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory's health ministry.

title: At risk Cumbrian in-person postpartum mums' groups saved
text:
At risk in-person postpartum mums' groups saved
A mothers' support service has said it is "absolutely thrilled" after it received £70,000 worth of grants to maintain its in-person wellbeing groups.
The Happy Mums Foundation, which supports women experiencing postpartum mental health challenges, was set up in 2015 and has helped more than 1,000 families across Cumbria.
Last month the organisation said its in-person peer support groups were at risk due to funding pressures.
But grants from both the Postcode and National Lottery mean that the immediate risk has been lifted, said director Lucinda Bray. "We can keep supporting mums," she said.
Due to funding pressures, the organisation had been considering moving its in-person peer support groups online.
But Bray previously told the BBC that the loss of these real world safe spaces could worsen the mental health of vulnerable women in the county.
She said that being able to talk about suicidal thinking was actually "quite a good preventative factor".
"If that doesn't have an outlet and you don't have a safe space to talk about those things, where might they go?" she said.
The foundation has since been awarded £50,000 by the Postcode Lottery and £20,000 from the National Lottery.
"I'm absolutely thrilled," said Bray.
"It means that we can continue the groups we are running and we can continue working on ways to make our organisation more sustainable for the future."

title: Henry Nowak: Southampton student’s family on police footage
text:
Nowak family say police footage deepened trauma
The family of Henry Nowak have said the trauma of learning he had been murdered was made worse by watching police footage of officers handcuffing him as he lay dying.
They told ITV their "world has changed twice", first when they were told he had died, and again when they watched the body-worn camera video.
His killer, Vickrum Digwa, falsely told police Henry had racially abused him, and officers handcuffed the student as he repeatedly said he had been stabbed.
His father Mark, stepmother Katie, mother Lucy and sister Olivia were speaking to ITV for the documentary Dear Henry: Our Fight For Justice.
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has announced an independent review into the murder, led by former lord chancellor Alex Chalk, which will look at "any missed opportunities to intervene".
Henry, 18, from Chafford Hundred in Essex, was a first-year accountancy and finance student at the University of Southampton when he was murdered.
He was stabbed five times as he walked home from a night out with friends from his football team in Southampton on 3 December 2025.
It took officers another 24 hours to identify Henry's body and tell his family.
"I jumped out of bed and I saw the police car on our driveway," said Katie.
"One of the police officers was holding his hat in his hand, and I just knew straight away that something horrific had happened."
She said Mark fell to his knees when he heard the news.
"He let out a cry that I'll never forget," she said.
"I just remember saying 'it's Henry' and breaking down in tears," Mark said. "It's just unbelievable pain."
Officers went to Lucy's home at the same time.
"We got that dreaded knock on the door at one o'clock in the morning," she said.
"They said to me, 'Do you have a son called Henry?… There's been an altercation. And unfortunately, your son has passed away'.
"No words, no words can explain that feeling."
Olivia said she rang her father after hearing the news. "I just remember this scream. It was awful. He screamed 'My boy, my boy'," she said.
She now keeps some of Henry's T-shirts on his bed and told ITV they still smell of him and give her comfort.
But Lucy said she could no longer enter his bedroom because of the memories it holds.
"I can't go in there," she said.
Coats now hang over the bedroom door so she does not have to look at it as she passes.
The murder caused widespread political outrage when the footage emerged.
In the video, Henry can be heard repeatedly saying "I've been stabbed", to which an officer replies: "Don't think you have, mate."
It is also looking at whether race, religion or prejudice affected police decisions.
The watchdog said it expected its investigation to conclude early next year.
"In the last year, our world has changed twice," Katie said.
"The first time was the night that we were told that Henry had died. And the second time was when we watched that video."
Digwa's mother, Kiran Kaur, was jailed for three years for assisting an offender after she removed the knife used by her son.
Chalk said: "Serious questions have been raised about whether agencies and organisations failed to act on complaints about Digwa's violent and erratic behaviour.
"My review will follow the evidence without fear or favour. It will also examine how public authorities treated the Nowak family at a time of unimaginable pain."
Dear Henry: Our Fight For Justice, a Tonight special, airs on Thursday 5 November at 21:00 GMT on ITV, ITVX and the ITV News YouTube channel.

title: Recognition for 105-year-old Sutton Coldfield veteran Joan Langley
text:
Recognition for 105-year-old veteran Joan
A 105-year-old veteran who served in the Women's Auxiliary Air Force (WAAF) in World War Two has been honoured with a special presentation from a deputy lieutenant of the West Midlands.
Joan Langley, from Sutton Coldfield, served from 1940-1945, mainly on barrage balloon defence, helping to protect Birmingham, the Black Country, Coventry, Worcestershire and Gloucestershire.
Speaking after the presentation on Saturday, during a sold-out Remembrance Day concert at Sutton Coldfield Town Hall, Langley said the recognition had been wonderful and surprising.
In May, she also had high tea with Birmingham's Lord Mayor at The Council House to celebrate her 105th birthday.
Langley still has a fantastic memory, saying she can remember things from when she was four years old.
The 105-year-old spoke about her time in the WAAF, saying: "It was the best time of my life. It was wonderful companionship.
"I've told the cadets if they go in the forces and they take to it, they'll have friends for life.
"From the top to the bottom, everybody on my unit was smashing."
Langley and her husband missed D-Day due to her WAAF officer's insistence that her wedding go ahead, despite unknowingly being scheduled at the same time.
It meant she was puzzled about the extra men mysteriously arriving daily at RAF Wythall living in tents.
She was also evacuated on Winston Churchill's instructions the night before the Coventry Blitz as part of a team of balloon defence that he felt could not be lost to the German's raid.
After retiring from housekeeping work at 97 years old in 2018, she has since thrown herself into local veteran affairs such as encouraging veterans and war widows to avoid social isolation.
During the summer, she received a letter of thanks and recognition from Sir David Jason in his role as honorary vice-patron of the RAF Charitable Trust.
As a former military musician playing the trumpet and bugle, she has also recently received a special recording of 'Coming in on a wing and a prayer', her favourite wartime song, from RAF Music based in RAF Northolt.
