title: Exhibition explores mountaineering's Cumbrian origins
text:
Exhibition explores mountaineering's origins
Mountain climbing's Cumbrian origins are being explored in a new exhibition.
The show at the Beacon Museum in Whitehaven opened on Saturday and details the sport's 200-year history in England and Wales.
It highlights the nation's first known mountain climb for recreational purposes which took place on Pillar Rock in the Lake District in 1826, according to the display's curator Ian Smith.
He said he wanted visitors to leave the exhibition knowing more about the sport, and to learn climbers were not "all mad".
Smith said research from the past few years had revealed that farmer John Atkinson, from Ennerdale, was the most likely person to have first climbed a mountain in England for fun.
He said the local newspaper the Cumberland Paquet had written about Atkinson in a short article which said he had "succeeded in attaining the summit of the rock called Pillarstone".
The mountain is the eighth highest summit in the Lake District.
Smith said no future references to Atkinson had been found in newspapers and the sport eventually became more widespread when wealthy Victorian gentlemen started holidaying to the mountains.
"People just started walking up the mountains then started thinking 'oh I could climb up that cliff as well'," he said.
'Great companionship'
He also said the exhibition, by the Mountain Heritage Trust, "details the little we know about Atkinson and the major safety innovations that have since come about in the sport".
"In the 19th Century climbing was pretty dangerous and it was only done by people who had that level of commitment and skill," Smith said.
"Now we have better ropes, safety harnesses and lots of different things… climbing is no longer the preserve of the very elite."
Smith said he hoped that non-climbers who visited the exhibition took away a better sense of why the sport was so popular.
"It's physical, it's exercise, you're in the great outdoors - it's great companionship," he said.
The show runs until 12 February.

title: Former Bradford City chairman Geoffrey Richmond, 85, dies
text:
Former Bradford City chairman Richmond, 85, dies
The former chairman of Bradford City, Geoffrey Richmond, has died at the age of 85.
Richmond helped oversee the Bantams' promotion to the Premier League in 1999, marking the first time the club had played in the top flight for 77 years.
Announcing his death on Sunday, the club said Richmond had also "played an important role in the redevelopment" of its Valley Parade ground during his eight years as chairman.
A City spokesperson added: "The thoughts of everyone at Bradford City AFC are with Geoffrey's family and friends at this difficult time."
Richmond, who was born in Leeds and also served as chairman of Scarborough, took over at Valley Parade in 1994.
The club was promoted to the First Division two years later after beating Notts County in a play-off final on its Wembley debut, before reaching the top flight in 1999.
A famous David Wetherall header against Liverpool ensured survival on the final day of the season, but the club was relegated the following year after spending big on wages for players such as Benito Carbone and Stan Collymore.
With the club in financial turmoil, Richmond left in 2002.
Paying tribute on X, Collymore said: "Incredibly sad news to hear. Larger than life character, gave me an opportunity to play for a fine football club, however brief.
"Rest in peace, Geoffrey."
Football reporter Alan Biggs described Richmond as "charismatic and controversial in equal measure".
He added: "Can only speak from personal experience; provided many a story. Friendly, though could be cantankerous if you disagreed with him eg. over manager turnover."
Scarborough Athletic, the club formed after its predecessor Scarborough FC folded in 2007, said it was "saddened" to hear the news.
The Leeds-based New Rover Cricket Club, where Richmond was also a chairman and player, said he had played a "significant role" in its history.
The club, based in Adel, said: "His contribution to New Rover, both on and off the field, will never be forgotten.
"He was a valued member of our club family, and his commitment helped shape the club we are proud to be today."

title: Radiologists warn cancer patients 'deteriorating' amid staff shortages
text:
Cancer patients 'deteriorating' due to staff shortages, radiologists warn
Cancer patients have warned delays in scans could be the difference between life and death as Wales faces a shortage of radiologists.
The Royal College of Radiologists said NHS Wales currently had 88 fewer radiologists than it needed - a 28% shortfall.
For the first time, it has reported seeing some patients' conditions "deteriorating" while waiting for diagnostic scans and tests.
Radiologists are doctors who specialise in using images to diagnose and manage medical conditions and diseases.
Betsi Cadwaladr health board, which covers one of the areas most affected by shortages, said recruitment was ongoing and, despite a substantial increase in demand for scans, reporting times had improved.
Beverly Scott, who was first diagnosed with ovarian and peritoneal cancer 14 years ago, said treatment was keeping her condition stable but without timely scans it was at risk of spreading unnoticed.
Scott, who is a member of Pwllheli and Pen Llŷn cancer support group in Gwynedd, was given five years to live when she was first diagnosed.
She took part in medical trials at the Royal Marsden Hospital in London and said that while there was no cure, continual treatment was now keeping her cancer stable.
Scott said the shortage of radiologists could threaten this stability.
"For the past 14 years, I have lived with scans," she said.
"In cases like mine, delays could cause the cancer to spread further and treatments wouldn't work."
Another member of the group, Karen Jones, was first diagnosed with breast cancer in 2015. She was subsequently diagnosed with colon cancer, and her breast cancer also returned in 2021.
She said: "Waiting for results is the worst part, will it be clear or not?
"It is terrible, horrific and horrendous. You are in total limbo."
North and west Wales are among the areas worst affected by shortages in the UK, with a 42% shortfall in consultant radiologists compared to 22% in south Wales, according to data published in the Royal College of Radiologists' 2025 clinical radiology census.
Clara Day, executive medical director at Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board in north Wales, said she understood the figures "can be very worrying for patients", adding the health board was "actively recruiting" into both radiology and oncology - the department which handles cancer diagnoses and treatment.
"We are also strengthening our links with the North Wales Medical School to support future workforce development."
She said the health board's clinical strategy for oncology had led to "key developments", including nurse-led clinics and the introduction of colorectal and breast metastatic nurse specialist teams.
"Robust arrangements are in place to maintain safe services, prioritise patients according to clinical need and to continue delivering high-quality oncology care for the people of north Wales," she said.
Day added that "despite a substantial increase in demand for imaging services", partnering with a third-party provider had contributed to a decline in waiting times for scans and results since April.
She said these reporting times were also closely and consistently monitored.
One of the main reasons for the shortage is that Wales has more radiology departments affected by recruitment freezes than anywhere in the UK.
In 2024, the radiology workforce in Wales grew by just 1.1%, far below the UK average of 5%.
Dr Owen Nicholas, a consultant oncologist in Swansea and chair of the Welsh committee for the Royal College of Radiologists, said: "It is not getting better and the patients are now getting affected."
He said the shortage was also impacting staff, adding: "There is a challenge, where you sit in front of a patient who is extremely anxious to know has the treatment worked or has it come back.
"For you to have to say, 'sorry I don't know, because I don't have the report in front of me', or perhaps you cancel an appointment because a scan report has not come back.
"The primary concern is for the patient, but it is not very nice for a clinician to have to do that over and over again."

title: City status will not be lost in council shake-up, says minister
text:
City status will not be lost in shake-up - minister
A city's status will not be lost as a result of local authority reorganisation, the government has said.
Gloucester attained city status following the dissolution of the monasteries and the subsequent transformation of St Peter's Abbey into a cathedral in 1541.
But councillors are concerned this could be lost or removed during a proposed council shake-up that will see Gloucester City Council abolished and merged with six Gloucestershire districts to become a "super council".
Local government minister Jim McMahon has said the government will do whatever it has to do "to ensure no city loses its city status through reorganisation".
McMahon told the Local Democracy Reporting Service it "would be absolutely wrong if a city risked losing its status just because its city status is aligned to a local authority that is being abolished rather than to a geographical area".
"I can give an absolute assurance that even if we have to introduce new legislation to preserve that status, we will do whatever we have to do to ensure that no city loses its city status through reorganisation," he said.
"City status and ceremonial matters play a valuable role for local pride."
Councillor Jeremy Hilton, for Kingsholm and Wotton, said he was relieved and pleased.
"We are still waiting to find out how they will make sure that is done but previously we were getting pushback from people working in Whitehall," he said.
"But the fact we have now had it from Jim McMahon is really positive.
"It now means it is on their agenda and they are not going to let the system fall apart because they haven't thought about it."

title: How the European question impacts on Scotland's future
text:
How the European question impacts on Scotland's future
Rachel Reeves must have been smarting this week as the new Chancellor stood on the steps of No 11 Downing Street - but she's now using her former platform to make a clarion call for Britain's re-entry into the European Union.
Her former rank carries weight and adds fuel to the prime minister's arguments on re-opening the EU debate.
That also opens up a Pandora's box of inter-twining constitutional questions here in Scotland.
The Reeves argument is clear. From her position in His Majesty's Treasury, she saw a United Kingdom that was "poorer, weaker and less secure" post-Brexit.
She therefore believes "Britain's future lies in the EU".
Her intervention may leave many people questioning - why make it now, after leaving office?
It has been up to the new prime minister to make the running, with Andy Burnham looking forward to an EU summit in Brussels on 20 November.
He's looking to lock-in deals on food and drink, emissions trading, and a youth mobility scheme.
It adds to the impression there has been almost seven years of the UK trying to patch things over with the EU, sector-by-sector.
Speaking on BBC Scotland's Sunday Show, the UK government minister Martyn McCluskey was asked when the people might be consulted about this?
He said: "I'm not going to get ahead of myself on process here. What we need to focus on is we're having a conversation.
"A conversation that was happening already in the country, that I think Andy Burnham has just said very clearly. It's a conversation we're all having, so we may as well have it in public about what the benefits are."
It's certainly clear that, after the summit, the prime minister wants to "explore options" for the longer-term relationship. But there will be no major changes before the next general election
All this rather horrifies the Conservatives.
Their leader Kemi Badenoch said on Sunday it was "yet another Westminster bubble argument".
Her Shadow Scottish Secretary Harriet Cross told the Sunday Show: "When we have a vote, that should be respected. That is the point of a democracy and it's incumbent on everybody to make that work and there have been benefits to leaving the EU".
What is particularly horrifying for the Conservative leadership is the prospect of re-opening the decades of Tory in-fighting on a matter they thought had been put to bed.
Far from horror, the SNP view the prime minister's European stance with some glee.
Brexit is so woven in with the issue of Scottish independence that it can be hard to unpick the threads.
The SNP's Westminster leader, Dave Doogan, told me he "really welcomed" Rachel Reeves' comments, and a majority of Scots had already known that leaving the EU was a "retrograde" step.
He said: "When you are sold a false prospectus, it's ok to go back to re-visit that after a reasonable period of time and I would say that, whilst that's appropriate for the European Union referendum, it's also appropriate for the referendum that happened two years prior to that in 2014 over Scottish independence."
The leader warned it would be "hypocrisy" not to re-visit the independence issue.
However, when the prime minister was in Glasgow on Friday, Downing Street was clear that a second independence referendum is "off the table".
It's unclear at this early stage what impact there could be on the SNP's "independence in Europe" argument if the UK does seek ever-closer union, or even re-joins the EU.
Given all these arguments, it is striking how often people outside the political bubble tell me they just want "certainty" over all these constitutional issues.
It's probably a very human reaction but their hope is maybe misplaced.
These arguments never really lie still.
For hundreds of years the relationship with our neighbours was fought in cross-border skirmishes or in battles across the English Channel.
Now, it's down to democratic votes and arguments in air-conditioned summit rooms.
With the prime minister re-opening this Pandora's Box, be prepared for plenty more constitutional debate.
description: Former Chancellor Rachel Reeves says the UK should be back in the European Union and that has implications for Scotland.

title: BrickTokker says her Lego passion helps her focus
text:
BrickTokker says Lego passion helps her focus
A TikTok creator who estimates she has about £3,000 worth of Lego says it helps her focus.
Al Palmer, 23, who lives near Norwich, is part of the AFOL - adult fan of Lego - community, and documents her hobby on social media, calling herself a "BrickTokker".
Palmer has autism and ADHD and became interested in the brick-building phenomenon as an adult during university.
The primary school teacher said she found the building process "therapeutic" as it offered her a distraction from the everyday stresses of life.
She got up at 05:00 GMT on Thursday to be one of the first through the door of the new Norwich Lego store, and ended up as the third customer inside.
Palmer said her hobby helped her unwind between essays and lectures at university.
"I love collecting it, displaying it. I love finding out about it - going to Denmark, going to the museum they've got there, learning about how Lego has developed over time," she said.
"It's so therapeutic to do; it takes your mind off of things.
"It allows you to focus and also online I've made such an amazing community of other people that love Lego, and getting to talk about it with other people that love it just as much as I do."
Palmer saves a small amount of money each month to fund her passion.
"You do have to save up and it's a nice thing to save up for," she said.
"It's what I've achieved through working hard at [my job]... this is what I choose to spend my money on, in the same way that someone might want to go on lots of holidays or buy handbags.
"That's my thing that I want to collect and be proud of."
Palmer said she was "always trying to get it into my lessons", and she also shares her love for bricks with her 4,000 TikTok followers.

title: Ciara Mageean: Tributes to 'inspirational' Olympic athlete after death at 34
text:
Tributes to 'inspirational' Olympian Ciara Mageean after death at 34
Tributes have been paid to former European champion and two-time Olympic runner Ciara Mageean, who has died at the age of 34.
Mageean, from Portaferry in County Down, was diagnosed with stage four bowel cancer in May 2025.
She died on Sunday morning, surrounded by her loved ones, a statement posted on her social media accounts said.
"A beloved daughter, sister, wife, friend and inspiration to so many, she will be deeply missed," it said.
Mageean's funeral will take place near her family home on Tuesday, with a ceremony at St Patrick's Church, Ballyphilip, followed by burial in the adjoining cemetery.
Her death comes less than three weeks after her marriage to her long-term partner Thomas Moran.
The athlete represented Ireland at the 2016 and 2020 Olympics and won gold in the 1500m at the European Athletics Championships in Rome in 2024.
She also represented Northern Ireland at the Commonwealth Games, winning silver in Birmingham in 2022.
'One of our own'
Olympic legend Lady Mary Peters said Mageean was a "wonderful lady" who was "gracious, beautiful, talented and inspirational to the next generation".
"We knew she was very ill and we knew that it was inevitable but we didn't expect it so soon," said the 1972 Olympic pentathlon gold medallist.
Lady Mary's charity the Mary Peters Trust, which supports Northern Ireland athletes, had helped Mageean in her athletics career.
"My charity supported her for as long as we could because she was so talented and we recognised that in her," said Lady Mary.
She said that Mageean had continued to inspire young athletes even while undergoing treatment for cancer and would be "sorely missed in the world of sport".
Sean Young, the secretary of Portaferry Gaelic Athletic Club, where Mageean played camogie in her younger years, said its members were in "disbelief and shock" at her death.
He said Mageean had been a "fierce competitor" who began her sporting journey at the club before pursuing athletics.
"Outside the sporting arena she is the most inspirational, humble person we have ever had within our club," he said.
Down Gaelic Athletic Association (GAA) said it was "honoured and privileged" to call Mageean one of its own, describing her as someone who never forgot her roots.
"She touched the lives of so many people and she helped change the lives of so many," it said.
"In her battle with illness she showed us courage, positivity and the value of life."
Her former school, Assumption Grammar in Ballynahinch, County Down, said it was "deeply saddened and heartbroken" by the death of its "cherished past pupil".
"Ciara's kindness, strength, faith and unwavering determination were an inspiration to us all," it said.
"She touched countless lives with her warmth, humility and generosity of spirit."
'A champion in every sense of the word'
Northern Ireland's First Minister Michelle O'Neill described Mageean as "a champion in every sense of the word and a role model for all athletes".
"She represented her country with pride and helped put Irish athletics on the map," said O'Neill.
She said Mageean had faced her cancer diagnosis with the same "bravery and determination" she had shown throughout her sporting career.
"Ciara's legacy will live on and she will continue to be an inspiration to many."
Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly said people across Northern Ireland had been "deeply proud and inspired" by the athlete.
She described Mageean as an "outstanding athlete and ambassador for her sport" who had spoken with honesty and bravery about her health battles.
Irish President Catherine Connolly said Mageean had stood out for "her strength and perseverance, for her clear speaking and for her determination to succeed".
"It was these qualities that led the public to appreciate her so much and to be so thrilled for her achievement in Rome," said Connolly.
"Since Ciara shared the news of her illness, the public have stood with her and their affection for her has only grown."
Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) Micheál Martin said he was "deeply saddened" by her untimely death and extended his sympathies to her husband, family and friends.
Tánaiste (Irish Deputy Prime Minister) Simon Harris said Mageean had inspired people both through her achievements on the track and her openness about her illness.
"She gave so many others strength and hope," he said.
'Great fun'
Speaking to BBC Good Morning Ulster athlete Katie Kirk, who competed alongside Mageean, recalled her first experience of training with her at Mary Peters tracks in Belfast for a cross-country session.
"Even then she was great fun, very determined, focused".
Kirk commended Mageean's success saying "she achieved so much" even through "incredibly difficult" times.
"She still came out, she still spoke to people, she still took pictures with children and participated fully in life.
"That for me is just the essence of who she is," she added.
'Self-belief and commitment'
World Athletics described her as "an inspiration to many, on and off the track", highlighting her historic European gold medal in Rome in 2024.
Athletics Ireland, the country's governing body for the sport, said Mageean was "much-loved and inspirational".
"Her courage, warmth and spirit will leave a lasting legacy," the organisation said.
The Camogie Association also paid tribute to Mageean, with its president Brian Molloy describing her as a great friend of the sport, both as a player and a supporter.
"In her all-too-short life, Ciara touched the hearts of so many," he said.
"Her self-belief and commitment to her craft will always be inspirational and she will be fondly remembered by all who had the privilege of knowing her."
'A light has gone out in the world'
Mageean was named the 2023 BBC Northern Ireland Sports Personality of the Year after an impressive year, in which she broke national records and was fourth in a competitive World Championships final.
BBC Sport NI broadcaster Thomas Niblock, who interviewed Mageean in July for The GAA Social podcast, described her as a "one off".
"A light has gone out in the world. Authentic, talented, decent. Her kindness and wonderful personality was a joy to watch and see," he wrote on social media.
Niblock recalled how Mageean had received disappointing news the day before their interview but had insisted on going ahead with the recording.
"It's 90 minutes [co-presenter] Oisin [McConville] and myself will always treasure. She was the best of us," he said.
He also paid tribute to her husband and the wider Portaferry community.
"I've never met a person who met Ciara, who didn't love her," he added.
Patrick Kielty, who said it was a "privilege" to interview Mageean on Irish national broadcaster RTÉ's The Late Late Show, said "she wasn't just a champion on the track".
"She was a champion of others who showed us all how to live."
In many interviews that she gave following her diagnosis last year, Mageean spoke candidly about the symptoms she experienced which led her to seek medical help.
She also worked with a charity that promotes bowel cancer awareness.
Noticing blood in your poo - which may appear black or dark red in the toilet bowl - can be a sign of bowel cancer.
If there is no other obvious cause for the bleeding, such as piles, the NHS recommends that you ask for an appointment with your GP.
The NHS also advises a check-up if you notice changes in your regular toilet habits, such as having to poo more often, or a pattern of diarrhoea or constipation.
Abdominal pain or lumps, stomach bloating and unexplained weight loss are also among symptoms which should lead to a bowel cancer test.
Bowel cancer can also cause anaemia, the features of which include extreme tiredness and shortness of breath.
The earlier bowel cancer is detected, the easier it is to treat.
description: The former European 1500m champion had bowel cancer and died just three weeks after marrying her partner.

title: Green Party at a "crossroads", says former co-leader Adrian Ramsay
text:
Green Party at 'crossroads', says former co-leader
The Green Party is at a "crossroads" and needs to focus on its "core values", a former party co-leader has told the BBC, weeks after members adopted a motion declaring Zionism a form of racism.
Adrian Ramsay suggested the Greens need their policies to appeal to a majority of British voters if they want to bring the "environmental changes that we need" and advised against taking an approach that risks being "quite divisive".
Green Party leader Zack Polanski responded by saying there was "no environmental justice without social, racial and economic justice".
The motion, which Polanski did not take part in or vote upon, defined Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" that had led to the "disenfranchisement and destruction" of Palestinians.
It backed the creation of a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.
Members of the Green Party of England and Wales adopted the policy motion last month.
It led to a backlash from some Jewish groups, as well as criticism from senior Green figures, including Ramsay and other Green MPs.
Israel's foreign ministry said it had banned Polanski, who is Jewish, from entering the country.
The Equality and Human Rights Commission also wrote to the Green Party asking for more information about the motion after concerns were raised by dozens of Labour and Lib Dem MPs and Jewish campaigners.
Labour later said it would end power-sharing agreements with the Greens on local councils, unless its councillors disowned the policy.
Speaking to Newscast, Ramsay replied "no, it's not" when asked if he thought Zionism is racist before adding he agreed with Polanski and others in believing that what is happening in Gaza is "appalling".
The MP for Waveney Valley, who joined the party in 1998, said he does think Israel has a right to exist, something Polanski has stopped short of saying.
Ramsay also said he has made it clear he is "deeply uncomfortable" with the motion adopted and suggested there is an "opportunity to take some action in relation to the motion in the run-up" to the party's spring conference next year.
He said the question now is how Polanski and the party as a whole responds to the motion.
Ramsay said: "I think there's a real crossroads point for the party at the moment.
"One option is to sort of dig in more down this approach, not only in relation to this motion, but I think that there's a risk it brings with it - a quite divisive, a quite internally focused approach to politics."
Ramsay said this is "perhaps seen from small groups of people on the hard left of politics who go around different parties try to influence how those parties are run".
He added: "What I want to see is the party really focus back in on our core aims as a party and our core values."
Ramsay said this includes ensuring the party is "consensus-building in how we approach our politics" and that "we engage the grassroots of our membership".
He added the party needs to be "very externally focused, because we're only going to be able to bring the environmental changes that we need to have to safeguard our society for now and for the future if the majority of the British public come behind that".
Ramsay served as co-leader of the Greens from 2021 to 2025 alongside Carla Denyer, who is also now an MP.
He unsuccessfully stood on a joint ticket with fellow MP Ellie Chowns in 2025, with the pair losing to Polanski in the leadership contest.
Polanski, who missed the conference vote to unsuccessfully campaign for election in a Westminster by-election, previously said he wants to see the "imperfect" motion amended in future.
However, he said the "substantial part of the motion", that "the displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people is clearly underpinned by a racist ideology" was "obvious". Israel has repeatedly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide.
Under Green Party rules, motions supported by members become official party policy, but will not necessarily be included in the party's manifesto at the next general election.
description: Adrian Ramsay suggested the party needs to focus on its "core values", including environmental issues.

title: Police probe video of officer hitting youth with handcuffs in Speke
text:
Police probe video of officer hitting youth with handcuffs
A police force has said it is reviewing a video which shows one of its officers punching a boy.
The footage circulated on social media shows a Merseyside Police officer punching what appears to be teenage boy three times while holding a pair of metal handcuffs in the hand he is striking him with.
The force said officers had been responding on Friday to reports of about 20 youths in the Alder Wood Avenue area of Speke, Liverpool, blocking roads with wheelie bins and "aiming fireworks at anyone who tried to remove them".
"We would like to stress that a short clip doesn't always show the full context," a Merseyside Police spokesman said.
The footage being circulated on social media - which has been viewed more than 40,000 times - begins moments before the officer strikes the boy.
It does not show anything that happened in the run-up to the incident.
Merseyside Police said youths had reportedly "smashed windows of nearby flats, tried to start fires and threatened members of the public".
'Complaint Received'
In the video, the boy is punched in the stomach, chest and throat before he is handcuffed and dragged off the ground by the officer, then led to a police van.
Another teenager can be seen being pulled from the ground as he is arrested.
After a complaint was made on Saturday, the force said its professional standards team would look into the incident.
"While we look to establish the full circumstances of what happened, we would urge people not to speculate and avoid sharing rumours or misinformation," the force said in a statement published on its website.
The incident happened the night before Halloween, on what in Liverpool has become known as "Mischief Night".
"We are determined to protect our communities from the sort of appalling behaviour that we historically see at this time of year.
"We have a contempt for criminality and a commitment to cracking down on people committing serious offences in Merseyside," a force spokesman added.

title: More than 300 arrests at Palestine Action support protest outside US embassy
text:
More than 300 arrests at Palestine Action support protest outside US embassy
More than 300 people have been arrested during a protest supporting the banned Palestine Action group outside the US embassy, police have said.
Hundreds of people gathered at Nine Elms in London on Saturday, with many holding signs reading phrases such as: "I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action."
The Metropolitan Police said on Sunday that 325 arrests were made. The force added on social media that 320 of them were for "expressing support for a proscribed organisation under the Terrorism Act".
At least 4,000 arrests have been made in relation to the group, which was proscribed in July 2025.
The UK Supreme Court is due to review Palestine Action's ban under terrorism legislation, after the group's co-founder was granted permission to appeal it.
The Home Office has said that it will robustly defend against the appeal.
Officers on Saturday made arrests into the evening, taking people to police vans for transfer, to the applause of many protesters, some of whom chanted: "Free, free Palestine."
In some instances, officers had to carry demonstrators who refused to walk.
Retired lawyer Charles Allison - who was taken by police in the afternoon - had travelled from Cumbria to participate. He said he feared for people's civil liberties, which he said were "being devalued and watered down".
"I hope the Supreme Court justices - they won't necessarily be influenced by it [the protest] - but I hope that they will take a long-term view of what is happening in this country and decide that the proscription was unlawful, as I believe it was," the 75-year-old said.
David Bolden, another protester awaiting arrest called the ban an "absurd law".
Defend Our Juries, which has been co-ordinating a series of protests over the ban, said the number of people detained this weekend took the total over 4,000 arrests since the group was proscribed, calling it "truly dystopian".
According to Home Office figures seen by the BBC, 3,630 arrests were made in the year ending June 2026. Along with the 134 people arrested outside Westminster Magistrates Court earlier this year and those on Saturday brings the total up to 4,089.
The BBC has contacted the Met to confirm any figures it might hold.
Amnesty International UK has criticised the arrests and called for the government to drop the proscription of Palestine Action.
Defend Our Juries called the arrests "unjust" and an assault on free speech.

title: Somerset MP facing voice loss after surgery shows recovery signs
text:
MP facing voice loss after surgery shows recovery signs
The "whispering MP" who feared she may never be able to speak confidently again revealed she has seen signs of recovery after suffering nerve damage to her vocal cords during surgery.
Liberal Democrat Anna Sabine lost her voice for several months following a thyroid operation in June, which cut one of the nerves to her vocal cords, leaving her with a condition called vocal cord paralysis.
The MP for Frome and East Somerset said the loss of her voice had made her want to "hide" when Parliament returned in September.
But in a surprise turn of events, Sabine said she awoke a few weeks ago to find it had regained some of its natural strength and "broadly speaking, it's back to where it should be".
The 46-year-old said she first realised something was wrong when she woke up from surgery in hospital in Bath.
"I had been warned it might feel strange, so I was trying to reassure myself hopefully this was just what it was going to feel like," she said.
"But the next morning, my surgeon did come around and say, 'I'm really sorry, but there has been a mistake and we have caused permanent damage'.
"At that time I could speak, but only just. I was kind of whispering."
When Parliament returned after the summer, she had to use a microphone to take part in debates.
'I can't hide away'
Sabine said the experience had been a shock and had left her feeling quite lonely.
"Your voice is a really key point of who you are, whether you are an MP or not," she said.
"When I came back to work in September I really wanted to hide, I did not want to speak in the chamber with my voice, because it actually, at that point, when you stood up to speak, you weren't really sure what was going to come out."
She added: "But over that summer, I had heard from so many people because I'd done various radio and TV about it, and people had emailed me.
"I can't now hide away, so I kind of felt inspired by them really to stand up in the chamber, which I did feel really embarrassed about. Even though no-one made me feel embarrassed, it felt extremely exposing."
Sabine said she would be doing a campaign about getting more therapy for adults.
Her voice is now the closest since the surgery to how it was before.
"During recess, one morning I woke up and my voice was like it is now, and my family said 'Your voice is stronger'," she added.
"My friends would say I don't sound quite like I used to, and I can feel that my voice is still really wobbly. But, broadly speaking, it's back to where it should be."

title: Seven arrested after Birmingham city centre firework disorder

Seven arrested after city centre firework disorder
Seven people have been arrested after disorder, involving fireworks being set off, in a city centre.
Footage posted on social media showed crowds gathered on Corporation Street in Birmingham, with fireworks being set off close to police officers and vehicles.
West Midlands Police had warned firm action would be taken against anyone involved in fireworks-related disorder, following serious incidents in the city during Bonfire Night last year.

The arrests were made in and around Stephenson Street and Corporation Street, after officers responded to "pockets of disorder," involving fireworks being set off in a dangerous manner, said the force.
Ch Supt Tom Boyce said: "Misusing fireworks is not only dangerous: it's illegal and can lead to fines, arrest and criminal charges."
The force said extra officers had been deployed at key locations to prevent a repeat of last year's violence.

title: Guildford mother calls for taller barriers after son's death
text:
Teen's mother calls for taller barriers after death
The mother of a teenager who fell from a multi-storey car park has said planned safety barriers must be high enough to properly protect people.
Tom Combeer, 17, died after falling from a car park in Guildford in the early hours of 8 March 2025.
Coroner Susan Ridge later warned there were insufficient measures in place to prevent falls and suicides, and raised concerns about public access, CCTV coverage and barrier heights.
Guildford Borough Council has said it aims to install edge protection in all of its multi-storey car parks by February 2027.
Tom's mother, Liz Combeer, is backing a campaign for a legal minimum barrier height of 270cm (8ft 10in), compared with the council's proposed minimum of 110cm (3ft 7in).
She said: "It would mean that anyone, in the middle of the night, would not have the opportunity to do what Tom did.
"If a full barrier would be in the way, they would have time for their mental state to change."
An inquest into Tom's death heard how he had messaged his family's WhatsApp group to say he loved them minutes before the incident.
Liz and Andy Combeer have since supported the Multi-Storey Car Parks Bill, which aims to increase the legal height.
The bill, known as Gabe's Law, is named after 15-year-old Gabriel Santer, who died after falling from the rooftop of a Liverpool car park.
Guildford Borough Council said it planned to appoint contractors in December 2026 before carrying out the work in the new year.
The authority said interim fencing would be installed at relevant locations in its multi-storey car parks by the end of 2026.
Vanessa King, the council's lead on parking, said: "The safety and wellbeing of everyone who uses our multi-storey car parks is extremely important to us, and we remain committed to taking proactive steps to improve safety and support for those who may be vulnerable."
The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government said it recognised the seriousness of the concerns raised by the coroner.
The department said the issues would be considered as part of a forthcoming review into protection measures in and around buildings.

title: Crochet novices in Friston create cascading poppy memorial
text:
Crochet novices create cascading poppy memorial
Novice crocheters have transformed a village church with a cascade of woollen memorial poppies.
Caroline Moore and Wendy Ireland took up their crochet hooks last November with the aim of creating a display for their village of Friston in Suffolk.
The pair said they came up with the idea after "a few glasses of wine" after being inspired by a display on Southend Pier in Essex last November which they saw on social media.
"Many hours of love and thought have gone into this," said Ireland.
"This has been a year in the making but this is our first time - so we're novices and we've only just learnt to crochet," she added.
Moore said they decided to invite other people in the village which led to a group of women joining for a "knit and natter" over a cup of tea and cake.
The exact number of poppies on the installation is being kept secret, so as not to spoil a competition for people to guess the total.
However, the pair said the amount meant they had slashed their poppy making time from an hour to just 20 minutes per poppy thanks to all the practice.

title: Five teenagers stabbed at Halloween party in Chandler's Ford
text:
Five teenagers stabbed at Halloween party
Five teenagers have been seriously injured after being stabbed at a Halloween party in Hampshire, police have said.
Officers were called to Park Road in Chandler's Ford, near Eastleigh, shortly after 22:30 GMT on Saturday.
The injured teens - three boys aged 16 and two aged 17 - were taken to hospital.
Hampshire Police said it believes an unknown group gained entry to a party at an address on Park Road before the stabbings.
The force has appealed for witnesses and anyone with information to come forward.
A police cordon remained in place on Sunday while officers continued their investigation.
An eyewitness told the BBC ambulances and an air ambulance had attended.
Another eyewitness said they saw someone running out of the house involved, shouting that he had been stabbed and that he was being chased by two people.
Senior investigating officer Det Ch Insp Elizabeth Pirie acknowledged the impact on local residents and thanked the community for its patience.
Speaking to the BBC on Monday, Eastleigh MP Liz Jarvis said: "The community is in just shock this morning that such an awful thing could have occurred.
"My thoughts are with the parents of the boys, the boys and the whole community.
"It is very sad to think that these five boys have been put in hospital as a result of this incident."
Jarvis urged people to "stay calm, don't be tempted to share information online, let the police do their job".
Two churches in Chandler's Ford have opened their doors to offer support.
St Boniface in Hursley Road will be open 09:00-17:00 through the week, while St Martin in the Wood in Queen's Road will open Monday-Wednesday from 15:00 to 17:00.

title: Mummified remains could return to Egypt after removal from public view
text:
Mummified remains could return to Egypt after removal from public view
Remains of an Egyptian mummy could be returned to Egypt after they were removed from display over ethical concerns.
The Sunday Post newspaper reported "Egyptian authorities" have asked for the repatriation of the mummified corpse of the priest Nekht, which was taken out of public view at Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum last month.
It came after the International Council of Museums (Icom) revised its code of ethics, recommending the "inherent dignity" of human remains be upheld.
Glasgow Life, which operates the museum, confirmed it had received a request to send the Nekht remains back to Egypt.
The organisation decided to remove the painted coffin containing the remains of Nekht in the "absence of consent from the deceased individual or their descendants".
Nekht is thought to have lived at some point between 1985 and 1797BC and was excavated at Beni Hasan in Middle Egypt during digs carried out in the early 20th century.
The remains were donated to the city of Glasgow in 1923.
There have been repeated calls and online petitions for the return of Egyptian artefacts following the opening of the 120-acre Grand Egyptian Museum (GEM) near the pyramids of Giza last year.
It is described as the world's largest archaeological museum, containing more than 100,000 artefacts including the entire contents of the intact tomb of boy king Tutankhamun.
A spokesperson for Glasgow Life said: "We have received a request in the last few days to repatriate the Nekht remains to Egypt."
The organisation could not confirm where the request had come from but added it has a "well-established" process for repatriation requests.
GEM has been contacted for comment.
The Hunterian Museum in Glasgow also covered Lady Shep-En-Hor's body in a specifically designed textile to protect it from being seen by visitors.
Her ornate sarcophagus, which has been on display almost continuously since 1820, will remain on public view as a "fine work of late period ancient Egyptian funerary art".
Lady Shep-En-Hor has never been removed from the coffin, but has been X-rayed and CT scanned in the last 50 years.
Kelvingrove and the Hunterian Museum said the decisions followed a reassessment of their duty of care towards the deceased.
Both museums previously stated they would consider the repatriation of the remains should they receive an approach from a country or institution.
The Icom code, which was revised in June, states museums should "uphold the inherent dignity of human remains and promote respect for their significance".
It adds: "Decisions about these items and collections should be made in collaboration with descendants or communities from which they originate, if known."

title: Colder and darker school days 'tricky' for Jersey pupils
text:
Colder and darker school days 'tricky' for pupils
Heading back to school as the days get colder and darker can be challenging for pupils, a child psychologist has warned.
Gemma Daniel, who lives and works in Jersey, said the change in the weather and the clocks going back brought difficulties for children as they returned to their classrooms after the October half term.
She said the change in routine can also be hard for parents to handle as they balance family life, childcare and work.
Her advice for people heading into winter was to get a bit of sunshine in the morning and listen to their body when it needs a rest, as it is "OK to take a break".
'Sensory overload'
Daniel said she found that children in Jersey had a lot of pressure socially and academically to "really achieve", which can lead to a lot of comparison and anxiety.
She said changes in routine could be "tricky" for children and their parents to manage.
"For parents, the added stress of childcare during the school holidays and balancing going to clubs and work still can then impact how a child feels about going back into school," Daniel said.
"I think by the October half term, they know what their school year's going to look like now and what their class looks like and who their friends might be.
"If that's not gone so smoothly, or they struggle with the demands or the sensory overload of school, it can be really anxiety-provoking."
She added that finding the motivation to get out during the winter could provide a lot of benefits for children.
"It's easy to forget because, as adults, we tend to manage, and it's just what we're expected to do," Daniel said.
"But it even impacts us - we don't really want to get out of bed in the morning, or we struggle to have that motivation to go outside or exercise.
"Children need encouragement, structure and routine to keep these things going, especially in the darker months."

title: Crève Coeur returned to National Trust after more than 30 years
text:
Land returned to charity after more than 30 years
Charity bosses said they needed to take a "deep breath" before deciding what to do with land which has been returned to them after more than 30 years.
The National Trust of Guernsey said it had secured land at Crève Coeur on the island's north coast.
A five-year lease started in September 1995 to allow the States of Guernsey to use fields owned by the trust as an emergency landfill, but despite this not being extended, talks to return the area to the charity came up against several issues.
Trust president Mike Brown said he was "extremely pleased" to have the land back but no decisions had been made about what it would be used for.
Under the original lease, which had an annual nominal rent of £1, the States agreed to restore and reseed the land once the agreement had expired.
Arrangements were also discussed for the transfer of additional States-owned land to the trust for £1.
However, the trust said the process became complicated with matters including proposals for green-waste facilities and questions about surrounding boundaries causing delays.
Brown said wildlife at the site, which is fenced off, had been able to thrive in the fields while the negotiations continued.
He said the site would be the biggest owned by the trust, but it was uncertain whether it would be opened to the public.
"What we're going to do is take a deep breath and sit down and think about what we should do with it," Brown added.
"This site has been fenced off for 30 years and therefore the wildlife is superb.
"We have ground nesting birds and we want to make sure that what we do is the right thing for the site, the right thing for nature and the wildlife and the right thing for islanders."

title: Plymouth aquarium shark that helped 'dispel myths' dies
text:
Aquarium shark that helped 'dispel myths' dies
A sand tiger shark that had been at an aquarium since its opening almost 30 years ago has died.
Staff at the National Marine Aquarium (NMA) in Plymouth said they had noticed changes in the behaviour and condition of Howard, also known as Howie, and she was put to sleep after not responding to medical intervention.
She was initially living in the Great Barrier Reef habitat before moving to the Atlantic Ocean habitat where she grew to 9ft (2.7m) long.
The team said the shark was believed to have been almost 30 years old and acted as an "incredible ambassador, helping to dispel many of the myths around this critically endangered species".
Staff said: "The team at the NMA are very sad to lose such a presence from the aquarium.
"A huge thank you to our valued visitors for your support and understanding at this time.
"Rest assured, our beautiful sand tigers, Ushaka and Mandela, can still be seen in our Atlantic Ocean habitat."

title: Devon footballer 'doing well' in brain tumour treatment
text:
Positive steps in footballer's brain tumour treatment
A teenage footballer who is undergoing treatment for a brain tumour is "doing well", her family have said.
Roxy Thomas, 18, who plays for Torquay United Women, was diagnosed in August and is in intensive care at Bristol Royal Infirmary after two operations.
A statement on behalf of her family said for the first time since the operation Roxy had been "able to breathe on her own for short periods" and "although these spells are still brief, this is a positive step forward".
She started radiotherapy at the end of October, which "has gone well" but will remain in hospital for the next six weeks while she "undergoes her course of treatment".
A fundraiser was set up to support Roxy and her family, which has raised just shy of £28,000.
The funds raised will be put towards cover travel costs, accommodation during hospital stays, loss of income during treatment and further medical expenses not covered by the NHS.
Both Plymouth Argyle and Marine Academy Plymouth donated the gate receipts from recent matches against Torquay to the fundraiser.
Roxy came through the ranks at Argyle before signing for the Gulls in 2025 where she played a significant role in a treble-winning season and was named Young Player of the Season.
Torquay United said everyone at the club "continues to keep Roxy and her family in their thoughts during what remains an incredibly difficult time".
"We are grateful to the Thomas family for sharing this update and send Roxy our very best wishes as she continues her treatment."

title: New Isles of Scilly passenger ferry sets off to UK from Vietnam
text:
New Isles of Scilly passenger ferry on way to UK
A new passenger ferry, set to start a "new era of travel" to the Isles of Scilly, has set off on its journey to the UK.
The Isles of Scilly Steamship Group's new passenger ferry, Scillonian IV, departed Vietnam for the UK at 06:00 local time on Saturday (23:00 GMT on Friday), ahead of entering service in March 2027.
The 75m (246ft) vessel started the two-month voyage, travelling from Ho Chi Minh City via the Cape of Good Hope, which was the same route taken by freight vessel Menawethan earlier this year.
Scillonian IV has the capacity to carry 600 passengers and will replace Scillonian III.
Ian Howard, chairman of the Isles of Scilly Steamship Group, was in Vietnam for the occasion. He said: "Watching Scillonian IV leave Vietnam and begin her journey home was a hugely significant moment for everyone involved in bringing the vessel to life.
"Reaching this stage reflects the tremendous work, expertise and commitment of the teams who have overseen her construction and the many people who have contributed to the project.
"We're now looking forward to welcoming her closer to home and beginning the next phase of preparations ahead of her entry into service in March.
"We know how important Scillonian IV is to the future of the Isles of Scilly, and we're excited to be one step closer to introducing her to the communities and visitors she will serve."

title: Snow-clearing tractors added to North Yorkshire gritter fleet

Snow-clearing tractors added to gritter fleet
Mini tractors will be deployed in North Yorkshire's towns this winter to keep the county moving during bad weather.
The compact machines will be used in urban areas which are difficult to access by larger vehicles, to clear roads and paths during challenging weather conditions.
North Yorkshire Council said they would initially be tasked with trimming flower beds and hedges, as well as carrying fencing supplies, but were fitted with snow-clearing attachments to provide assistance to the gritting fleet.
The authority said keeping the county moving was a "key priority" and it was always looking to strengthen its winter maintenance fleet.
The tractors will be stationed in Harrogate, Richmond and Scarborough and will be deployed in the worst affected parts of the county during severe weather.
The council operates 70 gritters, works with more than 100 farming contractors and has several snow ploughs and snowblowers available.
The local authority said more than 2,700 miles (4,345 km) of the county's roads were gritted during the winter months.
About 50,000 tonnes of salt is in storage with about 5,000 salt bins and heaps across the county.

title: Cate McHugh wins The Voice UK after being mentored by Sir Tom Jones
text:
Sir Tom Jones mentors Welsh singer to victory on The Voice UK
A singer who began her career as a teenager busking on the streets of Cardiff has been crowned winner of The Voice UK.
Cate McHugh, from Llantwit Major in the Vale of Glamorgan, appeared stunned when she heard her name announced on the ITV show, telling viewers "I did it" when asked how she was feeling.
The performer, who has a degenerative sight condition which has left her registered blind, was given a congratulatory hug by her coach Sir Tom Jones on his final appearance on the show after previously announcing he had been "fired".
Speaking after the show, McHugh, 32, said: "I won The Voice! I'm entirely gobsmacked and absolutely haven't fully processed this information just yet."
Footage shared by McHugh on social media showed her laughing and smiling with family and friends screaming in delight as they celebrated her victory at a watch party in Cardiff.
McHugh's prizes include a £50,000 cash prize and a recording contract, with her first ever single, a cover of The Beatles classic Blackbird, now released.
Posting on social media, she said: "From the bottom of my heart I want to say THANK YOU for following my journey, and joining my world! This is where it's going to REALLY get fun!"
In an interview with BBC Radio Wales Breakfast in September, McHugh said being chosen to be on Team Tom at the blind audition was "absolutely undescribable".
Her rendition of Lady Gaga and Bruno Mars song Die With A Smile prompted Sir Tom to hit the button to turn his chair around after hearing her.
McHugh said she began singing "before I was talking" and started singing lessons aged six, turning professional when she was about 15.
At 22 she was diagnosed with degenerative sight condition Stargardt disease during her second year at music school and is registered blind.
As it affects the centre of her vision, it meant the singer was not sure if anyone had turned around at her audition until she heard Sir Tom's voice, she added.
"I just waited because I didn't know that anything had happened and then Tom Jones started talking," McHugh said.
She said her "fantastic mother" has the same condition and has been an inspiration to her over the years, "working around anything that might be affecting her physically or mentally".
McHugh said when she phoned her parents to tell them she was on Team Tom "there was this massive roar".
McHugh performed a duet of John Denver's Take Me Home, Country Roads during the final.
Some of her family members could be seen celebrating in the audience during the show.
It was also a poignant night for Sir Tom as he made his final appearance on the show, having been a coach on and off since it first aired in 2012.
The It's Not Unusual and What's New Pussycat? singer made headlines after revealing that ITV had "made the decision" to "fire" him from the show's coaching panel.
He shared the news on Instagram in September, amid speculation he had been "dropped" from its 2027 series.
The 86-year-old singer from Pontypridd, Rhondda Cynon Taf, is currently on his Come Gather Round world tour but announced at the end of October that he would have to reschedule or cancel some of his scheduled concerts in the United States due to "a bad case of the flu", telling fans he was "truly sorry".

title: Noise complaint sees Kent rescue cockerel returned
text:
Noise complaint sees rescue cockerel returned
A woman said she has returned her rescue cockerel to an animal charity after she was issued an anti-social behaviour notice and threatened with a £1,500 fine following complaints over his early morning crowing.
Laura-Jane Wain, from Upper Halling, Kent, took in Bruce Almighty in 2025 and said she had not received a complaint until July, when the council first warned her to take steps to minimise the noise.
"It's not a constant sound, it was only every so often, and I loved it," she said. "I thought it was a gentle crowing."
Medway Council said it had a "statutory responsibility to investigate complaints that may be considered excessive, regular or constant - and that unreasonably interfere with the wellbeing, comfort or enjoyment of a resident's property".
Wain told the Local Democracy Reporting Service: "They [neighbours] never came to us to say, 'can you do something about it?'.
"They did not even put a letter through saying it was getting on their nerves or whatever. Nothing. Nobody ever commented on it.
"I have had supportive messages from people saying they like hearing the cockerel, that it feels like the country.
"It's a semi-rural area and the houses are quite far apart with a decent amount of land between them."
Following the first complaint, she said the council wrote to her with suggestions about possible ways to remedy the situation, including placing Bruce in a darkened space to make him think it was still night-time.
Wain said she followed the advice and took the cockerel into her home's cellar in the evening, bringing him out again later in the morning.
"That seemed to take the sting [out] but then we still got the second complaint," she said.
After receiving the second letter from Medway Council with the anti-social behaviour notice in September, Wain said she decided to return the cockerel.
"It's just quite sad that so many people did say to me they enjoyed hearing the cockerel," she said.
A spokesperson for the local authority added: "The evidence collected by the council included diary sheets from residents, which logged dates, times and how they were being affected by a noise disturbance, which was then following by an investigation by officers."

title: Changes to local council planning systems come into force
text:
What you need to know about changes to the planning system
New rules on who decides planning applications have been introduced to councils across the country.
The government says planning officers, rather than councillors, should decide most applications unless exemptions apply.
The government says the changes will provide greater clarity and consistency on how planning decisions are made across England.
But critics say that reducing the role of elected councillors will make the system less democratic and transparent. They raise concerns that this will erode public confidence in the planning process.
Mayors, including the Mayor of the West Midlands, will also be given new powers to overrule local councils on some planning decisions.
The new National Scheme of Delegation, which came into effect on Saturday, sets out when a planning decision can and cannot go to committee, leaving councils with less discretion.
Determination by officers is now the default position for all planning applications.
Some councils are refusing to implement the changes.
What is changing?
The new scheme means unelected but fully trained officials will make decisions on most planning applications.
Planning committees may still consider:
- some commercial and residential developments
- listed building consent applications
- tree preservation order applications
- advertisement consent applications
Even these applications will be decided by planning officers unless they raise issues of economic, social or environmental significance.
The size of planning committees will be limited to 13 under the scheme.
In Herefordshire the amendment was voted through by a full meeting of county councillors last month, though without enthusiasm.
Chair of the county's audit and governance committee and former council leader David Hitchiner called it "an unacceptable change to our democracy", but said he would "reluctantly" second it.
Residents in his Stoney Street ward west of Hereford were already "irritated" that a seven-home proposal locally could no longer be determined by councillors, he added.
Peter Wilkinson, chair of planning at Staffordshire Moorlands District Council, has described the changes as an "erosion of local democracy", while councillor Tony Holmes went as far as to resign from the planning committee in protest.
Supporters of the old system say that when applications are determined by committee, it allows planning issues to be debated in public, making the system more transparent and accountable - something they say will be lost under the new system.
Councillors have been particularly concerned by the removal of the right to call in applications to the committee.
Moorlands councillor James Aberley said the call-in system allows ward councillors to act as a link between residents and the planning system, ensuring that the public feel involved in decisions that could have a major impact on their lives.
But the changes being implemented by the Labour government have had more support from local Labour councillors.
Councillor Finlay Gordon-McCusker, cabinet member for regeneration at the Labour-led Stoke-on-Trent City Council, suggested that "not a lot will change" in the city, as the council already delegates most applications to officers.
But he insisted that the biggest planning applications would still go to committee for a decision.
David Walker, Shropshire Council's cabinet member for planning, said, despite the changes "people will still be able to have their say".
Comments that raise relevant planning matters such as highways, flooding, heritage, ecology, landscape, residential amenity or planning policy will continue to be carefully considered as part of the decision-making process, he said.
"Shropshire Council is already recognised as a high-performing planning authority and has an established process for reviewing which applications should be considered by committee," he said.
"As a result, whilst we must comply with the new national requirements, the practical impact in Shropshire is expected to be less significant than in many other areas which differ more substantially from the new national framework."
Ahead of the changes, Solihull Council held an extra planning committee meeting on 21 October to consider five applications.
Addressing the meeting, planning officer Mark Andrews reassured the committee they would "take full regard" to concerns raised by members and residents in determining applications.
Councillor Bob Grinsell, chairman of the committee, told members the changes would not mean they would be "let off the hook".
"Maybe the load will be lessened, but it will be equally as onerous," he said.
Mayors given 'call-in' powers
Under government proposals the Mayor of the West Midlands could overrule local councils, including Coventry, Birmingham and Wolverhampton on some planning decisions.
The change would apply to proposals with more than 150 homes, more than 15,000 square metres of commercial space or buildings over 30 metres.
In addition to gaining the new "call-in" powers, mayors are set to be able to grant "up-front permission", which the government says will allow building to begin "without a developer having to apply".

title: Pero's Bridge in Bristol collapses into water after damage
text:
Bridge collapses into water after malfunction
A landmark bridge which was left partially hanging after a major malfunction earlier this year has now collapsed, leaving part of it submerged in water.
Photographs show a section of Pero's Bridge in Bristol Harbour twisted downwards, leaving one of its horn-shaped sculptures in the water.
Workers were set to remove damaged parts of the bridge last week after it was closed in August when a lifting mechanism failed.
Bristol City Council said the collapse happened shortly before 23:00 GMT on Saturday, adding there is "no confirmed impact to the maintenance and refurbishment programme" which would see it reopen in Spring 2027.
The bridge has been closed since it failed a test lift in the summer, leaving it stuck in a raised position.
Andrew Brown, the council's chair of the harbour committee, said the centre span of the bridge "slipped" and caused damage to the hydraulic ram.
He added a small amount of hydraulic oil leaked into the water by the Arnolfini, and workers were currently on site to clear the oil.
Brown said no one was injured.
"Engineers are also on site assessing the structure and we are reviewing our plans to lift the bridge next week," he said.
"At present there is no confirmed impact to the maintenance and refurbishment programme.
"However, this remains under review pending engineering assessment and approval of the revised plans."
Concerns about the bridge's condition emerged months before the incident, after engineers warned of "significant rusting" and said there was a possibility of the lifting section becoming stuck or misaligned.
It was planned to take damaged parts of the bridge to Albion Dry Dock last week for repair work.
An inspection carried out on the bridge in July 2025 found several "major structural issues" that required "urgent attention" on the crossing, which was built in 1999 and links Queen Square and Millennium Square.
In September last year, the council agreed to spend £200,000 on emergency investigation works and brought in a ban on lifting the bridge and a weight restrictions.

title: Rush to finish West Denton leisure centre frame before winter
text:
Rush to finish leisure centre frame before winter
Workers are "racing against time" to get the steel frame of a new leisure centre in place before winter sets in.
The new centre at West Denton in Newcastle has been beset by multiple setbacks.
Construction on the new facility began earlier this year and Newcastle City Council recently announced the concrete walls had been finished.
Council cabinet member for communities Rob Austin said the "weather has taken a turn for the worse" but workers were "ploughing on".
It is still hoped that the centre will be completed by the end of 2027.
It will have two swimming pools, sports hall, a gym, a café, a children's play area, a library, and a sauna and steam rooms.
The senior project manager for the contractors, Carl Maddison, said: "Work is progressing after a couple of challenging weeks.
"We are hoping for calm weather in the coming weeks so we can manoeuvre the last roof girder in place, put the roof on and the external walls before we begin work on the interior of the building."
The West Denton facility will be the first council-owned leisure centre to be built in Newcastle for 26 years.
Originally set to open in summer 2024, the scheme suffered a series of delays linked to cost inflation, the need to move a high voltage power cable running across the site, and old underground mine workings.
It is estimated cost has risen from an original £22.3 million to just shy of £40 million for the entire project.
The leisure centre was backed by a £19.8 million grant from the previous government's Levelling Up Fund in 2021, as well as £2.5 million from Sport England and a £1.4 million loan from North East mayor Kim McGuinness.
The city council has promised to cover the remaining costs from its own reserves, Community Infrastructure Levy funding, and borrowing.

Bert Bingham, cabinet member for transport and environment, said: "It is great news that these pre-construction works will start at Ollerton roundabout from November.

title: Smoke control area expanded to whole of York
text:
Smoke control area expanded to whole city
Households across the whole of York are now covered by a smoke control area, the council has said.
The rules, which limit the way residents use wood-burning stoves, aim to improve air quality and protect people's health.
Previously, about 80% of the city was covered by a smoke control area which has now been expanded to the whole of York.
The council said the expansion would make the rules "easier to understand" and "reduce preventable deaths".
According to the authority, smoke from open fires and stoves is one of the main sources of tiny air pollution particles known as PM2.5, which can enter the lungs and bloodstream.
Peter Roderick, director of public health for York, said: "Solid fuel burning accounts for nearly a third of PM2.5 emissions in York.
"There are no safe levels of these particles - they harm everyone, especially children and older people.
"Expanding the smoke control area is a proportionate, evidence-based step to protect health and reduce preventable deaths."
'Cleaner air'
Residents can continue to use wood-burning stoves or open fires but must follow certain restrictions.
Wood can still be burned indoors if it is dry and properly-seasoned but only in a stove that meets modern standards set by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs.
Older wood burners or open fireplaces can also still be used as long as "smokeless" fuels such as anthracite is used.
Other rules mean prolonged smoke from chimneys attached to buildings will not be allowed for more than 15 minutes after initially lighting a fire.
People who repeatedly break the rules following advice could face a fine of up to £300.
Labour councillor Jenny Kent said: "This is not about saying people can't use stoves or open fires.
"It is about helping people use the right fuel in the right way, so we can all benefit from cleaner air."

title: Seven-week Sandbanks Ferry closure due to begin
text:
Seven-week chain ferry closure due to begin
A major refit of a chain ferry is due to get under way on Monday, with the service expected to be out of action for about seven weeks.
The Sandbanks Ferry, which runs across the entrance to Poole Harbour between Sandbanks and Studland, will undergo a scheduled maintenance programme after its final crossing from Shell Bay at 23:10 GMT on Sunday.
The work will be carried out at Poole Quay, Dorset, and in Falmouth, Cornwall, with the timetable subject to weather and sea conditions.
Maintenance work on the ferry is carried out every two years, alternating between major and minor refits. Its last major overhaul took place in 2022.
General manager Wayne Row said extensive planning had gone into the project, with parts ordered well in advance and sections of the work prepared before the ferry is taken out of the water.
He thanked passengers for their patience and said the aim was to complete the work as thoroughly and efficiently as possible.
"We appreciate the ferry is part of the critical transport network," he said. "We're doing everything we can to ensure works are both thorough and efficient, so we can be back on the chains quickly."
The Sandbanks Ferry takes about four minutes to cross Poole Harbour and helps motorists avoid a road journey of up to 25 miles (40km).

title: Delayed discharges costing Tees Wear trust £21.5m a year
text:
Delayed discharges costing trust £21.5m a year
Patients stuck in hospital beds despite being medically fit to leave are costing an NHS trust about £21.5m a year.
Tees, Esk and Valleys NHS Foundation Trust (TEWV), which covers mental health and learning disability services in areas including County Durham and Teesside, said it had 68 adult patients taking up bed spaces at the end of August despite it not being clinically necessary.
Reasons for the issue included delays in moving people to external care placements, it said in a report. The 68 patients made up about 18% of the trust's total number of acute beds.
The trust said it was seeking to curb the problem by improving its community services.
Hospital beds being occupied for longer than necessary is a national issue caused by various factors including a lack of care home space.
The average hospital bed takes £562 a day to staff and maintain, according to NHS England, which means the health service is losing more than £225m every month supporting patients who could be elsewhere.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has touted his plan for a free NHS-style social care system as a way to solve the problem.
In a report, TEWV said the bed space problem was its "most significant performance, quality and financial risk".
It said it had devised an outline business care for a new crisis assessment centre in Durham which it hoped would divert demand from its acute wards.

title: New Mills roads reopen after double decker bus hit building
text:
Roads reopen after double decker bus hit building
Several roads that were closed after a double decker bus struck a building in New Mills have reopened.
The bus crashed into a building at the junction of Union Road and Market Street at 17:20 GMT on Saturday, Derbyshire Police said. A number of people suffered minor injuries and were treated by paramedics at the scene, it added.
A cordon was put in place on Saturday due to concerns over a "potential gas leak", but gas distribution company Cadent confirmed on Sunday it had isolated the supply to a damaged pipe.
In an update on Sunday, police said Union Road, Market Street as well as St Mary's Road had reopened and the building affected had been declared safe by a structural engineer.
The force also confirmed the bus - which was running on the 358 route between Hayfield and Stockport - had been recovered.
Elliott Nelson, network director for Cadent, said: "We were called out yesterday to support the emergency service response to an incident involving damage to a gas service pipe.
"The service pipe is the pipe which carries gas into a building from the bigger main in the road.
"Our priority in an incident like this is to make sure everything associated with gas is made safe, which we have been able to do by isolating gas supply to just this damaged pipe.
"Our teams have checked all gas assets in the vicinity and there is no additional impact."
A spokesperson for Transport for Greater Manchester said it was working with the police and the operator to "understand the exact circumstances" of the crash.
"Our thoughts are with those who were injured and we wish them a speedy recovery," the spokesperson added.

title: 'Right place, right time' for student at Boxgrove Man dig site
text:
'We were lucky to dig at UK's oldest human site'
A member of the team that started excavations at the Boxgrove archaeology site says he and his friends were "very lucky to be in the right place at the right time".
Tony Tynan was an archaeology student in 1982 when he and others became the first to dig at the site near Chichester in West Sussex.
The "Boxgrove Man" fossils, considered the oldest human fossils found in Britain, were later unearthed at the site in 1993.
Tynan told Secret Sussex that work may not have begun at the site "had we had other preoccupations on a summer's evening".
He was among the University College London students working at a nearby Roman archaeology site in 1982.
"Because we were impoverished students who couldn't go down to the pub every night, we decided to explore the bottom of the quarry," Tynan said.
The group found "60 or 80-odd feet of gravel" had been removed, uncovering a land surface from about 500,000 years ago.
"It's from that that we started to find hand axes, flint tools, subsequently then animal bones," Tynan told the BBC.
"We were lucky being in the right place at the right time and it just flourished from there, from those humble beginnings."
The South Downs nearby would have been "a lot more impressive" during the age of the fossils while the land site would have been a grassy savanna, according to Tynan.
Remains of animals including rhinoceroses and an elephant were later found.
After receiving a grant to do exploratory work, the project "snowballed over the subsequent years".
Tynan said: "The more we dug the more we found really, and the more other specialists got involved."
The early human remains, thought to belong to the species Homo heidelbergensis, consist of a shin bone and two teeth belonging to a separate individual.
Tynan said he and his colleagues had to endure "gruesome winters" with temperatures as low as -12C in the early years of the site, as well as accommodation "full of rats" and no electricity or warm water.
But he told Secret Sussex he had "very happy memories of the times we shared", including "riotous parties" and "general camaraderie" as well as digging.
