title: Police tackle 144 Halloween fireworks incidents across Scotland
text:
Police tackle 144 Halloween fireworks incidents across Scotland
Police Scotland received 144 fireworks-related calls on Saturday night - down on 160 on 31 October last year.
Fireworks were thrown at people, buildings and vehicles in some parts of Scotland on Halloween.
Officers said in general there was "outstanding behaviour and co-operation" around the country but were working to identify to those responsible for disorder.
Firework Control Zones (FCZs) - where it is an offence to set off fireworks - are in place in 14 areas in Edinburgh and four in Glasgow until early November, and dispersal zones are in force in some places.
On Halloween there were reports of fireworks lit in the street and some thrown at members of the public in Glasgow, Tranent in East Lothian and Bonnyrigg in Midlothian.
Police said no officers were injured and inquiries to identify those involved were ongoing.
Operation Moonbeam, which runs up to the evening of 5 November, means police can call on specially trained officers to deal with violence and disorder.
It is the annual police response to firework-linked criminality, which is now in its ninth year.
This year, FCZs banning the use of pyrotechnics in certain areas run from 30 October to 8 November in Edinburgh and until 9 November in Glasgow.
Seven dispersal orders were also issued in Edinburgh and work was ongoing to establish the number issued in Glasgow that relate to Operation Moonbeam.
Ch Supt David Robertson said: "The overwhelming majority of Scotland's communities have celebrated Halloween in the proper spirit and I'm really grateful for the support of our efforts tonight to deter criminality, respond to reports of disorder and protect the public and emergency services from harm.
"Sadly, however, we have again experienced incidents of fireworks used as projectiles at buildings, vehicles and members of the public.
"This type of behaviour is completely unacceptable and has to stop before there are serious consequences."
He said investigations would be launched immediately and Operation Moonbeam officers would continue to support local policing teams on fireworks-related crime over the next week.

title: Blackpool charity hits back at probe over Reform link claim
text:
Charity hits back at probe over Reform link claim
Allegations that a charity allowed its premises to be used for political campaigning for Reform UK are being assessed by the sector's watchdog.
The Charity Commission has said it is looking at claims that soup kitchen Amazing Grace in Blackpool hired out a room upstairs that was used for campaigning by the party, for which the charity's founder Mark Butcher has stood in elections.
Amazing Grace - which faced complaints to the Charity Commission two years ago when it shared on Facebook photos of Butcher with Reform leader Richard Tice - said hiring out a room did not indicate political affiliation.
Butcher said the complaint was "another move by political opponents to discredit me".
Butcher added that it was "really unfair to a charity which is doing good work to help homeless and vulnerable people in our community".
No political affiliation
Charity Commission guidance states charities can take part in political activity which "supports their purpose and is in their best interests".
However, it adds charities "must remain independent and must not give their support to a political party".
A spokesman for the Charity Commission said: "We have previously engaged with the charity on political engagement and that will be considered in our assessment of these concerns."
A spokesperson for Amazing Graze said the charity had received no direct complaints about its facilities being used for political purposes.
They added: "Our purpose is to support vulnerable individuals and families within our community, regardless of their background, beliefs or political affiliations."
The spokesperson said it operated as a community hub, providing facilities that are available for "straight forward and transparent" hire at a cost of £20 to £25.
"At no point during that conversation did the Charity Commission tell us that we could not rent out space within our building," the spokesperson said, adding the arrangement was comparable with hotels, churches and community hubs hiring out a function room, including as polling stations during elections.
"We are concerned that attempts to associate our charity with political activity simply because an external organisation may have hired a room could ultimately affect the vulnerable people who depend on our services," the spokesperson added.
Butcher stood against Labour's Chris Webb in Blackpool South in 2024, receiving 10,068 votes to Webb's winning 16, 919.

title: New music venue bids to revive Wakefield's gigging glory days
text:
Music venue bids to revive city's gigging glory days
There was a time when Wakefield buzzed with live music as crowds packed into pubs to watch bands such as The Cribs and The Kooks during their rise to fame. Although much of the grassroots scene has since faded, a new live music venue hopes to bring back the glory days for emerging talent.
The Backroom, which opened this week inside the city's Hop and Cobble pub, aims to give young musicians a taste of performing to an audience in a purpose-built space.
For musician Adam Schofield, a singer in a band during Wakefield's music scene heyday, the inspiration came from a lack of opportunities for young bands to hone their craft.
It struck a chord with Hop owner Jamie Lawson and, over a pint, the pair came up with the idea for the Backroom.
Schofield, 47, says: "As a band we used to talk about getting back together.
"We'd say 'let's just do that one gig' but then we were like, 'yeah that's great, but where do we play in Wakefield nowadays?' All the places that used to exist have gone."
Players, Escobar and the Snooty Fox were among the venues where Schofield and many local bands gigged.
Wakefield's internationally acclaimed indie rockers The Cribs performed at Escobar in their early days, while acts including The Kooks and Arctic Monkeys also played the venue.
"It was this tiny little place which wasn't really set up as somewhere for bands to play - it had this pillar down the middle stage," Schofield remembers.
"But it had a really good reputation for live music - so much so that emerging bands would put it on their UK tours.
"For local bands, what that meant was they'd get these opportunities to support a band coming up from London.
"You'd say 'yeah OK I'll play that gig' and it turned out to be The Kooks or Razorlight."
Those venues may have been popular, but Schofield says the Backroom offers something they did not - a space built for live music.
"The Backroom has got all the things you'd associate with playing a big venue like the O2 but in a smaller space.
"There's a green room so the band gets to sit backstage, have a few drinks and come out onto the stage instead of having to clamber through the crowd.
"It's got a great sound system and it's dark so you're always able to create a vibe."
When it opened in 2009, live music was at the heart of The Hop. Although that focus faded over time, Lawson, who is also the owner of Ossett Brewery, said he had always wanted to bring it back.
"Bands all need to start somewhere and I think without a grassroots venue then it's very difficult to do that.
"As a company we've grown a lot since then, so now it's about investing in the local area and giving people the opportunity to play live music again."
The impact of The Hop can be seen in some of Wakefield's more recent successful acts who credit the pub as a place that enabled them to shine.
Ryan Johnston, lead singer of Skinny Living, says it played a pivotal role in the band's formation.
"The Hop played a huge part in Skinny Living forming. It's where Danny and I first met and we've had some unforgettable gigs there," he recalls.
"It's a proper grassroots music venue with a real passion for the local community.
"It's great to see the opening of a new stage for new artists to come through and play in Wakefield."
Similar support came from Embrace drummer Mike Heaton who remembers playing some of the most memorable gigs of the band's career there.
He says: "We did two nights at The Hop to road test the songs after such a long time away and they became two of the most memorable shows of our career."
For Schofield, he wants to provide the same opportunities for the next generation of musicians.
A weekly grassroots night will take place at the Backroom every Thursday and bands are able to sign up to register their interest in playing.
"There's a trend with younger people where they're turning back to real instruments and forming bands again," Schofield says.
"We're probably the only purpose-built place in Wakefield where a group of kids can email us and say 'can we play?' and the answer is 'yeah, you can be on next week'.
"It doesn't matter how many people you can pull in. The bigger bands didn't start playing to huge crowds, they all had to start somewhere."
The venue will also work with local colleges and other music organisations to give people interested in the technical side of the industry opportunities to gain experience in areas such as production and engineering.
Schofield says: "Ultimately, I'd love to see Wakefield go back to 'Oh it's a Wednesday night, shall we go and watch a band?'
"Instead of, 'oh it's a Wednesday night, there's nothing to do'."

Women and children's hospital 'finished in 2032'
Hospital bosses have said work to build a new women and children's hospital will start soon.
Kim O' Keefe, acting chief executive of the Royal Cornwall Hospitals NHS Trust, said the project which was announced in 2023 as part of the national New Hospital Programme, would become a reality in the next few years.
"I feel like I've been talking about this for 20 plus years and it's finally feeling real, O' Keefe said.

In January the trust said a total of £15.5m had already been spent on the project, including design and planning, car parking provision and creating a contractors' compound.
In an update in July, it said Willmott Dixon had been appointed as construction partner for the hospital on the Treliske site in Truro.
It added the new hospital would bring acute women's, children's and maternity services together in a "purpose-built environment".
O'Keefe said: "The new plans are almost ready to launch."
"We are in the final throws of the revised business case, we have our new build partner Willmott Dixon, we've worked very very strongly with our clinical teams and our stakeholders," she added.
"It's a very different build to what was originally put forward 18 years ago," she said.

title: Consett group painting rocks and hiding them around country
text:
Artists hiding painted pebbles around the world
A craft group has hit 8,000 members six years after they began hiding painted pebbles around the world.
Stephanie Winter and her aunt Victoria Morris set up Consett Rocks in 2020 to help people stay creative during the coronavirus pandemic.
Since then, Winter has painted hundreds of stones and the group has amassed thousands of members on social media, all posting painted pebbles they have hidden or found.
Winter said she had been "amazed" to see how large the group had become and to know how many strangers they had made smile.
"We created the group to help people in and around the Consett area get creative and active again during lockdown," Winter said.
"Everyone who has found a rock and shared it on the group has always said it's made them happy."
She said some people who found the painted rocks left them where they were, others took them home for their gardens and some hid them in different locations.
Winter once hid a Consett Rock in Iceland and remarkably it made its way back to the UK.
Leanne Harris and her family first started painting rocks after discovering a Consett Rock while on a day out.
She said some of their creations had popped back up in entirely different countries months after being placed.
"My husband hid a rock in Durham in July 2025 and it was not seen again until it turned up in October in Australia," Harris said.
"We hid a little crab rock in Bowlees Visitor Centre [in Teesdale] and it was found by a family having a holiday before the mum's maternity leave ended, and they took it home and put it in their baby's memory box."
Harris recommended people give pebble painting a go because all you needed was "a simple little rock and a bit of paint which ends up making someone's day".

title: Police hunt for three men after Trowbridge Halloween stabbing
text:
Police hunt for three men after Halloween stabbing
Police are searching for three men after a man was left with life-changing injuries in a stabbing.
Wiltshire Police said the attack happened near the car park at Tesco Extra in Trowbridge shortly before 14:00 GMT on 31 October.
The force said three men wanted in connection with the attack are Redouane Bendhiyaf, 47, Dion Barrett, 50, and Joshua Galbraith, 35, who all have links to Trowbridge.
The victim, a man in his 20s, was taken to hospital with potentially life-changing injuries, police said.
The three men are believed to have targeted the victim near the car park before fleeing the scene, police said.
Det Sgt Jonathan Dean, from Wiltshire Police, said: "Our investigation into this incident is continuing at pace and we are asking for the public's help to locate these three men.
"Members of the public are advised not to approach the men, but to contact us immediately if they have any information about their whereabouts."
There will be an increased police presence in the area as inquiries continue, he added.

title: Heidi Klum's Halloween costume revealed as Traitors' Maya Jama dresses as Mo Farah
text:
From Maya as Sir Mo Farah to Heidi as her own left hand: The best Halloween looks
Supermodel and TV host Heidi Klum confirmed her position as the queen of Halloween by transforming into a giant, bloodied and severed hand for her annual costume party in New York.
Klum, 53, was completely unrecognisable arriving at her event in what she described as her own chopped-off "left hand".
This year marks the 25th anniversary of Klum's party, which brings celebrities across the globe together dressed in their wild, weird and wonderful costumes.
And the revelry didn't stop there, with celebrities such as Maya Jama wowing attendees at her own Halloween party in London dressed as four-time Olympic champion Sir Mo Farah.
"It took a lot of hands putting this hand together," Klum told reporters as she posed for pictures on the red carpet. "I think about 10 or 20 hands."
Explaining the inspiration for the idea, she said: "I looked at my hand and I thought 'Hey, I think that I can fit my body inside of this somehow.'
"I always try to come up with something unusual and I don't think I've seen an actual person walking around like a hand. I thought that was something new and different."
Klum is never one to shy away from dressing up on the scariest day of the year, with previous looks including a worm, Medusa and the ogre Princess Fiona from the Shrek films.
Other attendees at Klum's party this year included actors Neil Patrick Harris and David Burtka, who surprised attendees by dressing as the twins from the horror film The Shining.
Pop star Jade Thirlwall also attended the party in New York dressed as a stone statue of an angel, while Severance and Spider-Man actor Tramell Tillman turned up with intricate face makeup and prosthetics.
Meanwhile in London, broadcaster Maya Jama hosted her annual Halloween Party dressed as Sir Mo Farah.
Jama told Elle UK magazine she wanted to dress as the "bald headed icon" to honour the Olympian, adding that she has wanted to dress up as a man for years for Halloween.
"[Sir Mo] loved the idea," she explained.
"He's actually sent me all of his real life Olympic outfits, his real, actual medals he won for the Olympics.
"His real trainers. He's even done some TikToks for me. He is fully on board."
Comedian Katherine Ryan attended the event dressed as Jama, recreating one of her outfits from her recent stint on the Celebrity Traitors.
Elsewhere, singer Lily Allen dressed as every performer's worst nightmare - a Ticketmaster seating map covered in unsold blue concert tickets.

title: Lime bike jousting is performance art, say organisers
text:
'Lime bike jousting is a form of performance art'
The organisers of two Lime bike jousting events in east London have said they wanted to bring people together in a free experience to help them "feel alive".
On Saturday, actor Cameron Carnegie-Brown, who jousts as Camtholomew the First, and artist Jack Carden met in London Fields Park, Hackney for a second duel on the hire e-bikes, with the match raising funds for five charities.
On Friday, a professional jouster from Leeds said that jousting on the Lime bikes was "absolutely a legitimate form" of the medieval sport.
Lime previously said its bikes were "not for jousting", and added: "While we appreciate the medieval spirit, safety must always come first".
Both Carden and Carnegie-Brown said that crowd safety was their "biggest priority".
Carnegie-Brown told BBC London that after the large turnout at their first duel, the pair had planned a bigger space for the joust, with an action zone, a dead zone and a spectator area.
They said they had stewards to help with crowd control, and health professionals were on hand.
Describing the joust, Carnegie-Brown said: "You have this moment where you put the visor down and you're suddenly very alone.
You're suddenly, it's you, the helmet, and all you can see through this little slit is another guy who's probably feeling the exact same way."
"You can kind of hear the crowd, but you can also hear your breath," he said.
"It's quite exhilarating because your heart starts to beat and you do get nervous.
"Your adrenaline just like pumps through your veins. The second you start pedalling, you forget it all - just ram and hope for the best.
"It makes you feel alive, and I think the audience feel that as well."
Tommy Moore, a 28-year-old content creator from London who is involved in the event, said: "Horses are quite hard to source in London, so we thought we'd go for lime bikes and bring it into the 21st Century.
"It's a bit of fun and an opportunity to get dressed up and have a nice time. It's community-building. Everyone is very respectful and are all here in good spirit. I feel I'm in good company."
Carnegie-Brown said it was an "amazing feeling" to bring "so many people together" in London.
To manage the crowd, they released the event location two hours beforehand to those who had submitted an RSVP to the event, which was capped at online at 5,000 people.
Hackney Council said it had not given permission for the event to be held in the borough.
Reflecting on the first duel's turnout, Carnegie-Brown said: "I expected a crowd. But as big as it was, no way.
"People probably made friends there that they'll remember forever, because you don't forget something like that."
He described the joust as a British "performance art", and said that nationally, there was a love of watching "a crazy sport".
"I like to consider myself a bit of a showman.
"We do think it's pretty British. The bikes, they're very London. The armour is extremely British."
He told BBC London ahead of Saturday's duel: "I think Jack wants to win, I think I want to win, but we never did it for a competition.
"We did it because it was a fun thing to do. We're not trying to sell tickets.
"I think that's what makes it art. We kind of just wanted to give people a free experience.
"And they deserve it just as much as we deserve that feeling of being a bit wild and free on the bikes."
The pair launched an online charity fundraiser as part of the event, with any donations being split between five charities.

title: Italian-themed festival on Richmond Green rejected by council
text:
Richmond Italian-themed festival plans refused
Plans to host a Sicilian-themed festival on Richmond Green next summer have been rejected over concerns about safety, anti-social behaviour and noise.
Richmond Council refused an application for the Marzamemi Festival, which organisers wanted to bring to Richmond Green for the first time from 25 to 27 June 2027.
The event features Italian music, food, wine tasting, workshops, shopping and children's activities and was previously held in Old Deer Park in Richmond, south-west London.
A licensing committee ruled that the site, which it said experienced anti-social behaviour, could not safely accommodate an event attracting up to 4,999 people.
Festival founder Emily Ceraudo said the event would be a "boutique, family-friendly celebration of Italian food, craft and culture on Richmond Green" that would support local businesses.
Ceraudo said concerns had been addressed by reducing the festival's footprint to just over a third of the green, introducing strict noise controls and providing security staff.
The festival was due to close at 21:00 BST on 25 and 26 June, and at 19:00 on 27 June.
The plans prompted 45 objections, including concerns that public access to the popular open space would be restricted and that nearby residents would be disturbed by noise.
Among those objecting were Friends of Richmond Green and the Richmond Society.
Robert Tuday, representing the Richmond Society, told a licensing hearing on 19 October that he objected to removing "public access to a large area of Richmond Green for a substantial period, to the point of constituting a public nuisance".
Tuday said it would be to the "detriment of the non-paying public at large, who may wish to use the green and enjoy it as an amenity".
Resident Vivien Harris added: "The nuisance would not be limited to residents. Visitors wishing to enjoy the remaining accessible areas of Richmond Green for relaxation, recreation or family outings would also be subjected to the noise."
Ten letters did back the plans, describing the festival as a well-managed, family-friendly event that benefited the borough.
Local mother and business owner Tara Stevens said: "We are begging for more activities like this, that are super curated for young families, to be closer to home."
In its decision report, the committee said there was a significant risk of people breaking into the festival, and that its website gave the impression it was "alcohol led".
The report said that although the festival had previously been run successfully at Old Deer Park, staging a similar event on Richmond Green would not meet licensing objectives around public safety, crime and disorder, and public nuisance.

title: Hackney drops opposition to £1.5bn Edmonton incinerator
text:
Hackney drops opposition to waste incinerator
Hackney Council has dropped its opposition to a £1.5bn waste incinerator project, which is now forecast to cost the authority millions of pounds more than expected earlier this year.
Ahead of the 2026 local elections, the Hackney Green Party pledged in its manifesto to "explore every option to cancel" the reconstruction of an ageing rubbish incinerator serving seven north London councils.
But after winning control of the council in May, the party says abandoning the project would be financially and environmentally "devastating".
Work to rebuild the ageing Edmonton plant began in 2022, but the scheme has faced opposition for decades over concerns about air pollution and carbon emissions.
Councillor Jacob Cable, the council's cabinet member for climate, said it was "clear" that failing to complete the project would be "devastating both financially for the seven constituent boroughs" which use it.
Cable, who is also chair of the North London Waste Authority (NLWA), said cancelling the rebuild would "also massively worsen environmental and operational outcomes, as we would have to pay to transport our waste to lower performing incinerators than that which is being built".
He told the Local Democracy Reporting Service he reached that conclusion after commissioning a review into the "costs and risks associated with not completing the project".
The U-turn comes as the cost of rebuilding the incinerator has soared, directly affecting the borough's projected budget deficit over the next three years.
Hackney Council said the multi-year construction budget for the 50-year-old plant had risen by 80%.
A council spokesperson said the authority's predicted budget shortfall had increased by £9m, partly because it has to contribute more money towards the rising cost of rebuilding the Edmonton waste plant.
The council now expects its budget gap to grow to more than £21m by 2030.
'Unforeseen complications'
In 2024, Hackney's Labour administration defended the scheme after a BBC investigation found that burning rubbish was the UK's "dirtiest form of power".
The scheme has been delayed by rising construction costs, high interest rates and supply chain pressures.
The NLWA said work had also been hindered by "unforeseen complications for working on an old industrial site", including the discovery of asbestos, unmapped water pipes and a "sewer diversion" that proved "more complex than planned".
According to the project's website, the incinerator is due to enter its commissioning phase in 2027.

title: Halloween: Young child hit by firework in Carrickmore
text:
Young child injured by firework on Halloween night
A toddler was taken to hospital after being burnt by a firework in County Tyrone on Halloween night.
It was one of numerous Halloween-related incidents that the emergency services responded to across Northern Ireland on Saturday night and into Sunday.
Fireworks were deliberately directed at fire crews in six separate incidents.
The injury to the toddler - a girl under two years old - happened outside a filling station on Main Street in Carrickmore at about 20:30 GMT.
Insp McDonagh of the Police Service of Northern Ireland said the firework was thrown on the road by teenage boys and "partially exploded" before bouncing back and "exploding for a second time" beside the child, who was with her parents.
The girl sustained a burn to her forearm, which required hospital treatment.
"It's only by sheer luck that the consequences of this reckless act weren't even more serious," said Insp McDonagh.
"The irresponsibility of throwing fireworks near a petrol station is shocking."
Halloween celebrations took place in Northern Ireland over the weekend, with the biggest festival being held in Londonderry on Saturday evening.
Across Northern Ireland, the fire service responded to 89 incidents, many of which were Halloween-related with 23 of them involving bonfires, between 18:00 on Saturday and 01:00 on Sunday.
Fireworks were directed at fire crews in Drumquin in County Tyrone, Enniskillen in County Fermamagh and Kilkeel in County Down.
"No damage or injuries resulted and operational response for local communities was maintained throughout," said a Northern Ireland Fire and Rescue Service spokesperson.
"We cannot emphasise enough how dangerous fireworks are as they can result in life changing injuries if used inappropriately.
"We acknowledge these incidents were isolated to a small minority of individuals, but this antisocial behaviour could have had devastating consequences."
'Perfect storm' in Dublin
In the Republic of Ireland, the Dublin Fire Brigade reported the highest number of Halloween calls in more than a decade.
Chief fire officer Greg O'Dwyer said that, as of midnight the service had received 558 calls, an increase from 320 calls last year.
O'Dwyer described it as a "very busy night" resulting from a "perfect storm" of dry weather and Halloween falling on a Saturday.

title: Cambridge scientist Marta Shahbazi dies in Spanish train crash
text:
Cambridge scientist dies in Spanish train crash
An award-winning University of Cambridge researcher died in the Spanish train disaster while on her way to collect a prize for scientific excellence.
Dr Marta Shahbazi was travelling to an awards ceremony on Wednesday when the train she was on crashed into another near Urda, south of Madrid, killing 69 people.
The mother of two was an affiliate associate professor leading a group of researchers at MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB) in Cambridge and had earned several awards for work on human embryos and cell biology.
In a statement, the LMB paid tribute to the "inspiring, talented and passionate scientist" and described her death as a "profound shock and a huge loss".
The expert in cell biology ran the Shahbazi Laboratory at the LMB, based on the Cambridge Biomedical Campus.
She had been announced as the winner of a Spanish Society for Developmental Biology award for her contributions to the study of early human development and was due to collect the award at a conference in El Rompido in Andalusia.
The LMB said: "As a wife and mother of two young children, Marta wrote eloquently about balancing her family and career, serving as a much-admired role model for a 'mother scientist', a term she used to describe herself.
"Marta was an inspiring, talented and passionate scientist whose research shed light on the earliest steps in the development of human embryos and how errors occur that lead to failed pregnancies," the LMB said.
The institute said her death was "a profound shock and a huge loss for LMB".
Her work had been recognised with "many awards and prizes", the laboratory added.
Shahbazi is listed on the University of Cambridge website as a principal investigator at its Stem Cell Institute (CSCI).
Institute director Prof Bertie Gottgens said its community was "shocked and deeply saddened" by her death.
"Marta led her primary research group at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB) alongside her roles as an affiliate principal investigator and affiliate assistant professor at the CSCI," he said.
"Across both institutes, she was highly respected for her pioneering research on early human development and valued for her collaborative spirit.
"Her creativity, passion, and generosity will be greatly missed."
The news of her death was first confirmed in a social media post by the CiMUS, based in Santiago de Compostela where Shahbazi's aunt works.
Shahbazi undertook her PhD at the Spanish National Cancer Research Centre, before joining the University of Cambridge as a post-doctoral fellow and then the LMB in 2020.
The crash in Spain happened when a state-operated Renfe high-speed train smashed into the back of a stationary train operated by the Iryo company.
It is one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history, and Spain's worst crash since 2013.
Three days of national mourning were declared in the country.
More than 540 people were on board both trains.

title: New charity uses outdoors to improve men's mental health
text:
New charity uses outdoors to improve mental health
A new charity hopes to use activities ranging from cold-water swimming and archery to hill walking and breathwork to improve men's mental health and reduce isolation.
Connect Outdoors is being officially launched alongside an International Men's Day event at the Venture Centre in Maughold, where organisers expect about 80 people to take part in a range of outdoor activities.
The charity said it wanted to gather research on what kind of support men are most likely to engage with, arguing that services have often been designed without asking men first.
Chief executive Kate Bergquist said it had grown out of years of work in social care, public services and outdoor wellbeing programmes.
She said: "We have this abundance of landscape on the island that is never used enough for health.
"This should be embedded into everyone's health and wellbeing routine every week."
'Blue and green health'
Activities on offer include high ropes, bushcraft, mindfulness, breathwork, yoga, archery, ice baths and guided walks, alongside informal spaces designed to encourage men to connect with one another.
The charity is built around what is known as "green and blue health", which encourages people to use natural environments such as forests, beaches and the sea to improve their health.
Bergquist said a key focus would be addressing men's mental health through activities that encourage conversation without making mental health the main selling point.
As part of Sunday's event, attendees will be invited to complete surveys that organisers hope will help identify which activities and approaches are most effective at engaging men.
Among those supporting the event is Gary Thomas, who runs Walking for Wellness and takes people on Manx hill walks where they can talk through any challenges.
The former serviceman and mountain leader said many people found it easier to open up outdoors than in a traditional counselling setting.
"It gives them that opportunity to feel secure and have that ability to open up in an environment that's not oppressive," he said.
"Nature's not clinical, nature's natural."
Thomas said group activities could also help tackle loneliness by creating new social connections.
"We've had people turn up and find their own circle of friends and common interests," he said.
"Then they go off afterwards and explore things together, which is brilliant."
Also involved in the event is Douglas barber Joshua Moore, who completed suicide prevention training through the Lions Barber Collective.
Moore runs Renegade: Cuts and Clobber, and said barber shops often became places where men felt comfortable discussing difficult issues.
"The barber chair is a very special place," he said.
"You can leave feeling a little bit better about yourself, whether that's having a nice haircut, but also just having the opportunity for somebody to listen to you."
Moore said he had seen first-hand the impact mental health struggles could have on families and communities, and wanted to support initiatives aimed at encouraging conversation and early intervention.
The International Men's Day event aimed to introduce men to new activities and point participants to support available to improve both their physical and mental wellbeing.

title: When will Preston's Grade II-listed red telephone boxes return?
text:
When will Preston's red telephone boxes return?
A Lancashire city's famous row of red telephone boxes have undergone a £75,000 refurbishment, but are not set to return to their home in Preston city centre any time soon.
The nine telephone booths on Market Street were due to return by the end of the year, but works are being carried out at the former Post Office property directly behind the kiosks.
With scaffolding being put up around the full building perimeter, the council said the phone boxes will have to wait to return until the building works have been completed.
What has been happening with them?
Preston's booths were disconnected from the network more than a decade ago.
Having become redundant, the kiosks were vandalised and fell into disrepair before been taken over by Preston City Council in 2021.
Their Grade II-listed status - designated in 1988 - meant planning permission was needed for the facelift, which began in December 2024 when they were lifted from the site.
The boxes - famously red so they stand out - have now been stripped out, sandblasted, and fitted with new toughened windowpanes and coloured lights and power sockets so art displays can be put in them.
What is the delay?
Blackfinch Investments, the company behind the works at the former Post Office property, have said work has started on the building with the initial phase focusing on essential repairs to make it watertight.
Valerie Wise, deputy leader and cabinet member for community wealth building and city regeneration at the council, said: "We are all eagerly anticipating the return of the telephone boxes.
"However, to protect the newly refurbished boxes from potential damage and ensure they are unveiled without scaffolding in the background, we believe it is best to wait.
"We hope their return isn't delayed for too long by the works at the former Post Office building and as such we are in close contact with the contractors on site to enable their return as soon as possible."
What is special about them?
The eight boxes form the longest continuous line of traditional call booths in the country, which is what won them their listed status.
A ninth stands slightly apart near the fish market canopy.
What is their history?
Designed by Sir Giles Gilbert Scott and introduced in 1935 in celebration of the Silver Jubilee of King George V, large numbers of the K6 - or Kiosk 6 - model were installed around the country, making them a recognised symbol of 20th Century Britain.
Preston City Council said there appeared to have been a telephone kiosk on Market Street, on the west side of the former head Post Office, in the 1930s.
A photo from about 1935 shows a single telephone kiosk at the northern end of the building, where it joins the Box/Fish Market, on the same spot as the lone kiosk that stands detached from the other eight.
This earlier telephone kiosk appears to have been cream-coloured and is likely to have been a K3.
It was replaced with the current K6, which, judging from the Tudor crown with a flatter base, was one of the earlier K6s models.
By the 1970s, a further eight K6s had been added.
Six of the kiosks are adorned with the Tudor crown and pre-date 1953, the council said.
Three kiosks have the St Edward's Crown. Of these, one has integral crowns, therefore dating to sometime between 1953 and 1955.
The remaining two have slots where the crown is placed, which would suggest that they date to 1955 or later.
What is the plan for their future?
The plan is to use them for digital art installations, which will change over time.
The nine kiosks will look different when they return, with Preston-based company, ADI.tv commissioned to install up to three digital screens in each box, alongside speakers that will provide ambient background music.
John Chesworth, chairperson of the Towns Fund Board, said the telephone boxes "will provide a big impact when they are completed".
"The delay is unavoidable, but it will be worth it to see them in full, glorious new technicolour."

title: Sheep return to roof of cinema complex to keep lawn in trim
text:
Sheep return to roof of cinema complex to keep lawn in trim
A cinema complex in Lancashire has come up with a lawn-mowing solution with a difference - by deploying sheep on to its grass-topped roof to help keep it in trim.
The six Dutch spotted sheep belong to Myerscough College but have been moved a mile or two down the road to the Flower Bowl in Preston, which houses a bowling alley, restaurants and sports facilities.
The centre had sheep in previous years but they were moved out for safety reasons during the coronavirus pandemic.
Director Peter Topping said: "We have mown it in the past but we have to carry the small mowing machines up the staircase so it's a lot easier to get the sheep up there and leave them to do their work."
Andrea Gardner, director of farm operations and innovations at the college, she was "so pleased" with how well the animals were doing, as part of a special joint project with the two sites.
The sheep, one of which has been named after BBC Radio Lancashire presenter Sharon Hartley, are kept safe by a five-foot high fence around the perimeter.
They have a wooden shelter and water in a trough that gets refilled with a stopcock.
Topping said the idea of having sheep on their roof came from his brother, the managing director of the centre.
He said they wanted to make the centre as environmentally friendly as possible, with a green roof "insulating the building" and making sure it "blends in with the countryside".
Gardner said the project showed off the sort of work that they do at the college, and was a good example of regenerative farming.
"They're not bothered about being up on a roof, they're quite happily looking around, the fantastic views that they're seeing", she said.
The college is hoping that the five female sheep will produce lambs in the spring.

title: Wife tells of husband's recovery from crash moments after buying lottery ticket
text:
Wife tells of husband's recovery from crash moments after buying lottery ticket
Every morning for three weeks, Sarah Rimmer would call the hospital where her husband was fighting for his life in the hope of being told the father-of-two had simply made it through the night.
Lewis was in an induced coma after being knocked down by a Range Rover in the car park of a Sainsbury's store in Bolton, Greater Manchester - just moments after he bought a lottery ticket.
The doting father was airlifted to the Royal Preston Hospital where his family were told he had just a 30% chance of pulling through.
Lewis spent weeks on life support and had more than 40 hours of surgery, including the amputation of his left foot.
"For three weeks, I couldn't hear his voice, tell him about the girls or ask him for advice," said Sarah, reflecting on how life had changed one year on.
"The girls couldn't understand why we couldn't Facetime daddy."
In the following three weeks, medics reduced the sedation and each day Sarah would hope to hear the words "settled overnight", indicating he had progressed and was comfortable.
"The next six weeks brought a whole new battle," she said.
"Waking up, piecing together what had happened, learning to eat and drink again and slowly seeing the tubes and machines disappear.
"The girls finally got to see their daddy and began to understand what had actually gone on."
On the day of the incident on 27 October 2025, Lewis had taken the afternoon off work to celebrate the birthday of his eldest daughter.
Driving straight from the car garage where he works, he met his wife and their two daughters at a cafe close to their Bolton home.
He was hit just minutes after buying the lottery ticket and waving goodbye to his family.
Lewis was left with a broken pelvis, fractures to both femurs, a compound fracture to his right shin and severe damage to his left foot, which could not be saved.
Six months after the crash, Lewis was finally able to go home.
Sarah said the family now faced "a completely different life" and "a long road to recovery" but were determined to stay positive.
"We're busy with appointments but it's all positive things moving forward," she said.
"It's just a new journey that we're doing now, navigating everything."
A 57-year-old man is due to stand trial in November after being charged with causing serious injury by dangerous driving.

title: Christmas lights switch-ons across the North West in 2026
text:
Christmas lights switch-ons across the North West
It's beginning to look a lot like Christmas in north-west England, as towns and cities in the region light up for the festive season.
As the countdown to 25 December begins, cities and towns across the region have set the date to switch on their Christmas lights, marking the start of the yuletide festivities.
Below are confirmed details of when and where events are taking place locally.
Merseyside
Southport: The annual ceremony takes place on Saturday 7 November, with free entertainment outside The Grand and performances from Regally Royal Parties from 16:00 GMT.
Huyton: The Christmas lights switch-on will take place in the village centre from 15:00 to 19:00 on Friday 13 November.
Prescot: The Christmas lights switch-on will take place in the town centre from 15:00 until 19:00 on Saturday 14 November.
Kirkby: The Christmas lights switch-on will take place in the town centre from 16:30 to 19:30 on Friday 20 November.
Greater Manchester
Manchester: There will not be an official Christmas lights switch-on in Manchester, but the lights will be turned on across the city on Friday 6 November.
Bury: The Rock Shopping Centre is marking its 15th year with a new tradition - its first Christmas parade and lights switch-on, on Saturday 7 November. Festivities start from 16:00 where visitors are asked to meet for the parade.
Oldham: The Christmas lights switch-on will be held on Saturday 14 November, starting with meet and greets with Peppa Pig, appearances from Oldham's mascots and activities by the Spindles Kids Club from 13:00. Celebrations will feature Father Christmas, Peppa Pig's Dance Party, Oldham Rock Choir and performances from Fierce Dance, followed by fireworks and a lights and laser show from 17:30.
Tameside: The Northern Lights Lantern Parade in Ashton returns on Saturday 14 November, setting off at 17:00 and wrapping up with a festive light switch-on at about 18:30.
Stockport: More than 200 performers and 50 free shows are set to take over the town centre on Sunday 15 November from 12:00 to 17:00, followed by a parade featuring more than 100 drummers, with the Christmas lights switch-on at 16:45.
Rochdale: The Christmas lights switch-on will take place on Sunday 22 November at 17:30 in front of the town hall following a countdown. Ignite Fire Festival continues opposite Rochdale Town Hall until 20:00.

title: Frodsham: Why a Cheshire town wants fewer councillors
text:
Why a Cheshire town wants fewer councillors
With around 10,000 parish and town councils across England, more than 100,000 local councillors represent them.
But one in Cheshire could have fewer councillors after residents backed plans to reduce its size, in a move one former mayor described as "quite sensible".
Frodsham Town Council (FTC) currently has 16 councillors, but that could be reduced to 12 if plans are approved by Cheshire West and Chester Council (CWAC).
The proposal follows a request by FTC for CWAC to review how the town council is run, although the council has since voted to oppose the change.
A former mayor of the town, Christine Lloyd, said the proposal seemed like a "good idea".
Christine and her husband Brian know a lot about town councils, having served as councillors and mayors.
Speaking in Frodsham's town centre, Christine said the plans were "quite sensible".
"People aren't coming forward and to make a quorum of how they have to do it, it's difficult to get things through," she said.
Brian said he was not sure if any changes would make a difference and preferred the way the council operated during his time in office.
He said when he was first elected, a fellow councillor told him there was "no room for hard politics".
"He was absolutely right," Brian said.
"He said, 'how can you get political over hanging baskets and Christmas lights?'. He was right and I stuck to that."
Anne Caulfield said she did not believe reducing the number of councillors "would make a great deal of difference".
"I think if they've got enough about them, with 12 councillors you can still do the same sort of thing 16 councillors could do," she said.
Another shopper said she liked the work of the town council, particularly a Christmas voucher scheme for residents aged over 70, and thought having fewer councillors could work.
"I think 12 is enough, because I've been on committees for a long time, it's hard to get everyone to agree," she said.
The National Association of Local Councils says there are around 10,000 parish and town councils across England.
They raise money through a precept, an additional charge collected as part of council tax to pay for local services and facilities.
In Frodsham, the town council raises around £300,000 a year through its precept. It's set at £79.88 for a band D property in 2026-27.
The process has not been straightforward.
Frodsham Town Council initially requested a governance review into reducing the number of councillors from 16 to 12 in September 2025.
Three rounds of consultation have since taken place.
However, the town council has now said it opposes the proposal.
Despite that, the consultation found support among residents for reducing the number of councillors.
In the second stage of consultation, which was sent to every resident in Frodsham, 148 people backed the proposal, while 21 opposed it and 24 said they were unsure.
The other rounds attracted fewer responses, but more respondents still favoured reducing the number of councillors than opposed it.
Feedback from the consultation will be discussed by CWAC councillors on 3 November before a recommendation is made to the full council on whether to approve the changes.
description: A consultation has found support for reducing the number of councillors on Frodsham Town Council.

title: Dog wedding chauffeurs and doggy roasts: The rise of the puppy experience economy
text:
Dog wedding chauffeurs and doggy roasts: The rise of the puppy experience economy
They are known as our best friends or as being part of the family, so it is only natural that owners want to shower their dogs in treats and take them wherever they go.
But over the past decade, this special relationship has evolved into a booming industry, fuelled by the rise of the so-called "doggy experience economy".
From pubs and restaurants serving up doggy roasts to cafes offering Puppuccinos and dog-friendly ice cream, catering for our four-legged friends has become a multi-billion-pound industry.
According to MoneySuperMarket, spending on pets and pet-related goods has surged from £2.9bn in 1997 to £11.95bn in 2025.
But what has caused owners to shift from bringing their dogs to a pub to wanting to feed them a chef-cooked meal while they are there? We spoke to pet owners, experts and businesses across the West of England to see what they think.
University of the West of England senior lecturer in marketing Dr Stelina Kanaki explained how social media could be influencing people.
"I think that social media has normalised premium pet care and services.
"A social media user compares themselves to other users and influencers.
"So, seeing, for example, someone's dog getting their professional photograph taken - this then becomes something the user feels they should do otherwise they get a fear of missing out, regardless of their financial situation," she said.
But, social media is not the sole reason in this change in consumer behaviour as Kanaki explains.
"There is something called the experience economy. This is what we're living in nowadays," she said.
This means businesses have shifted from selling traditional goods or services to creating memorable moments for customers.
"So people are now buying an experience with their dogs," she added.
Helen Barber started her dog wedding chauffeur company Together Furever Weddings in Weston-super-Mare, North Somerset, with her husband in 2022.
"There's a lot more acceptance now that people will want to be with their dog at their weddings," she said.
"Year-on-year we've seen the demand for our service and dog friendly venues increase. We've done just over 70 weddings this year already.
"There are now hundreds of chaperone services when there only used to be a handful."
She went on to attribute the rise in people spending money on their pets to social media.
"People see things online and realise it's an option to have their pets with them at their wedding or other family events," Barber added.
Rachel Morgan, from The Amberley Inn in Stroud, serves doggy roasts which have proved very popular.
She believes the "shift in attitudes" started after the pandemic.
"People spent more time with their dogs. They offered a degree of comfort in really difficult time and from then their relationship with their dogs has changed," she said.
"They want to be spending more time with them and if they're able to take their dogs out with them in the day they're more likely to go out and dine in that restaurant that caters for them.
Morgan explained their doggy roast includes meat vegetables and specially formulated doggy gravy.
"We're now organising a Christmas dog event called Santa Paws where we'll sell Puppuccinos, the dogs can go for a walk together and have a roast after when Santa will share presents," she added.
Wiltshire-based family-run dog walking service Potters Tails run by Shelly Potter and Casey Gumm believe social media has been the driving influence behind wanting to do more things with and for their dogs.
"Social media shows people what's out there, like what we do, which means there's now a huge demand out there," Potter said.
"Some of our dogs were bought during Covid. There's so many more dog lovers now.
"People treat them very well. You get things like dog birthday parties now and dog cafes."

title: Bristol Drugs Project: Changing lives for 40 years
text:
Charity celebrates 40 years as 'a beacon of hope'
It took ex-punk metal drummer Alison 25 years to find her love of music again while managing her drug use.
She was supported by the Bristol Drugs Project (BDP), established in 1986, which stuck by her through the good and bad days.
The charity has since reached 40 years of service and within that time started an arts-based recovery scheme called Creative Communities.
This is where Alison said she found herself again through connection and confidence - something she thought she had lost in the 1990s when things took a turn for the worse.
At the time, Alison had started smoking heroin with a partner from her band Corpus Vile and after many years reached out to BDP which helped her into a rehabilitation programme and has since become a rock in her life.
She said in the beginning she wanted the charity to "instantly cure" her, but soon realised she had to put in a lot of work.
When she got out of rehab, Alison started doing more creative things and took part in art classes which eventually led to her joining the charity's Bristol Recovery Orchestra.
"It was another step to get back into my music again. It's taken almost 30 years to get here," she said.
"It's not my style - orchestra to punk music - but I like it.
"It's an escape away from things for a while and the feeling of playing is just brilliant, it's so uplifting.
"I feel like me again. I've got freedom back, I've got myself back because the drugs just rob you of everything."
Alison said she feels "pride and privilege" to celebrate the organisation's 40th year.
"And getting behind the drums again - it just gives you goosebumps, it's great."
Delroy from Bristol, first sought help from BDP in his mid 20s.
"Having that creative and fun element to recovery has been huge for me. It was important to tap into that other part of me that was being stifled," he said.
"It allowed me to flourish."
Through BDP's Creative Communities programme he has been learning how to play the drums, write and perform poetry and take part in theatre and hip-hop groups - a life far removed from what he was living in his early 20s.
"Crack cocaine brought me to my knees," he said.
"I kept that a secret for around three years until I ran out of excuses. It was like hell," he said.
When he reached out, BDP helped him access a treatment centre, but he explained his journey was not "straightforward".
"It took many attempts, but at each relapse BDP was always there," Delroy said.
Now with support from BDP and a focus on performing he said he understands who he is again.
"The ability to express yourself though art is paramount to many addicts because they've spent to so many years suppressing themselves," he said.
"It holds up a beacon of light that says, 'anything is possible'."
'Like a rebirth'
Sophie Wilsdon, first started working with BDP 18 years ago as a student doing research, and now coordinates its Creative Communities projects.
She is also a musician and started the Recovery Orchestra as a way to channel what she knew through her passion.
"It's not like what I created was new - we had a music group - but what I did that was different was I created something that happened every week - our groups just perform and rehearse," she said.
Wilsdon said the music allowed people to heal without having to talk and "go into the darkness".
"For people new to performing on stage it's like a rebirth, it's amazing," she added.
"It's empowering."
To celebrate four decades of changing peoples lives through performance and art BDP will host a 40th anniversary event at St George's Hall on 3 November.

title: West Yorkshire mayor to meet airport bosses about parkway station
text:
Mayor to meet airport bosses about parkway station
West Yorkshire Mayor Tracy Brabin is to meet Leeds Bradford Airport bosses about a proposed parkway station.
Councillors from West Yorkshire have voted to move ahead with plans for a railway station that would serve the airport, with the leader of Bradford Council saying he was "delighted" to support the scheme.
West Yorkshire Combined Authority (WYCA) was given an update on the plans at a meeting on Thursday, with Brabin saying she was "determined" to make sure the proposed station was finally approved.
Brabin also said she would speak to airport bosses at an event in the coming days, where they would "set out the vision to get this delivered".
Plans for a railway station to serve the airport at Yeadon were first mooted over a decade ago, and an outline business case approved in 2020, but there has been little progress since.
'Game-changer'
A report to WYCA members said a parkway station could be built on the Harrogate line, between Horsforth Station and Bramhope Tunnel, and passengers would then travel to the airport by a shuttle bus.
The station was estimated to cost about £65m to build.
The report said the lack of a nearby station was a "drag" on the growth of the airport, and a new facility would dramatically increase the number of passengers able to arrive at Leeds Bradford Airport by public transport.
Introducing the report, Brabin said: "This station has long been an ambition for our region.
"I know some have been frustrated by the pace of progress, but this development will be a game-changer.
"I am determined to make sure this project finally gets approved."
The station parkway was also expected to help develop a North West Leeds Employment Hub, an 89 acre (36 hectare) strategic employment site adjacent to Leeds Bradford Airport, and allow the development of more homes in the area, members were told.
They were asked to "endorse continued development of the Leeds Bradford Airport Parkway project, including the completion of a full business case; completion of necessary ground investigation work at the site; identification of a workable timetable for Leeds Bradford Airport Parkway, including definition of any network enhancements required, and identification of a funding strategy for the station."
'Huge impact'
Leeds Labour councillor Salma Arif said: "I really welcome this and what it will mean for jobs in the area."
Stephen Place, Reform leader of Bradford Council, said: "I'm delighted to be supporting this. Leeds Bradford Airport is a vital hub for the region.
"I do believe a shuttle bus from Apperley Bridge Station would alleviate a lot of transport issues for passengers in the area."
Alan Lamb, a Conservative Leeds councillor, added: "This is absolutely critical for Leeds and the wider region. It is a tricky project to deliver because of the topography."
According to the Local Democracy Reporting service, he said it would also unlock jobs and housing land, saying it would have a "huge impact" beyond just transport to and from the airport.
Lamb also asked officers if they could give any timing for the works, adding: "Can you tell us when people will be able to start getting trains?"
Simon Pope, transport capital programme director, said it would take "at least two years to get to the point where we have a full business case".
That would involve investigations into what level of rail service the new station would be able to provide, Pope added.
Members voted to push ahead with the plans.
The West and North Yorkshire Chamber of Commerce has also thrown its weight behind the plans.
Mark Casci, its head of policy and representation, said the chamber was "massively supportive of any efforts" to build the parkway station.
"We would wish to see a positive and speedy decision made regarding its approval," he said.
"The leadership team at Leeds Bradford Airport is very ambitious and its recent refurbishment is delivering a much better passenger experience.
"But the key next step is connectivity and new routes, something the station will enable."

title: Brassed Off at 30: 'Community spirit has kept Grimethorpe going'
text:
Brassed Off at 30: 'Community spirit has kept this village going'
With its story of pit closures and brass bands wrapped up in pathos and northern humour, the 1996 film Brassed Off thrust the village of Grimethorpe and the nearby town of Barnsley into the international spotlight - and exactly 30 years after its release, its lasting impact can still be felt in the area.
Grimethorpe Colliery shut in 1993 and just three years later the village where it had stood at its heart was immortalised in Brassed Off as Grimley.
The Bafta-nominated film, starring Ewan McGregor, Sue Johnston, Pete Postlethwaite and Tara Fitzgerald, portrayed the fictional village's struggle to survive against the backdrop of mine closures across South Yorkshire.
"Grimethorpe was the most industrialised village in Europe at that time and when the colliery closed, it became the poorest village in Europe," explains Johnny Wood.
"Brassed Off tells you about the devastation it caused within the community."
If there is one person who knows about the impact of pit closures on the area, it is Johnny.
He worked at Grimethorpe Colliery and now, at the age of 68, he is chairman of Grimethorpe Miners Memorial and Reunion, an annual gathering of 300 ex-miners from the former pit.
As he stands by a marble memorial outside St Luke's Church in Grimethorpe, an unexpected cloudburst interrupts the sunny autumn day and briefly lashes it with rain. It is perhaps symbolic of a community which has weathered plenty of storms.
Over the road is Grimethorpe Working Men's Club where a large glass cabinet displays a National Union of Mineworkers flag and a framed poster listing all the pits which closed down in the 1980s and 90s.
"I would suggest everybody watches that film because it is historical and educational," Johnny says.
"This community wouldn't have existed without the collieries, and we have a memorial with 163 miners' names who paid the ultimate price."
Johnny recounts that two of the film's stars, Postlethwaite and Johnston, were both politically active, which endeared them to the local community during the filming of Brassed Off.
"Sue Johnston actually campaigned for Grimethorpe Colliery to stay open, so she had respect from people here without a shadow of a doubt," he recounts.
"When the media came, all they asked about was the band. There was no mention of what was going to happen with the 2,000 jobs since the colliery closed.
"I think Pete probably picked up on that when he was interviewed as he had sat and spoken with miners.
"His speech in the film, which I understand he wrote himself, was about the power of what community is all about."
"People come first," says Johnny.
"We had a world famous band, which the village is very proud of, but it wasn't about trophies. That community spirit, which in my opinion is second to none, has kept this village going."
'Brilliant people'
Johnny gives a tour of locations featured in the film. Some, like The Grimethorpe Hotel, which on screen was The Collier's Arms, have been demolished, and it is difficult to even reach the former colliery, which is now an industrial estate.
But while buildings may have come and gone, Johnny says community spirit is still strong.
Standing outside a baker's shop, which doubled up as a fish and chip shop in the film, and looking at the empty plot where the Grimethorpe Hotel once stood, he says: "We used to have six pubs, sports teams and a welfare club that belonged to the men that worked at the colliery.
"The strength of people built this community back up. They put pressure on ministers, MPs and councillors - and good on them for doing that.
"If there's somebody having problems, people are there, they are behind you. They are second to none, brilliant people."
Seven miles away in Barnsley town centre, Steve Fothergill sits in an office overlooking the town hall.
Labour ruled Barnsley Council for 50 years before Reform UK took control in the May local elections.
Steve is lead author of the State of the Coalfields 2024 report and an expert on former mining communities.
Brassed Off portrayed the trauma of the job losses which affected the area, and Steve has spent his career studying the after-effects of an entire industry disappearing.
"What everybody expected when the pits closed is that unemployment would go through the roof," he says.
"It didn't, or at least recorded official unemployment didn't, because a lot of the miners dropped completely out of the labour market.
"Some of them took early retirement, but a great many went on to what was then incapacity benefit with their health problems.
"The redundant miners could just about muddle through if they were in their 50s, picking up their pension early and with some benefits.
"But it created a problem for the generation behind them because there weren't any jobs for the younger people coming through."
Steve says that became "the problem we have all had to tackle since the pits shut".
"The challenge over the last 30 years has been to plug that gap in the labour market."
Steve remembers a conversation with then Deputy Prime Minister John Prescott, who was also secretary of state for environment, transport and the regions.
"Brassed Off was never intended to be a political tool, but it did have a big impact because John Prescott went to see it," Steve says.
"He came out of the cinema thinking, oh my goodness, somebody should do something about the problem in these former coalfields. Then he realised that somebody was him."
Steve says Prescott's realisation "led to all sorts of good things happening".
"He established the Coalfields Taskforce, which I was involved in, and that led to a massive expansion in the programme of colliery site reclamation which allowed new businesses to come on to some of those former colliery sites.
"He also established the Coalfields Regeneration Trust, which continues to do good work in the former mining areas.
"So, Brassed Off has had a really important long-term and positive impact."
According to the State of the Coalfields report, former mining areas have "moved on" since the job losses of the 1980s and 90s, and there has been substantial progress in new job creation.
But it adds that "in an era of international migration, the full benefits of job growth have not always filtered through to local residents".
"Conventional mass unemployment may have faded into the past, but worklessness and dependency on welfare benefits remains widespread," the report states.
Steve has the same pit closure poster on his wall as the one in Grimethorpe Working Men's Club.
"Even though we've grown jobs in the former coalfields, there are still very substantial problems," Steve explains.
"We have large numbers of people still out of work on benefits, we have poor health, and wages are not good in some of these new jobs.
"You have a situation where there has been job growth, but there still is quite a high proportion of people out of work on benefits and a lot of people getting by on low incomes.
"Really, the coalfields are still lagging quite a way behind the more prosperous parts of the country."
Brassed Off and pit closures may be a generation or more away now, but young people in Barnsley and the surrounding communities still have a strong connection with brass bands.
Alex Francis, music service manager for Barnsley Council and conductor of the Barnsley Metropolitan Band based at the Civic theatre, says miners once played for both relaxation and entertainment.
"It was something deep-rooted and it brought people together like a sport. There was real pride in the colliery that you were part of," Alex says.
"Brass bands are a strange musical genre in that they compete against each other. So, bringing trophies back to your village in the name of the band was something of great pride.
"Once the pits closed, some bands were sadly lost, but many bands survived and there is still a really active network of brass bands to the present day.
"Some of them are under different names instead of their original colliery names, but there are a lot of bands out there still making music and bringing people together."
Yorkshire is certainly synonymous with brass bands, many of them award-winning, and Brassed Off cemented that image in people's minds.
"A big part of our past is the music people played years ago such as hymn tunes and marches - and, of course, music from Brassed Off as it's famous," says Alex.
"We still perform that for audiences, and even if people don't really know much about brass bands, they will recognise the soundtrack from the film.
"We do a big outdoor performance called Brassed On every summer and when people hear William Tell or the March of the Cobblers, it really pulls them together. It's a special moment."
"A lot of grandparents have played brass music," Alex adds.
"It's good for the soul, as they say, so there's a real interest and support from families and they really want their children to carry on that tradition.
"We're really proud of how many young people are performing with brass bands and we really want to keep that tradition going.
"We have a whole programme of music in schools and instruments like the cornet, the tenor horn and the euphonium are really popular in our area.
"Some of these instruments people wouldn't have known about unless they watched Brassed Off. They certainly know what a flugelhorn is from that film."

title: Brighton's once grand West Pier and it's battle with nature
text:
Brighton's West Pier and its battle with nature
When Anthea Secker learned another section of Brighton's West Pier had collapsed into the sea, she said she was devastated.
The West Pier has become one of the city's most recognisable landmarks - the rugged lines of its metal skeleton have become a familiar part of the city's skyline, alongside the seagull and the Royal Pavilion.
Now, as more storm damage weakens its structure and sends more pieces underwater, residents are reflecting on what the pier means to Brighton and what its future may hold.
"You have to experience it to know how much it means to people. It's like a relationship, and I feel incredibly bonded to it," Secker said.
She added: "The pier has been just such a big part of my life in Brighton. It was a bit of a congregation of youth when I was younger, and now it's part of that view and in our day-to-day lives.
"Some people feel that it should just disappear now, but it's part of this environment that we live in."
Golden age for piers
As with the construction of many of Brighton's landmarks, the building of the West Pier marked the city's status as a premier getaway for the Victorian elite.
Designed by engineer Eugenius Birch, the 1,115ft (340m) structure opened in October 1866.
It was later expanded to include a 1,400 seat concert hall, which was also used as a 1,000 seat theatre.
The pier was built just a few years after the opening of The Grand Hotel, at a time when seaside piers were proving popular to build.
It became Brighton's second pier after the Chain Pier, which had opened in 1823.
The Chain Pier stood for over 70 years and was later replaced by the Palace Pier, which opened in 1899.
According to the West Pier Trust, the pier had its heyday on 11 July, 1919, less than a year after the end of war, when more than two million people visited it in a single day.
But the pier was hit by war again in 1939, when security around World War Two saw it close.
Burning and falling away
The pier saw some popularity after the war, including its use in Richard Attenborough's Oh, What A Lovely War! in 1969.
But it never regained its earlier popularity and closed over safety concerns in 1975.
The structure then stood largely unused for decades while multi-million pound restoration schemes were considered.
Age 21, Secker was part of a small group who were able to take a tour of the West Pier in 1997, while restoration attempts were underway.
Armed with a Kodak camera and an excitement to see what very few people had seen up to that point, she and her family were part of the small group able to see what the pier had become before its destruction.
"It was a great day - it felt monumental," she said.
"No one had been on it for a very long time, and you knew that if they were going to restore it, it would be different from then on."
However, two fires, in March and May 2003, decimated what was left of the structure, and it was declared beyond repair in July 2004.
The cause of the fires was never established.
Described at the time as "definitely of doubtful origin", there was unproven speculation in the years since that the fires were arson.
Fire inspectors could not access the pier due to the collapse of a walkway the previous year.
No-one has ever been prosecuted in connection with the blazes.
Since then, more damage has been done through storms, waves and the elements.
In 2004, the middle section of the pier collapsed.
Storm Claudio in November 2022 caused further damage.
The latest collapse, following Storm Austen, has altered the shape of the structure once again.
'Eventually disappear'
Questions about the pier's future have been raised many times over the years.
The Brighton i360 was put forward on the same site as a "vertical pier" to replace it.
The attraction has experienced mixed fortunes since opening in 2016.
Fred Gray, a professor at the University of Sussex and honorary historian for the West Pier Trust, said people should accept the structure will one day fall into the sea, and enjoy it for what it now is.
"People should accept it is changing. It may take decades but it will eventually disappear under the waves", he said.
Gray added: "Perhaps quite rightly there would be protests if they tried to clear it.
"I think people should enjoy it as it is now. They should see it as a battle between nature and society."
Gray hopes someone could rebuild a West Pier eventually, or something which celebrates the seaside structure, though he accepts that wreckage under the sea could present a challenge to any future projects.
For now, the West Pier will continue to fall away, and its changing structure will continue to be a focal point for visitors and residents alike.

title: Stories to make you smile from across Yorkshire 01/11/26
text:
Stories to make you smile from across Yorkshire
Every week in Yorkshire, we cover uplifting and feel-good stories across our region - and we like to shout about them.
This week, among other stories, we are featuring a daring dog rescue, a pool team's £10,000 victory and a portrait of a chip shop owner which boasts a surprising royal connection.
Family celebrates three generations in NHS
When Dorothy Henry arrived in the UK from Grenada in the 1950s, she started a dynasty - three generations of women who dedicated their lives to NHS patients.
She came to Huddersfield, with her daughter Jacquelin, and picked up a job at a care home.
Twenty years later, Jacquelin joined the NHS as a nurse at Huddersfield Royal Infirmary.
Today, Dorothy's grandchild, Emma Fleary, has carried on the tradition by working in midwifery at Bradford Royal Infirmary.
Their shared career path brought them all together in way "I never sort of expected", Fleary said
She added that she hoped the family legacy would continue through her 12-year-old son, Amos, who she was encouraging to pursue a career in physiotherapy.
Dog rescued after 30ft fall during storm
A dog which fell 30ft (9m) down a hole during Storm Boelo is "back to normal" after being saved by mountain rescuers, its owner has said.
Freddie, a Cocker Spaniel, had been out walking with owner Tom Hollingworth near The Stang, a moorland ridge at the border of North Yorkshire and County Durham.
The black and tan dog became stranded in a pothole, but thanks to the efforts of volunteer-run rescue team Swaledale MRT, was safely brought back to the surface.
Freddie was largely unharmed and was now "happier than ever, just back to normal", Hollingwood said, adding: "Without [the rescuers], Freddie would still be stuck."
Chippy owner honoured by royal artist
A Barnsley fish and chip shop owner has been immortalised by a royal portrait artist to celebrate the impact independent businesses have in their communities.
Pindy Kaur has been painted by artist Nicky Philipps, who has previously painted members of the Royal Family, including the late Queen Elizabeth II.
Kaur runs Monk Bretton's Ocean Fish Bar, and has been serving fish and chips since the early 2000s.
"To have me painted by someone that's painted the Queen, it's just amazing," she said.
The portrait is part of the Local Royalty campaign by Coca-Cola GB, and will go on show from 28 October at the Saatchi Gallery in London.
Volunteers restore vintage buses
As East Yorkshire Motor Services marks 100 years, a group of enthusiasts are helping to preserve its history by restoring a fleet of the company's vintage buses.
Hobbyists at Hull Bus Restorers are currently working on five heritage vehicles, including a bus that has a curved roof, designed to fit through Beverley's North Bar.
Volunteer and former bus driver Phil Russell has been working with engines for nearly five decades, and said restoring the fleet to its former glory gave the group "a real sense of achievement".
"I just enjoy it - it's our man cave," he joked, adding: "I don't get fed up of it. I'll have the odd days, but most of the time no, because we get an end result."
Pub pool team secures £10,000 win
A pool team from Keighley has won the Ultimate Pool League final, beating 200 teams to the £10,000 prize.
Breaking Bad, from Pilky's Cue Sports Club and Bar, beat Leicester's Rail Huggers 25-19 in the final at the Cue Club, in Leicester, just four months after they were formed.
The team consists of captain Dylan Mitchell and players Summer Ibbs, Logan Robinson, Luca and Sergio Dellucci, Jordan Kellett, Stephen Almond and Ian Taylor.
"It was an unbelievable night for the club and the team," said Pilky's manager Ryan Stewart, who said the team had "outdone all our expectations".
"Last night they were all phenomenal. All season they've been brilliant," he said.
