title: Could Margaret Clitherow’s execution have shaped Guy Fawkes?
text:
Did a woman's brutal death influence Guy Fawkes?
The "brutal" execution of a Catholic martyr in York may have helped shape the religious fervour of Guy Fawkes, a historian has claimed.
Margaret Clitherow was crushed to death in 1586 after refusing to enter a plea to charges she had harboured Catholic priests, a serious offence in Elizabethan England.
Almost two decades later, Fawkes and his co-conspirators would be caught attempting to blow up Parliament and destroy England's political elite including King James VI and I.
Dr Hannah Thomas, from York's Bar Convent museum, said a young Fawkes and fellow conspirators may have witnessed Clitherow's death.
She was crushed beneath heavy weights, with a sharp stone placed under her back.
"Even by the standards of that time, this is said to have been a really brutal execution," she said.
"This is a time where people go to executions for sport. They go to watch public hangings like we would go to a football match."
Clitherow's impact on Fawkes is explored in Gunpowder and Treason: The Real Guy Fawkes, available on BBC Sounds.
Under Queen Elizabeth I, Catholics faced penalties for refusing to attend Church of England services, while priests who continued to practice Catholicism risked arrest, torture and death.
Religious differences were seen as a threat to the Crown and Dr Thomas said the government feared Catholics' loyalties were divided between the Queen and the Pope.
"They're thinking 'does that mean they've got loyalty to an overseas crown'," she said.
Fellow historian Gillian Waters, from Leeds, believes 1586 would have been a critical year for Fawkes, who was about 16 when Clitherow died.
He was born and raised in York, educated at St Peter's School in the city, and inherited an estate in the Clifton area from his father.
"Well certainly Guy Fawkes would have been aware of Margaret Clitherow because she is executed on Good Friday," she said.
Another Catholic, Jesuit priest Francis Ingleby, was also hanged at York's Knavesmire in that year.
He had been a great-uncle of Christopher Wright, a schoolfriend of Fawkes along with his brother John.
They had a further connection to persecution as their mother had been imprisoned at times for her Catholic faith.
Both brothers would participate in the Gunpowder Plot and like Fawkes, paid for it with their lives.
Dr Thomas said Clitherow's death, among other forms of persecution, could have affected many young people who saw people being punished for protecting their religious communities.
"They would have had a lot of empathy and sympathy and perhaps thinking that could have been our mother," she said.
Clitherow's own decision not to enter a plea was largely to ensure her children and friends did not have to testify against her or face torture.
Jeremy Walker, headteacher at Fawkes's former school, St Peter's, said the city would have helped shape "his personality, his outlook on life and his beliefs".
The Gunpowder Plot involved the conspirators putting 36 barrels of gunpowder in a cellar underneath Parliament.
But they were betrayed by one of the plotters sending a letter to a member of Parliament.
The King's men searched the cellars and found and arrested Fawkes, who would face torture and execution himself.
His childhood friends, the Wright brothers, would flee but were eventually killed in a shoot-out with the King's men.
As to Margaret Clitherow, after her death, her body was thrown onto a rubbish heap because she was considered a traitor.
Dr Thomas said Catholic friends later recovered and buried her body secretly, keeping her hand as a relic, which remains preserved in a glass case at the Bar Convent.
More than four centuries later, it remains a physical reminder of the religious persecution that marked Fawkes's youth.
The convent, founded in secret in the 18th Century, is the oldest in England, and is a testament to the persecution of those who adhered to Catholicism in Protestant England.
Clitherow would be regarded as a martyr to the Catholic faith and was ultimately canonised in 1970 by Pope Paul VI.

title: Blind veteran pays tribute to fallen comrades at Alrewas
text:
Blind veteran pays tribute to fallen comrades
A former Welsh Guardsman whose military career ended when he was blinded in an assault is among thousands set to honour the lives of those lost in war.
Clive Jones, from Market Drayton, laid a tribute at the Royal British Legion's Field of Remembrance in Staffordshire at the opening of its annual display.
Around 30,000 handwritten messages are expected to be planted this year at the National Remembrance Gardens in Alrewas.
"It's phenomenal. It's emotional. It always pulls at the heartstrings for me," said Jones, a Royal British Legion ambassador.
The opening service on Friday concluded with prayers and a moment of reflection for those who have died and the families they left behind.
While many people associate the poppy with the First and Second World Wars, the tributes at Alrewas commemorate service and sacrifice across generations, including more recent conflicts such as the Gulf War and operations in Afghanistan.
Jones' army career was cut short when he suffered injuries that left him blind on his 26th birthday.
He said: "Waking up out of the coma, I was in total blackness. It was my wife and children that I worried for."
He said support from the Royal British Legion, including the Battle Back recovery programme at Lilleshall, helped him adapt to civilian life.
"They took me under their wing and looked after me fantastically well. It opened my eyes, so to speak.
"When I lay a tribute, I think about those I've lost from my regiment."
The Field of Remembrance has been a fixture at the National Remembrance Gardens since 2016 and raises funds for the Royal British Legion's annual Poppy Appeal.
This year's appeal, which launched on 22 October, highlights the sacrifices made by Armed Forces families and the challenges they face while supporting loved ones in service.
Each tribute carries a personal message of remembrance for a loved one, including those who lost their life serving their country.
Founded in 1921, the appeal aims to raise more than £50 million to help fund support services for serving personnel, veterans and their families.
Speaking at the event, Royal British Legion representatives reminded visitors that "when one service person serves, their whole family serves".
The field will remain open to visitors until 15 November.

title: How an introvert became a Shropshire storyteller
text:
How an introvert became a storyteller
Standing before an audience and holding their attention for an hour or more might sound like a nightmare to many introverts.
For Danielle Free, it once was.
The storyteller, who lives in rural Shropshire, now performs around the country, bringing to life tales of history, folklore and landscape in venues ranging from libraries and museums to ancient sites and windswept hillsides.
Many of her stories focus on historical women, as well as the landscapes and places connected to their lives.
"It's really nice to be right in the centre of where stories are," she said. "And to be able to just take them for a walk."
Yet not long ago, Free thought public speaking simply was not for her.
"People who know me laugh every time I tell them that I stand up in front of an audience and present or tell them a story," she said.
"It wasn't that long ago that I was having anxiety attacks and panic attacks about standing up and having to give presentations in front of people at work or when I was at university.
"I thought public speaking and telling stories is not something that's in me because it's too overwhelming."
Her route into storytelling was an unexpected one.
After completing a master's degree in Celtic Studies, she became fascinated by the bardic tradition and the centuries-old art of passing stories from one generation to another through the spoken word.
Then, during the Covid lockdowns, she signed up for an introductory storytelling course over Zoom.
The experience changed everything.
Free discovered telling a story felt completely different from giving a presentation.
"When you've got something that you're so passionate about and when you have something that you desperately want to tell, when you've got a good story, that seems to override some of the anxiety," she said.
"The anxiety shows up in a different way because I want to do the story justice. I want to tell it well."
She says she only tells stories she genuinely loves, and believes that passion helps bring them to life for audiences.
Today she can hold audiences' attention for an hour or more at a time, often without notes or a script.
People frequently ask how she remembers so much material.
The answer lies not in memorising every word, but in learning what she calls the "bones" of a story.
Rather than reciting a script, she builds a narrative around key scenes and images.
"I imagine it like a film in my head," she explained.
"If I were to ask you what your favourite film was, you could tell me what happens.
"It's being so in that world of the story that I can see it so clearly."
The approach means each performance is slightly different, shaped by the audience and the moment while still following the same path.
Beauty in silence
Free practices constantly, whether she is driving, walking or doing household chores.
"Story is always there," she said. "It's always on my mind and on my tongue."
These days, the silence of an attentive audience no longer feels intimidating.
In fact, it has become one of her favourite sounds.
"The silence that you get when people are completely enraptured by a story," she said, "is actually one of the most beautiful sounds that you can get."
For someone who once dreaded speaking in front of a room full of people, it marks a remarkable transformation.
But one thing, Free insists, has never changed.
"I am an introvert at heart," she said.

Lincoln's annual Remembrance Service will be held on Armistice Day from now on instead of Remembrance Sunday.

Kate Fenn, the council's civic and international partnerships manager, said: "We welcome residents, visitors, businesses and organisations to join us in paying tribute to all those who have served, and continue to serve, in the armed forces."

title: Renovation to begin for historical public toilets in Shere
text:
Renovation to begin for historical public toilets
A listed building which currently serves as a Surrey village's public toilets is to be renovated after receiving a £30,000 government grant.
The Grade II-listed Old Fire Station in Shere was built in 1885 for the Shere and Albury volunteer fire brigade.
It was converted into toilets in 1977, but the facilities are "showing their age and are too small for the number of visitors", according to Surrey Hills National Landscape.
A spokesperson said: "The planned improvements will provide better facilities while retaining the character of a building that forms part of Shere's distinctive heritage."
The statement added: "Looking after the Surrey Hills means caring for its villages and communities, as well as its landscapes and wildlife.
"Shere's historic buildings and its village character make it a much-loved destination.
"Although modest in scale, this project demonstrates how practical improvements can help support rural communities, care for historic places and enable people to enjoy the Surrey Hills responsibly."
The toilets will be closed temporarily for refurbishment from 2 November for approximately 10 weeks, according to Shere Parish Council.

title: West in Pictures: Tiger cubs, AI bat hunt and pumpkin time
text:
In Pictures: Tiger cubs, AI bat hunt and pumpkins
Thousands have been picking their perfect pumpkins across the West this week for Halloween.
Women have been lining up in their high visibility clothes and glow sticks to take to the streets, creating safe spaces for women to run as the evenings get darker.
Tiger cubs have been playing at Longleat, AI has been used to help identify bats and life on the home front has been recognised through a poppy display.
Here is our weekly round-up of photographs from across the region.
Wiltshire
Farming friends: Heddington and Stockley's annual poppy display tells the story of wartime life on the home front, with new silhouettes of the Women's Land Army, the "Land Girls".
The animals show the vital role farming played while so many men were away serving.
Fiesty felines: Two rare Amur tiger cubs have taken their first steps at Longleat Safari Park near Warminster.
The 14 week-old cubs, named Anya and Ginny, are being gradually introduced and will stay at the park until they are eventually re-homed as part of the European Breeding Programme.
Stunning reflections: Striking autumn colours were on display at Stourhead near Mere this week, with the bright reds and oranges offering a distinctive Halloween feel.
The National Trust Property is normally inundated with visitors during the autumn months due to its dramatic scenery.
Early bird: Photographer Gary Chalker captured this photo of a watchful Red Kite in a Swindon field on the look-out for its breakfast.
Super stars: Children in care were recognised for their accomplishments at a special Star Awards ceremony held in Trowbridge.
Young people were recognised for overcoming challenges and achieving educational milestones, while also performing and showcasing their skills on stage.
Somerset
Bat scan: Some of the rarest species of bat have been popping up in Somerset as part of Britain's largest ever woodland survey of bats, assisted by AI.
Some of Britain's rarest and most threatened bats, including the red-listed Barbastelle, have been recorded in the south-west of England, including Somerset, Devon, Cornwall and Dorset.
Stormy skies: The old clapper bridge at Tarr Steps, in Exmoor, was washed away during heavy rain.
Water levels on Exmoor rose substantially, with a lot of large tree branches washing down the river and becoming trapped.
Gloucestershire
Pumpkin power: Over Farm, in Gloucestershire, has been holding its annual pumpkin festival, where thousands go to pick their round orange treat every Halloween.
Pumpkins were first introduced to the farm in the 1990s and the number of pumpkin visitors has grown every year, with about 35,000 pumpkin picking last year.
Beetle Juice: One of the UK's rarest beetles has been spotted in two places in Gloucestershire.
The great silver water beetle, which is listed as near threatened, is usually found on the Somerset Levels and in the East of England, with recent sightings showing it is on the move.
Autumn colours: Autumn is a beautiful time of year with this rainbow of colours picked up in the village of Woodmancote.
Bristol
Garden joy: Wen Li, from Bristol, spent eight days in Southmead Hospital's Intensive Care Unit (ICU) after developing a rare, life-threatening condition and said visiting the hospital's ICU garden played an "essential part" in her recovery.
The garden is funded through charitable support.
Run ready: Bristol-based running group This Woman Runs is encouraging women to start their exercising journey and provide a safe space to bring women together.
The group headed out wearing head torches, glow sticks and high visibility clothing as part of the Let's lift the Curfew campaign which supports women running after dark.

title: Energy bills help doesn't go far enough, say families
text:
Energy bills help 'doesn't go far enough'
Households in the West Midlands said they want to see the government revisit energy bills in the wake of the Budget - amid concerns the help being offered won't go far enough.
Chancellor John Healey announced a £100 'household energy payment', and a future plan to remove gas standing charges, as part of a wider package to address the cost of living.
Families in the region told the BBC they were "grateful" for the assistance, but were concerned about their finances over the winter.
Kelly Birkett, a personal accountant from Redditch, said: "The £100 is good, but it's not great. It just gets absorbed into everything else families have to pay for, just to get by."
Birkett, a married mum-of-two, said her family was already considering what to cut back on in the wake of the Budget.
"I know I sound a little but ungrateful for the £100, and I don't want to be. I'm certainly not ungrateful," she said.
"But in reality we're no better off. With the temperatures dropping we know the heating will have to be on, the children can't be cold.
"We'll dig deep to make sure we're a little more conservative when it comes to the heating, but for sure it's something most families will be worried about (the winter.)"
Mark Sumner, a coach driver from Alcester, said him and his wife sold their previous home partly to clear old debts that had accrued from bills including energy.
He told the BBC they had fallen into "energy debt" and were concerned about this coming winter.
"We know our bill will go up again, you're just dreading it each time the increase comes around, as to how much it will be," he said.
"I very rarely take our children out for anything to eat anymore, and we're very careful about what we spend at the shops.
"What the government has announced is helpful. I don't want to be ungrateful so I will say it's helpful for us, but it probably only covers one month (of bills).
"So it's a slight help, but it's not enough."
'We are being fair to families'
The government said "millions of families" would benefit from the measures announced in the Budget, including freezing fuel duty, the 3.9% minimum wage increase and scrapping plans to reduce the £20,000 tax-free limit on ISAs.
Chancellor John Healey said the energy announcement was "just a small part" of what the government was doing to help families.
"Conflict in the Middle East and Europe is hitting families here at home through higher everyday costs," he said.
"We can't control global events, but we can act where we can make a difference."
There is no definitive date for scrapping the standing charge on gas, but the Treasury has committed to doing it either in 2027 or "as soon as possible after".
The VAT cut on electricity bills, which was due to end in April, will be extended to July next year.

title: Man struck off for doing nursing shifts at Prospect Park Hospital
text:
Unqualified man struck off for doing nursing shifts
A man who completed 10 shifts at a mental health hospital that he was not qualified to do has been struck off the nursing register.
Nana Kwasi Asabre got a job through an agency to work the shifts as a registered nurse in June 2022 and July 2022 at Prospect Park Hospital in Reading.
He was also found to have given medication to a patient without a nurse present and then left a medication cabinet unlocked during a shift on 24 July 2022.
Asabre told a Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC) panel that he "deeply regretted" his actions and "the concern they have caused to the profession [and] the public".
He said he had worked the shifts "under the belief that the roles assigned" by the Your World healthcare agency "were appropriate to my level of experience and training".
The NMC said he had been dishonest because he knew he was not qualified to complete the shifts "but did so anyway".
It said he had "sought to deflect blame onto the agency" for booking him onto shifts and that his conduct "could have put patients at significant risk of harm".
The NMC said Asabre worked for the Oxford Health NHS Trust as a healthcare assistant between September 2021 and July 2022.
He was qualified to work as a nursing associate.
The agency was contacted to comment.

title: Kent doctor wins award for improving neonatal jaundice care
text:
Doctor wins award for neonatal jaundice programme
An NHS consultant has won a national award for her work improving the recognition, assessment and care of neonatal jaundice in babies with darker skin tones.
Dr Helen Gbinigie, who works at Medway Maritime Hospital in Gillingham, Kent, has been named inclusive leader of the year at the BAME Health and Care Awards.
She was nominated for her Jaundice in Darker Skin Tone Babies Programme, which "tackles inequalities in the care of babies with neonatal jaundice and helps ensure fairer care for all newborns", the hospital said.
Gbinigie said: "Creating long-term change requires joint working, compassion and a shared commitment to equity."
She added: "I hope this award shines a light on the importance of building inclusive cultures and driving meaningful change for both our workforce and the communities we serve."
Jaundice is a common condition in newborns which presents as yellowing of the skin in babies with paler skin tones.
It is easily treatable if detected early, but it can appear differently in babies with darker skin tones, making it harder to detect and increasing the risk of delayed diagnosis and treatment.
The Jaundice in Darker Skin Tone Babies Programme has trained over 1,200 healthcare professionals across more than 80 NHS organisations across the UK.
The judges said: "This leader translated a clearly identified health inequality into sustained national change in neonatal care."

title: Cotswold Wildlife Park rhinos celebrate first birthday
text:
Rhino siblings celebrate first birthday with cake
Two rhino calves have celebrated their first birthday with cakes made of pellets, carrots and salad leaves.
Siblings Markus and Mo were born at Cotswold Wildlife Park, near Burford, last year.
The pair weighed about 70kg (11st) at birth, and now weigh about 500kg (78st) each. Their arrival took the number of rhinos at the park to nine, the most in its 56-year history.
White rhinos were close to extinction in the early 1900s, with fewer than 50 thought to remain in Africa. They are now the most numerous of the five rhino species, but the park says conservation remains vital.

title: Hundreds fill Diwali food hampers in Birmingham to bring hope
text:
Diwali hampers to bring hope to families in need
Hundreds of volunteers have packed food parcels to distribute to people across Birmingham struggling with the rising cost of living.
About 300 people turned up to the Diwali Basket Brigade event at the RSRS Centre in Hockley, which was organised by The Diwali Foundation.
It is the ninth time the charity has brought community volunteers from a variety of backgrounds together to make hampers in the build up to the religious festival.
Deepak Parekh, founder of the initiative, said: "[The] cost of living crisis hasn't gone away... but Diwali is a celebration of light over darkness, and this is our little way of bringing some light and some hope into the families that need it most."
The Diwali Foundation, who are based in Herefordshire, said that more than 12% of UK households are experiencing food poverty.
It works with about forty different food banks and charities to reach vulnerable households.
To date, the charity said it has provided around 23,470 food hampers to those in need.
Volunteer Clare Hannah said, while packing bags: "You're thinking about, 'oh I wonder what they're going to make with this'. And the fact that this is all that they've got, for some people."
Parcels were taken from Hockley to residents living in homes provided by Walsall Housing Group (whg).
Faye Shanahan from whg said: "It's really tough out there. Our customers are having a really hard time. The cost of living is not easing.
"Events like this today are really, really fantastic. It makes an absolutely fantastic difference to our customers."
Resident John Whiting, who turned 80 on Saturday, described his parcel as "unbelievable".
"There are a lot of people out there that've got nothing," he added.
"The food will be tremendous, thank you."
A London event was also held on Saturday, with similar events in Manchester and Leicester planned for Sunday.
Organisers have set a target of providing 6,000 food hampers this year, which would top a 2025 record when more than 80,000 meals were provided.

title: Thermal imaging cameras on loan from Kent libraries
text:
Thermal imaging cameras on loan from libraries
Residents across Kent will be able to borrow thermal imaging cameras from libraries for free, helping them to identify where heat may be escaping from their homes.
The cameras can help spot possible gaps in insulation to support informed decisions about improving energy efficiency.
A total of 23 cameras will be available through selected libraries across the county as part of a 12-month trial.
Richard Palmer, Kent County Council cabinet member for communities, said: "We are giving people free access to a practical tool that can help them make informed decisions about improving comfort, reducing energy waste and increasing energy efficiency in their homes."
The scheme will help residents better understand how their homes perform and identify practical opportunities to improve comfort and reduce energy waste, a spokesperson said.
The cameras connect to a compatible smartphone or tablet and use thermal imaging technology to show heat patterns that are not visible to the naked eye.
Residents can use them to inspect areas around windows, doors, walls, roofs and radiators, helping to identify potential sources of heat loss.
Palmer added: "This new 12-month trial gives residents the opportunity to better understand how their homes use energy and identify areas where heat may be escaping."

title: Your guide to West Midlands' Remembrance Sunday events
text:
Your guide to West Midlands' Remembrance events
Thousands of people are set to attend Remembrance Sunday services across the West Midlands next weekend to honour Armed forces personnel.
Members of the public will join veterans and current servicemen and women at events marking the annual occasion on 8 November.
Many will involve a parade before wreaths are laid ahead of the nationwide two-minute silence at 11:00 GMT.
People are encouraged to check with their local councils for details of road closures and changes to public transport timetables. Below is a selection of events in the region.
Birmingham
Birmingham's annual Remembrance Day Service will take place on Colmore Row, opposite St Philip's Cathedral.
Attended by military veterans and representatives from the armed forces, the Salvation Army Band will begin playing at 10:15 with the Birmingham City Council Choir also performing.
Civic dignitaries will walk from the council house at 10:40 ahead of a two-minute silence at 11:00.
Shropshire
Shrewsbury Town is to host a remembrance match in tribute to service personnel when the League Two team meet Gillingham on 31 October.
The club honours armed forces past and present each year and wreaths will be laid on the pitch by officials and representatives from both clubs.
On 8 November, a civic procession will take place from Shrewsbury Castle at 10:30 to the War Memorial in The Quarry.
There are several events being held across Telford between 6 and 11 November with parades in the town centre, Newport and Wellington on Remembrance Sunday.
Coventry and Warwickshire
The Warwickshire town of Bedworth will retain the tradition of celebrating Armistice Day at the exact hour, day and month each year on the 11 November.
One of the largest and most famous parades in Britain, the service will be held at the War Memorial in Bedworth's Coventry Road Cemetery, following a parade through the town starting at 10:00.
In Coventry a parade will end in War Memorial Park at the Cenotaph near the Leamington Road entrance on Sunday 8 November.
A Remembrance Sunday service will also take place at the War Memorial in Euston Place in Leamington Spa at 10:50 after a parade by local organisations.
In Warwick, a procession leaves the the Court House at 09:50 and will stop at St Mary's Church before a two-minute silence at the War Memorial where wreaths will be laid.
Other events will be held in Kenilworth, Whitnash and Nuneaton.
Herefordshire and Worcestershire
Hereford Cathedral will be bathed in red during the Remembrance period, from Saturday 31 October with a service being held from 10:00 on 8 November.
A service of commemoration and wreath laying will take place at the War Memorial in Ross-on-Wye Remembrance Sunday followed by a service at St Mary's Church.
Hereford will mark the anniversary with a civic parade and service at the War Memorial in St Peter's Square.
In Worcester city centre there will be a parade of veterans, members of the armed forces, and cadets starting at 09:15, setting off from the Cornmarket.
At 09:40 the Mayor of Worcester will lead a civic procession from the Guildhall to the cathedral ahead of the service, which begins at 10:00.
The parade will then return past the city's Guildhall.
Staffordshire
A free service is being held at the Royal British Legion National Remembrance Gardens, formerly the National Memorial Arboretum, on 8 November.
The ceremony will take place at the base of the Armed Forces Memorial and be relayed on a large screen in Heroes' Square, organisers said.
A service will also be held on the Armed Forces Memorial to mark Armistice Day on Wednesday 11 November.
In Stafford, members of the armed forces will parade through the town centre on 8 November with an open air service starting at 10:50.
On Wednesday 11 November, prayers and a two-minute silence will be held in the Market Square also from 10:50.
In Stoke-on-Trent, a service will be held at Stoke Cenotaph between 10:15 and 11:30 along with other services held at:
- Stoke (Kingsway)
- Bucknall (by St Marys Church)
- Goldenhill (St John's Church)
- Longton Park
- Fenton (by the Town Hall)
- Burslem (by Swann Bank)
- Hanley (by the Town Hall)
Wolverhampton and the Black Country
The West Midlands Fire Service Pipe Band will once again lead a parade through Wolverhampton when the city marks Remembrance Sunday on 8 November.
A two-minute silence will take place at 11:00 before the laying of wreaths at the city's cenotaph. This will be followed by a service of remembrance inside St Peter's Church.
A short service will also take place at the cenotaph at 11:00 on 11 November.
In Sandwell, seven parades and remembrance services will take place across the borough from 10:30 GMT at the following locations:
- Great Barr - St Margaret's Church
- Oldbury - Civic Square
- Rowley Regis - Powke Lane Cemetery
- Smethwick - Smethwick Council House
- Tipton - Victoria Park

Temporary road closures will be in place in some areas to accommodate the parades, organisers said.
In Walsall, the main Remembrance Sunday parade will take place in the town centre followed by a service with military veterans and armed forces representatives at the Cenotaph in Bradford Place.

title: Chipping Norton crowned baseball champions a century after win
text:
British baseball champions crowned a century after win
It's America's national pastime, but during the 1920s it was a small town in the Cotswolds that was flying the flag for baseball in the UK.
At the same time Babe Ruth was leading the New York Yankees to the top of the sport across the pond, Chipping Norton were being crowned British champions in back-to-back years.
But in a wait that's taken longer than the Red Sox needed to break the Curse of the Bambino, the Cotswold market town's success had never been officially recognised.
Now, a century on from the team's first triumph, the championship has finally been certified by the British Baseball Federation - with a plaque celebrating the team recently unveiled at a local museum.
At the forefront of 1926 Chipping Norton baseball team was its founder Fred Lewis - a local undertaker with a fine sporting pedigree.
"He didn't like cricket, he didn't like football, but otherwise he was a great sportsman. He played a very good game of tennis and golf," his granddaughter Jill Kelly said.
"But he just absolutely loved baseball, he really did."
Although most people associate baseball with the USA and its major league - the game was in fact first played on the landed estates of Surrey.
But it was in the US that the game was first truly associated and organised. Over the years, it has gone on to become just about as American as apple pie.
In the early 1900s, it was Lewis who brought the game to the rolling hills of the Cotswolds - founding the Chipping Norton Baseball Club after seeing baseball in a sporting pamphlet.
Bill Williams, a former PE teacher who now volunteers at Chipping Norton Museum, said Lewis was "just a man who had a finger in every Chipping Norton pie".
"In the early days, they had very little equipment, but he designed and, as far as I'm aware, made the kit that the [baseball] teams played in."
"He did do other things, obviously, but I think it was very much the centre of his life."
By the roaring 1920s, Lewis had adopted the Field of Dreams motto "If you build it, they will come" and turned Chipping Norton into a hotbed of British baseball.
"By all accounts, they would attract large crowds on a Sunday afternoon - sometimes two, three hundred people would come along," Williams said.
In 1926, Chipping Norton beat the London Americans at Stamford Bridge, now more famously known as the home of Chelsea FC - to win their first national title.
A local newspaper report from the time said Lewis had told his defeated opponents that the secret of his team's success was "in their blood".
The club would retain the title the following year, but Williams said "things started to fade as Fred got older".
"When he died in 1960 at age 81, the club sort of fizzled out."
Neither of their national titles had ever been officially recognised by what would go on to be the governing body of the sport in the UK, British Baseball.
That was until earlier this month, after Williams led a years-long campaign to have the Chipping Norton club's achievements officially acknowledged.
But that changed last Saturday, as Williams and Kelly unveiled a plaque at Chipping Norton Museum to celebrate the success. It was approved by British Baseball.
"[It's] fantastic, I'm so chuffed that we finally got to do this," Williams said.
"There was a point where I thought this might never happen, but thankfully the British Baseball Federation have now officially recognised Chippy."
"I suppose it is [mission accomplished] really."
Kelly, who is in her 90s and now lives in Tewkesbury, said her grandfather Fred Lewis would have been "so pleased" with the recognition.
"He'd be absolutely delighted that the game had been recognised, mind you, you wouldn't have been able to stop him talking about it."

title: Drivers urged to slow down after seven red squirrels hurt in a day
text:
Motorists urged to slow down for red squirrels
An animal shelter has issued a plea to drivers to slow down in woodland areas after seven red squirrels were injured on an island's roads in one day.
The JSPCA Animals' Shelter, in St Helier, Jersey, said that it had been called to a worrying number of casualties in "a short space of time".
Jersey has a thriving red squirrel population, due to the absence of grey squirrels, which carry a virus deadly to their red cousins.
Red squirrels are endangered in the UK, with about 120,000 to 160,000 left in the wild.
A post on the shelter's Facebook page urged drivers to reduce their speed when driving through areas where squirrels may be crossing and to keep an extra lookout, particularly near wooded areas and roads surrounded by trees.
'Care and attention'
If you hit a squirrel, the shelter have advised islanders to stop somewhere safe and either call the JSPCA for advice or bring the squirrel directly to them if it is safe to do so.
"These little animals are precious, and every life matters," the shelter said.
"A few extra seconds of care and attention behind the wheel could make all the difference.
"The little squirrel pictured escaped with just a split lip, which was expertly stitched back together by our wonderful JSPCA vets."

title: Weekly round-up: Five stories from the South you may have missed
text:
Weekly round-up: Five stories you may have missed
New pictures of a missing capybara that escaped from a zoo, a lottery win, and an urgent appeal to help blind twin sisters all feature among the most-popular stories in the south of England this week.
In case you missed them, we have picked five articles from the past seven days across Hampshire, the Isle of Wight, Dorset, Berkshire and Oxfordshire to keep you up to date.
RAF base chemical contamination worst in UK, report says
Chemical contamination at a former RAF base earmarked for 9,000 homes is the worst found in the UK, a report has said.
Testing at RAF Upper Heyford carried out on behalf of a developer found "unacceptable" levels of polyfluoroalkyl substances, referred to as forever chemicals.
Fears have been raised previously that the site could be the source of pollution in nearby waterways, after earlier testing by campaigners and the Environment Agency.
About 1,300 homes have already been built on the site.
Search to find blind twin sisters a forever home
An adoption charity based in Reading has made an urgent appeal to find a permanent home for "determined and affectionate" blind twin sisters.
Parents And Children Together is searching for an adoptive family for Lily and Rose, whose names have been changed to protect their identities.
The charity said the identical twins, who are nearly 22-months-old, were registered blind and have additional needs. One of the twins also has epilepsy, which is well-managed with medication.
The charity said despite the challenges they faced, both children had been making "positive progress and continue to develop in their own unique ways".
Private school shuts for good during half term
A century-old private school has announced its closure at short notice.
Leweston School, near Sherborne, Dorset, posted on its website that it would not reopen after half term, but gave no reason.
The Catholic boarding and day school wrote: "We are very sorry for what this means for our pupils, their families and our staff, and for how little notice we have been able to give."
The school's alumni include actress Kristin Scott Thomas and Baroness Dido Harding, who ran the government's Covid-19 Test and Trace programme in England.
Samba the missing capybara caught on camera
New pictures have emerged of a missing capybara that escaped from a zoo more than six months ago.
Marwell Zoo, near Winchester in Hampshire, is still trying to recover one-year-old Samba, who attracted global interest after she went on the run in March.
Grainy images were captured this month after wildlife cameras were set up following her last sighting in August.
Samba escaped from the zoo on 17 March, less than a day after arriving. She broke out of a temporary enclosure she shared with her sister, Tango, who was quickly recaptured.
'Lottery win means I can pursue my dream'
Abbie West-Long was preparing to change her dream to move to Canada with her partner, when she had a knock at the door.
After learning she'd won £333,332 in the Postcode Lottery, the charity volunteer said she "just started crying".
Now, the 34-year-old from Cowes on the Isle of Wight says she can chase her dream and build a new life with partner Daryl Marlow in the Canadian Rockies.
Ms West-Long is one of five neighbours in her street to share £1m worth of winnings.

title: Charities ask people to look out for hedgehogs after Storm Austen
text:
Charities warn of bonfire danger for hedgehogs
Wildlife charities have asked people to consider hedgehogs before disposing of any debris from Storm Austen in bonfires.
Animal welfare groups in both Guernsey and Jersey said more people may be planning to have bonfires after the storm brought down trees and branches. It comes as hedgehogs numbers have plummeted in the Channel Islands as the animals struggle to survive in hot summers.
Jersey Hedgehog Preservation Group advised people to build a bonfire on the day and not several days in advance as it "only takes one night for a hedgehog to move in".
Steve Byrne from the GSPCA in Guernsey advised people to check their bonfire carefully before setting light to it.
Gill Morgan, from the Jersey group, said: "Given that there will be plenty of raw material from the aftermath of the storm and the weather is due to improve over the next week people may be planning to get rid of their broken branches, twigs and leaves by burning them.
"Hedgehogs will be venturing out looking for food after the bad weather, and this is the sort of habitat they love to curl up in during the day."
The GSPCA has cared for 7,000 hedgehog since 2011.
Byrne said: "The winter weather causes challenges for our prickly friends so popping out water and food can really help them and with many thinking about bonfires next week we all need to help our hedgehog friends."
Byrne also advised people to check areas carefully before mowing or strimming, ensure netting is kept at a height that allows hedgehogs to pass safely under and check compost heaps before digging into them.
He also urged people to avoid using pesticides and poisons in their garden, to cover drains or deep holes and ensure there was an easy route out of ponds and pools for hedgehogs.
Guernsey Hedgehog Rescue Centre has previously reported a "steep" decline in numbers, while Jersey Hedgehog Preservation Group in St Helier has also reported a sharp drop.
The Jersey group said it had never had a casualty brought in after bonfire night but feared the animals would have been "killed outright and not rescued".
It said hedgehog numbers were in decline all over Europe, so any hazards that could be prevented would help their numbers recover.
Dru Burdon, another member of the group, said hedgehogs were under constant threat and would have struggled to raise their young this summer.
"With the very hot dry summers we have had the last three years, they have really been finding life difficult," said Burdon.
"Food has become very scarce just when they are trying to breed and increase their numbers again."

title: Newton Aycliffe hazardous waste incinerator set to be approved
text:
Hazardous waste incinerator minded for approval
The Environment Agency (EA) has announced its intention to approve a permit for a hazardous waste incinerator plant which attracted thousands of objections.
The structure on Heighington Lane in Newton Aycliffe, County Durham, has already been built by Fornax North East but requires additional building work and an environmental permit from the EA.
The EA said after exploring the issues and concerns raised, it could not find any reason to refuse the application but was yet to make a final decision.
Fornax welcomed the announcement and said it expected a final decision to be made early next year.
Area Environment Manager for the EA, Gary Wallace, said the organisation recognised the local interest in this facility and had "carefully considered all the information and consultation comments".
"We will only grant the permit if we are satisfied the application meets all legal requirements and provides a high level of protection to the environment and human health," he said.
A second period of consultation is now open until 1 December to allow residents time to comment on the draft decision.
Fornax CEO Ian Jones said: "We welcome the initial announcement from the Environment Agency that it's minded to grant a permit to operate.
"We must now allow the natural permitting process to run its course before a final decision is taken."
Newton Aycliffe Labour MP Alan Strickland said he was "disappointed" by the EA's announcement and urged locals to submit responses to the consultation.
'Deeply concerned'
Resident opposition group STOP Heighington Lane Incinerator said they were calling on local MPs and PM Andy Burnham "to intervene" in the proposal.
A spokesperson said: "Thousands of residents across Newton Aycliffe and surrounding villages oppose this development.
"We demand an extended consultation, disclosure of relevant evidence and sufficient time for independent expert review."
Independent councillor Gerald Lee said while he was impressed with the design of the facility, he remained "concerned" about the proposal to wait two full years before carrying out soil sampling once the plant became operational.
"Across Heighington Parish there is genuine fear, particularly among young parents, about the potential build‑up of dangerous particles in the soil," he said.
Fornax previously said all waste would be brought on to the site in sealed airtight containers, while emissions from the plant would be closely monitored.
About 70% of the waste treated in the plant would be clinical waste from across the North East and North Yorkshire. The remaining 30% would be classed as hazardous waste.
Fornax said clinical waste would include used needles and blades, scrubs and surgical materials from clinical theatres.
Hazardous waste would comprise waste medicines, pharmaceutical waste and packaging, along with some plastics from discarded electricals, paints and DIY chemicals, cleaning products from industrial settings and agricultural chemicals.

title: Special locations are 'holy grail' for blockbuster film makers
text:
Special locations are 'holy grail' for film makers
As some classic films are made and remade, location scouts face a constant challenge to find fresh filming locations.
So was the case with the 2026 version of the Jane Austen classic Sense and Sensibility which was previously shot in south-west England in 1995.
"The holy grail of location-finding is something new, that hasn't been seen before, and is very special, explains Eddy Pearce from location specialist The Westcountry Set.
Pearce said he discovered just that special place right on his doorstep when he came across Kingston Russell, a private home tucked away in west Dorset.
The house doubles as the family estate Norland, which Elinor Dashwood and her sisters are forced to leave when their half-brother inherits it from their father.
The film's creators favoured the location as it had not featured in a film before, while the director also liked its weathered facade.
In the 1995 version of the film, Saltram House at Plympton in Devon was used for Norland, prompting decades of film tourism at the National Trust property.
Kingston Russell owner Sam Carter and his family moved out of the property to allow the film crew full access.
"It's the first time I've ever been on a big budget film set," said Carter. It was amazing to witness."
The estate is now running special tours for Jane Austen fans.
Parnham Park's lake in nearby Beaminster was also part of the film. The location is used to explore Elinor Dashwood and Edward Ferrers' burgeoning relationship.
Kingston Russell is among several locations in south-west England given a starring role in the new adaptation of Sense and Sensibility.
Dartmoor, Mothecombe and a second country home in West Dorset also feature.
The locations were chosen for their raw natural beauty, mirroring the changes in financial situation of the Dashwood women, as they navigate the societal constraints of the Georgian marriage market, in their pursuit of love.
But while some new locations are used, the 2026 film also features some old favourites.
It is the second time Mothecombe beach in South Devon has been used to portray Barton Beach in the Jane Austen story.
The beach is part of the Flete Estate which also acted as a film set for the version directed by Ang Lee, starring Emma Thompson, Kate Winslet, Greg Wise and Hugh Grant.
The 1995 film also made use of Efford House with its view down to the water and the drive below. The property is now used as a holiday let.
The estate's current owner, John Mildmay-White, said: "This was 31 years ago and in terms of the estate, its been a real big driver for tourism here."
"We get people still coming now from around the UK and even from America to stay where Sense and Sensibility was filmed."
Audiences might recognise some other Devon places in the film, including Ditsworthy Warren House on Dartmoor which was also used by Steven Spielberg for Warhorse.
The Sense and Sensibility team were attracted to the area's remoteness and beauty, but a lot of work was needed to transform the roof and inside of the derelict cottage and garden into the Dashwood's home.
Production designer Francesca Di Mottola said she felt inspired by the moors and said it was a "fantastic location to work with" and it was like "working in a painting".
She added the weather also brought its challenges during the four-week set construction.
"We had days of extreme heat when our construction team were on the roof so that was a struggle and then there were days when we could only work inside because it was so stormy."
Lee Morgan from the Devon Film Office said Sense and Sensibility dug deep into an "emotional use of landscape."
He added that big productions were an opportunity "to show the county off to its best".

title: Monster cabbage gift helps feed hungry animals at Devon sanctuary
text:
Monster cabbage gift helps feed rescue animals
Giant cabbages grown for a National Trust competition have been donated to a rescue centre to feed hungry animals.
Gardeners at Buckland Abbey in Yelverton grew a number of Cornish Giant cabbages, one of which was 1.2 metres (47.2 inches) across and weighed about 10kg (22lbs) - which won the competition for the biggest across trust sites in Devon and Cornwall "by a country mile".
Three of the large brassicas were taken to the Woodside Animal Sanctuary in Plympton to help feed its sheep, pigs, goats, turkeys, rabbits and guinea pigs.
Gardener Sam Brown said the cabbages, which are "often bred for exhibition", were "really good fun to grow" but were best suited for animal consumption.
"Giant veg typically doesn't taste very good," Brown said.
"The bigger the veg, it's kind of a bit more watery, a bit more tasteless, so it's not that suitable for human consumption."
He said the Cornish Giant variety was not the easiest to grow as animals wanted to eat them but the warm summer had helped them thrive.
Woodside Animal Sanctuary's senior manager Debbie Haynes said staff laughed when they first heard of the possible donation but thought it would "be great as the animals would love it".
Haynes said the donation would really help the sanctuary as "fresh fruit and veggies are really expensive, so any donations for that is just brilliant".
She said the animals "seem quite excited" by them and were "really enjoying them".
"I've worked here for over 30 years and I've never seen a giant cabbage that big before in my life."
"They're all munching away" but "it may take a guinea pig a long time to get through one of them".

title: Northumberland Youth MP says young voices matter
text:
Young voices need to be heard, youth MP says
A member of the youth parliament (MYP) has joined calls for the scheme to be continued as it faces an uncertain future.
The parliament has more than 300 elected members aged between 11 and 18, but the government has not committed to supporting the programme in its current form beyond March 2027.
Ryan Parsons, an MYP from Northumberland, said young people's voices "deserve to be heard", adding: "We are the future and our voices do matter."
The government said it was working with young people and youth organisations to design a new scheme aimed at increasing their involvement in democracy and decision-making, with further announcements to be made this autumn.
The Youth Parliament was launched 26 years ago to boost interest in politics among young people.
Members are elected by their peers, and campaign on issues they are passionate about and which they believe are important to young people.
Once a year, the members are allowed to hold debates in the House of Commons chamber, on a day when MPs are not sitting.
The parliament is run by the National Youth Alliance, and funded by the Department of Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) using taxpayers money.
Last year the parliament cost £453,000 to run.
Following a review last year, which found only a quarter of young people knew about the Youth Parliament and some schools felt "excluded from the process", DCMS said it would not commit to continue the programme in its current form.
Ryan, 15, who was elected in February, said he was inspired to put himself forward after seeing Prime Minister's Questions last year.
"I just thought, you know what, I want that to be me one day," he said.
"I want to help people."
Ryan is passionate about campaigning for free bus travel for young people, and improving their mental health.
"Too often young people don't get a say in decisions that are going to affect them in the future," he said.
Since being elected to the Youth Parliament, Ryan has met numerous local politicians including MPs, councillors and the North East Mayor.
He said he was "gutted" when he heard it could be lost.
"I understand the government has to make cuts, but if the government also wants to lower the voting age to 16 then young people have to take part in democracy," he said.
A bill to lower the voting age from 18 to 16 for all UK elections is currently making its way through Parliament.
One former member of the Youth Parliament believes it needs to modernise.
Luke Hall, 21, represented South Tyneside in 2023-24 and is now studying politics at university while working part-time as a parliamentary researcher for Labour Washington and Gateshead South MP Sharon Hodgson.
He said it was a big achievement "for a 16-year-old to be able to go from South Shields down to London and speak in the House of Commons".
However, the youth parliament did have some flaws, he said, mainly around attracting young people in the first place.
"A lot of the people that were involved probably would have been involved in politics and democratic participation anyway," he said.
He said any new model would need to be " truly inclusive" and engage a broader range of secondary and special educational needs schools.
The government said it was working to design a new scheme with a "particular focus on under-represented groups".

title: WW2 Cinderella Service crew remembered after 'ultimate sacrifice'
text:
Forgotten WW2 coastal airmen added to memorial
Three World War Two veterans who served in the South West and died in the conflict, are among those being added to a memorial.
Sqn Ldr George Crawford and Pilot Officer Kenneth Brian Willson were both based at St Eval RAF base in Cornwall while Sgt Jack Saul Lockwood was based at RAF Chivenor in Devon, as part of Coastal Command.
Coastal Command was tasked with keeping British seas safe from German U-boats along with escorting allied shipping convoys of troops, food and munitions.
It was recently announced 12,500 men and women who died while serving with the Coastal Command, part of the Royal Air Force, would be added to International Bomber Command Centre's Losses Database.
Crawford was a pilot with No. 53 Squadron Coastal Command and flew Consolidated B-24 Liberator aircraft from St Eval.
He flew with a multi-national crew which included people from Canada and New Zealand. He took part in 21 operations and had been tasked with patrolling the English Channel during the D-Day landings.
It was during this mission his plane was hit by anti-aircraft fire from a U-boat, leading to the death of him and the whole crew. Crawford was 29 and the only body found was that of a crew member from New Zealand.
The International Bomber Command Centre said the project was poignant as more than half the people who made the "ultimate sacrifice" had no known grave.
Crawford - who was from Ham, which was then part of Surrey but now in the London Borough of Richmond upon Thames - was given a Distinguished Flying Cross medal in January 1944 for an attack on a U-boat.
"As is the case with more than half of the airmen who were lost in the service of Coastal Command, the remainder of the crew have no known grave, and their names are instead included on the Runnymede Memorial," a spokesperson from International Bomber Command Centre said.
Four months after his death, Crawford's wife Leslie gave birth to a son in Belfast and named him George David Hugh Crawford.
Coastal Command was also known as the 'Cinderella Service' due to how it was overlooked and underfunded as Bomber Command and Fighter Command took priority during the war.
Many of the crews were based in south-west England as they headed out to protect waters off Devon and Cornwall's coast.
Willson served with No. 58 Squadron Coastal Command at RAF St Eval.
The International Bomber Command Centre said Willson, who was born in Dartmouth, Devon, on 11 April 1923, was part of missions including bombing attacks on the port area of German city Bremen and anti-submarine patrols in the Bay of Biscay.
The centre said during the latter, squadron record books said: "P/O Willson had the good fortune to sight two separate U-Boats.
"The first one was attacked and six depth charges dropped on the track on the submarine.
"An oil patch 100 yards in diameter was visible but nothing further seen.
"The second U-boat was attacked by the front guns and bullets seem to strike the conning tower and the U-boat crash-dived; nothing further was seen of this submarine."
Willson was on another anti-submarine patrol on 12 June 1942 when the crew in his aircraft became disorientated in dense fog and crashed near Cabo Ortegal in Galicia on the northern tip of Spain.
All six crew were killed and were buried side-by-side in the Bilbao British Cemetery.
Lockwood grew up in the Lincolnshire village of Scampton, which had its own RAF connections as the location where the Dambusters set off for Operation Chastise.
He trained as a pilot in Canada and the US before being posted to No. 179 Squadron Coastal Command at RAF Chivenor in Devon.
He flew modified Wellington bombers with special headlights known as Leigh Lights, which helped locate submarines just below the surface at night.
On his crew's third operation on 12 and 13 August 1943, Lockwood died as their aircraft returned to Chivenor.
Due to poor visibility, the crew decided to make another circuit to establish their position, but crashed into a nearby hill before the aircraft exploded due to unused depth charges still being on board.
The International Bomber Command Centre said the body of Lockwood, who was 23, was returned to Scampton where he was laid to rest within sight of the family farm he grew up on.
His epitaph reads: "He died that we might live in freedom."

title: Workington Town Women braced for FA Cup first round debut
text:
Team braced for debut in FA Cup first round
A women's football team is braced to make history having qualified for the first round of the Women's FA Cup for the first time in the club's history.
Workington Town Women will make their first round debut against Mancunian Unity Women at 14:00 GMT on 1 November after the fixture was postponed due to Storm Boelo.
Injured former club captain Naomi Foster said the achievement was "absolutely phenomenal" and a testament to the way the women's game had grown in west Cumbria.
The sixth-tier side reached the first round proper with a surprise win against six-time FA Women's Cup champions Doncaster Rovers Belles in the final qualifying round.
Workington beat the 13-time finalists 4-3 on penalties after a late Cassie Donald equaliser brought the score to 1-1 in normal time.
Since the win, the club has featured on Colin Murray's BBC 5 Live Sport show and the players have enjoyed seeing their faces on a billboard in the town.
Foster said the attention had been "surreal".
"It just goes to show what we're really trying to build," she said, adding: "To be able to advertise that in our local area and beyond is fantastic."
Manager Paul Mackenzie hoped the cup run would inspire the next generation.
"It's a great achievement for us and hopefully this will be the start of a momentum that will build for years to come with some of the younger women that are in the team and the girls that are playing junior football locally," Mackenzie said.
Workington will host Oldham-based side Mancunian Unity Women, who are in the division above.
Foster said: "Hopefully that home crowd will be there in great numbers to support us.
"We know we need to pull something off and we're kind of looking at the magic of Fleetwood Town this week and hoping that rubs off on us as well," she added, a reference to the Leaue Two team beating Arsenal in the League Cup.
The winner of Sunday's game at the Fibrus Community Stadium in Workington will face Notts County Women in the second round on 15 November.

title: Cancer survivor racks up 250th parkrun
text:
Cancer survivor racks up 250th parkrun
A man who was given six months to live after being diagnosed with terminal cancer has completed his 250th parkrun, 10 years on from his initial diagnosis.
Robin Ford, from Ruddington, Nottinghamshire, was diagnosed with kidney cancer in 2016, aged 45, and was told he would most likely not make it to Christmas.
He quickly married his partner, Litza, and underwent two rounds of chemotherapy which shrank the tumour to the point where it could be safely removed, along with parts of his liver and pancreas.
Following surgery, he joined the cancer support movement 5k Your Way and began taking part in parkruns as part of his recovery.
Bleak prognosis
Robin told the BBC he first began noticing symptoms in March 2016.
"I eventually went to the GP, who sent me for a CT scan which found a huge tumour on my kidney," he said.
"I went to see the consultant, who was great, but basically told me it was too big and there was no way they were going to shrink it. He said I probably wouldn't see Christmas.
"I was in shock, but I felt it was all kind of OK. I'm quite stubborn as well, so I didn't really believe it."
But then came the twist.
It turned out he had a Wilms tumour, a rare form of kidney cancer more commonly found in children and babies.
"It was quite unusual and only a few people have it - but it did mean there were chemotherapy options that we could try to shrink it," he said.
"There were three different treatment options and, after six months, one of them managed to start shrinking it."
Robin's tumour was removed along with his kidney, as well as parts of his liver and pancreas. He then faced a long road to recovery.
"I'd lost a lot of weight. I was in a wheelchair because I didn't have the energy to walk around and could hardly get up the stairs," he said.
"My wife persuaded me to use a wheelchair, which helped. It was nice having her pushing me around the park.
"I was just sitting at home and wasn't even meant to do anything hard.
"I had big surgery scars and found a free leaflet for CARE, (Cancer Rehabilitation and Exercise) which is a programme run by the Notts County Foundation at the Portland Centre.
"I met people there who were from Move Against Cancer and, between us, we came up with the idea of doing something at parkrun, just to get cancer patients out and moving.
"So in June 2018, we held our first 5k Your Way parkrun."
Now a regular parkrunner with 250 runs under his belt, Robin has set himself personal targets for the 5km event, improving from an initial time of 45 minutes to 26 minutes.
"I'm hoping to get under 25 minutes one day before I start getting slower again. But I don't mind too much. It's about getting out there. Every time I get there, it's a win," he said.
"I wasn't working straight away afterwards because I was too ill, but I could look forward to something that was in the calendar, and there were always going to be people there that I knew."
Following surgery, Robin's progress was monitored with regular tests for eight years until there were no signs of cancer remaining.
"Ten years ago, I couldn't have imagined doing one parkrun, so 250 is quite amazing. Looking back on all the photos from the last eight years, it's really been lovely.
"I'm just so grateful to all the different people involved in my survival.
"I had a fantastic oncologist called Professor Pulum Patel from the University of Nottingham, and he really helped. He's an incredibly kind, clever and wonderful man.
"He must have saved so many lives, so I owe a huge thanks to him and his team.
"Exercise is really important. Having something to do every month gives you structure during your rehabilitation and in your life."

Construction for a new housing estate in Newark has started, councillors have confirmed.

title: Council plans new team to tackle Loughborough nuisances
text:
Council wants new team to tackle town nuisances
Plans for a team of new public space officers to patrol Loughborough to tackle anti-social behaviour are set to given the go-ahead.
Charnwood Borough Council's cabinet has been advised by the authority's community safety team to approve proposals on 12 November to create a new public spaces officer patrol in the town.
According to the Labour-run council the service would cost about £250,000 a year, and would comprise of four full-time public space officers plus a part-time business support role.
It comes as the council carries out a final consultation on proposals to introduce a new public spaces protection order (PSPO), which includes a ban on wearing face coverings.
The council said the proposed new patrols would help enforce new powers being proposed in the PSPO.
As well as the balaclava ban, the proposed extension of the PSPO would also ban riding bicycles, e-bikes or e-scooters in a manner that is "dangerous, careless or inconsiderate".
The proposed PSPO would also prohibit loitering in any public place either alone or as part of a group in a manner that is "causing, or is likely to cause, nuisance, harassment, alarm or distress to others".
Alongside this it would target urinating or defecating in streets, parks, car parks, open spaces, or any other publicly accessible outdoor location.
Failing to comply with the PSPO would result in a fixed penalty notice of £100, reduced to £50 if paid within a certain time.
Officers would patrol in pairs, with the council anticipating the officers could be introduced in April 2027.
A final consultation is being held on the new PSPO, with its introduction set for next year, the council said.
Liz Blackshaw, the council's lead member for communities and neighbourhoods, said: "We know anti-social behaviour can affect how residents, visitors and workers feel when they spend time in our town centre.
"These proposals would introduce a visible presence to help deter anti-social behaviour, support businesses and provide reassurance for people using the town centre.
"This would be a significant investment by the council, but it is an investment in the future of our town centre.
"A welcoming, safe environment benefits businesses, encourages people to visit and supports the local economy."
The move comes after Leicester City Council recruited six officers in June to reinforce its existing team of street wardens in an effort to make the city centre feel safer.
They have the power to issue £100 penalty notices for offences such as dangerous riding of e-bikes and scooters, street drinking and aggressive begging, which became offences under a public spaces protection order (PSPO) established in 2025.
The officers, equipped with stab vests and body-worn CCTV cameras, are patrolling the city centre 12 hours a day, six days a week, the council said.

title: Mums need more support after Caesarean sections - I'm still recovering
text:
Mums need more support after C-sections - I'm still recovering
After undergoing two emergency Caesarean sections in 2018 and 2021, Kyra had hoped a planned procedure to deliver her third child would be different.
The surgery, on 22 October 2025, had been scheduled because her baby was in the breech position, with his feet positioned first.
Recalling the operation, the 36-year-old says: "They make it as comfortable as possible for you. There's chatter and music playing, it's only afterwards you realise this is major surgery."
Kyra, of Kibworth Beachamp in Leicestershire, says her recovery was "horrific" and she is still left with physical trauma.
"Because I'd had two emergency Caesareans before, I had a baseline to go off," she says. "As it was planned, I thought it would be a lot better.
"Granted, on the day of the Caesarean I was really well looked after, but afterwards everything drops off. Everything's focused on the baby, but you've just had open surgery. I took ages to heal."
A year on, Kyra has pelvic floor problems, bladder symptoms and is still dealing with pain around her scar, which she says took five months to fully close.
She adds: "My scar, especially on one side, is very pulled in. It affects day-to-day life; just walking, any physical activity that I do, even when I laugh there is a tug, there's pulling. And also just the look of it, it's a big change."
Kyra felt she received "standard care" after her first two Caesarean sections for daughter Thea and son Elijah, but found her recovery from her most recent procedure "a lot worse".
She is now backing a campaign calling for improvements to postnatal care for new mums whose children are delivered by Caesarean section.
A Caesarean section, or C-section, is a major operation to deliver a baby through a cut in the mother's abdomen.
According to NHS data, about 45% of babies born in England are delivered by Caesarean.
The NHS website states most women can go home one or two days after having a Caesarean, if there are no complications, and that they may experience discomfort for the first few days.
It adds: "When you go home, you'll need to take things easy at first.
"You may need to avoid some activities, such as driving, until you have had your postnatal check-up with the doctor at six weeks."
Before leaving hospital following a Caesarean section, women may receive advice from a physiotherapy team about exercises and recovery after childbirth, depending on local hospital arrangements.
Women are encouraged to inform their midwife if they need stronger pain relief. Healthcare professionals should also assess each woman's risk of developing deep vein thrombosis, as Caesarean sections increase the risk of blood clots.
Kyra and her baby, Tobiah, were discharged from hospital the day after the surgery and received routine visits from midwives and health visitors, and attended a six-week post-birth check-up with a GP, as is standard.
At an early midwife appointment, she was referred back to hospital due to an infection and how her scar was healing, but due to the condition of her scar, Kyra eventually sought help from private healthcare services.
She says: "I felt left to manage my recovery by myself and if there was better postnatal support, then I wouldn't be suffering the way that I am today.
"If you're having other major surgery like a knee or a hip operation, you'd probably expect to have some type of rehabilitation afterwards like physiotherapy. There is nothing offered to C-section mums. It's sad."
Kyra is backing a petition, which is calling on the government to fund improved post-Caesarean care across the NHS, which has been signed more than 2,000 times.
The government will respond to the petition if it reaches 10,000 signatures, and if it reaches 100,000, it will be considered for a debate in Parliament.
Started by Hannah Poulton, from Broughton Astley in Leicestershire, it says standardised scar care, abdominal rehabilitation, pelvic health and mental health support "should be basic care following major abdominal surgery".
The petition states: "'Rest and don't lift anything heavy' is not enough now.
"Mothers deserve consistent, evidence-based support and properly trained professionals to improve recovery and outcomes."
Hannah, a women's health physiotherapist, says recovery from her own Caesarean was difficult.
"I found it painful to move and I was unsure of how I should be recovering even though I'm a women's health physio," the 47-year-old adds.
"You feel very vulnerable and isolated and, while I received the standard care available, I didn't feel it was enough.
"Nine years later, I'm seeing women come to my clinic with similar concerns every day and their experiences of birth and recovery are getting worse."
'Basic level care'
Hannah says the stories she hears are "so similar" and the women she sees feel they have not received enough support and guidance on how to recover.
She adds: "They want to care for themselves, recover well, but they have no idea how to.
"I'm not asking for a huge amount, for basic level care."
Kyra has thrown her weight behind the petition, adding her experience had been physically and mentally exhausting.
"Instead of enjoying those precious early months with Tobiah, so much of my time and energy went into worrying about my health, attending appointments and fighting to be heard," she says.
"You only get those newborn days once, and I feel like some of that time was taken away from me - that's why the petition means so much to me."
Maxine Palmer, from the charity National Childbirth Trust, says most women are signed off from midwifery care 10 days after giving birth, when health visitors and GPs in the primary care sector take over.
She adds: "Women are faced with a very fragmented system that isn't joined up between maternity care and their postnatal care, which spreads across multiple different services and as a result of that women are failing to get the physical and mental health support they need following Caesarean birth."
According to the Department of Health and Social Care, all women should be offered a GP postnatal consultation six to eight weeks after birth with perinatal pelvic health services and maternal mental health services now available.
In a statement, a spokesperson said: "Every woman and baby deserves safe, compassionate maternity and neonatal care and the health and social care secretary is determined to improve standards across the country as a personal priority.
"Through the National Maternity and Neonatal Taskforce that she is chairing, this government will deliver the reforms needed to ensure the very highest standards of safety and care for every mother and baby.
"Our renewed Women's Health Strategy commits to improving postnatal support for women's physical and mental health in the community, while the updated Healthy Child Programme guidance sets clearer standards to assess mothers' physical and mental health needs and ensures that support is available after pregnancy."

title: Derby sets out 2026 Christmas programme of events
text:
Derby sets out Christmas programme of events
Derby is gearing up to celebrate the beginning of the festive season with a programme of events.
This year's Christmas lights switch-on will be taking place on Saturday 28 November.
The flicking of the festive switch will follow a lantern parade and coincide with the official opening of the city's temporary ice rink.
Derby City Council cabinet member for city centre, culture and tourism Gurkiran Kaur, said: "Christmas is a time for making memories with family and friends, and we're delighted to be bringing a fantastic programme of festive events to Derby once again."
In the run up to the switch-on, Surtal Arts are holding a series of lantern making workshops up until 21 November at the Market Hall and other venues across the city.
These can then be showcased in the free Heroes-themed lantern parade which will gather at St Peter's Church at 17:00 GMT on 28 November.
The switch-on will then take place at 17:30 in the Market Place, where the Cathedral Quarter Ice Rink and Nordic Bar will both be up and running until 31 December.
The Cathedral Quarter Santa's Grotto will also open on 28 November, inside the Market Hall.
Children will be able to meet Santa and his elves there and receive a gift until Christmas Eve.
Brad Worley, manager of both the Cathedral Quarter and St Peter's Quarter Business Improvement Districts, said: "Christmas is a special time in Derby, and we're delighted to be supporting Santa's Grotto at Derby Market Hall once again.
"It's a wonderful opportunity for children and families to enjoy the magic of Christmas together while also discovering everything our city centre has to offer."
Derby's family Snow White panto will run at Derby Arena from 4 December until New Year's Eve, while the family show Help! Santa's Missing will run at Chapel Street Arts Centre from 10-23 December.

Christmas lights switch-on events are also planned across Derbyshire.
The Matlock Christmas parade and lights switch-on and the Ashbourne Christmas lights switch-on both take place on Saturday 21 November, while the lights switch-on in Chesterfield will take place on Sunday 22 November.
The Long Eaton lights switch on takes place on Thursday 26 November, with Ilkeston lit up for the festive season the following day, Friday 27 November.
Dronfield Christmas lights switch-on takes place on Friday 27 November, while Swadlincote's Lights Before Christmas event takes place on Saturday 28 November.
