title: Queen's University Belfast: Staff warned of 'difficult decisions' ahead
text:
University staff warned of 'difficult decisions' ahead over finances
Staff at Queen's University of Belfast (QUB) have been warned of "difficult decisions" ahead due to the university's finances.
Pay deals with staff, and childcare and gym fees for staff and students are under review while staff car-parking charges are going up.
The details came in an message to staff from the university's vice-chancellor Prof Sir Ian Greer.
His message came after the grant paid by the Northern Ireland Executive to universities had a "significant" cut in 2025/26.
What is the state of Queen's University's finances?
According to Greer, the university had a deficit of about £12.5m in the last financial year.
While the university hoped to reduce that, he said that a combination of cuts in funding from Stormont and a fall in student fee income meant the university had to "control costs".
There have been tougher visa requirements for international students coming to UK universities in recent years.
According to the university's annual accounts, the income QUB received from international student fees recently fell by around £5m - from more than £60m in 2024 to around £55m in 2025.
Greer also said that student recruitment income was expected to be around £7m "below target" in the current year.
He said that the university still hoped to deliver agreed pay deals to staff.
"However, given the Department for the Economy's position, we have no choice but to keep the position under review," he said.
Some other charges, including for staff car-parking on campus are going up.
Costs for university services that staff and students use, like childcare and membership of the university Physical Education Centre (PEC) are also under review and may rise.
However, plans for a new university heritage and visitor centre, to be built in the Quad on the site of the current administration building, are going ahead.
But there may be more savings measures to come.
"The University Management Board has agreed to identify approximately £10m of savings this year and, depending on the final position with public funding, further difficult choices may have to follow this academic year," Greer said.
How are students affected?
Greer said that due to a cap on student numbers, QUB had turned away "around 500 students who had the grades to attend Queen's".
The number of local students both QUB and Ulster University (UU) can admit is decided by Stormont's Department for the Economy and depends on available funding.
Current QUB students who use university childcare or the PEC may also face higher fees for the services.
But Greer said that "the student experience must remain central to our decisions".
What has the university said?
In a further statement to BBC News NI, a QUB spokesperson said that the university was "facing increasing financial pressures arising from reduced public funding, lower student recruitment income and rising costs".
"Our planned approach is centred on both stability and growth, to secure the university's long-term future while supporting our students and staff," it said.
"Strategic investment in projects such as the Public Engagement and Discovery Centre are part of a commercial growth strategy to help generate income while providing teaching and research space to further enhance the student experience."
description: Pay deals with staff, and childcare and gym fees for staff and students are under review.

title: The WW1 Ipswich soldier given his name back after 111 years
text:
The WW1 soldier given his name back after 100 years
In 1915 Cpl George Thomas Manning of Ipswich was killed in World War One - but it would take more than 100 years to find his body.
The soldier from the Suffolk Regiment 2nd Battalion was killed fighting in Belgium and his wife and two daughters died never knowing where he was buried.
In 2019 human remains were found in a ditch near Ypres and confirmed to be his. Alexia Clark, the Ministry of Defence (MOD) detective who solved the mystery said: "It's always a nice feeling to be able to give a man back his name."
With a full military funeral in Belgium now planned, the MOD and the Ipswich War Memorial are searching for Manning's descendants so they might attend.
Manning was born in 1881 in Ipswich and was one of nine siblings.
In 1905 he married Florence Elizabeth Bayles and they had two daughters.
When war broke out in 1914 Manning found himself fighting in Kemmel near Ypres in Belgium the following year.
The men dealt with sniper fire and shelling and 140 lives were lost, including Manning who died on 9 March 1915 aged 34.
His name was memorialised on the Menin Gate in Ypres that honours 55,000 British and Commonwealth soldiers who died in the area and have no known grave.
Alexia Clark, an MOD war detective, said the human remains were found in Kemmel in 2019 during ditch clearance work.
They were recovered and taken by the Commonwealth War Graves Commission to a mortuary in France.
In 2024, the MOD received a report stating artefacts with the body included two brass badges with the word Suffolk on them.
The MOD determined that only the 2nd Battalion of the Suffolk Regiment was ever in this area of Belgium and that 26 of the bodies of the men killed were still missing.
Clark started to build family trees of the missing men to locate living relatives and ask them to provide a DNA sample to see if they matched with the remains.
Clark said: "I had been through six other men before I actually managed to get a match and prove that this particular man is George Thomas Manning.
"It's a really thrilling feeling when you get that report that comes through from the DNA contractors and it is, 'Yes, you've got it this time'.
"Especially when you've potentially got quite a lot of casualties to work through and to try and narrow it down from."
The person who matched with Manning was a two-times great-nephew. Two other relatives have since been found including one in Australia.
It is not believed Manning's daughters had children of their own. However as he was one of nine children, Clark expected there to be many relatives out there.
The MOD sought the help of Ipswich War Memorial to find other possible relatives still in Suffolk.
Andrew Beal from the group said they had researched Manning about 10 years ago and it was "wonderful" his relatives would at last be given closure.
He said: "It probably was quite upsetting after the war [for Manning's family] to realise there was no grave and they couldn't find it.
"Over the years, we've come across letters and things from families, and they're absolutely heartbroken that there is no grave to visit.
"There's just a plaque on the wall – it's not the same really."
A full military funeral for Manning will be held next spring in Belgium, with his remains laid to rest in a cemetery with others from the Suffolk Regiment.
Anyone who thinks they may be a relation of Manning is encouraged to get in touch with the MOD and Ipswich War Memorial so they might be able to attend.

title: Broughshane Waterfowl Park: Recovery effort continues after oil tank vandalism
text:
Oil tank vandalism results in waterfowl park 'nightmare'
Recovery efforts are continuing after an oil spill caused by the vandalism of a nearby home heating oil tank resulted in the death of 13 birds from Broughshane Waterfowl Park.
More than 20 birds were transported to the USPCA's headquarters last week for urgent specialist care, but the death toll has continued to rise.
The popular attraction in County Antrim has been forced to close while efforts continue to remove oil from the pond.
Police have appealed for anyone with information to come forward.
Broughshane Environment Wildfowl and Wildlife Trust's chairman, Gary Hayward, said they incident had been a "nightmare".
"We are devastated," he told BBC News NI.
"One of our volunteers appeared on the Thursday morning to feed [the birds], and walked down through the park and smelt this kerosene smell and saw the black swans completely oiled."
The park is home to 120 "collection birds", as well as wild birds, he explained.
"So far we have lost 13 birds, some of which are really close to us."
Hayward praised the efforts of the USPCA and Northern Ireland Environment Agency (NIEA), who have been instrumental in treating the sick birds and clearing up the spillage.
The Northern Ireland Environment Agency (NIEA) was first alerted to the incident on Thursday 22 October and have been involved in trying to remove the oil waste.
"The incident was quickly confirmed as having had a significant impact on the ponds and NIEA inspectors deployed oil absorbent booms and other countermeasures as mitigation," a spokesperson said.
The agency said the substance involved had been identified as home heating oil, or kerosene, and that the source had been traced to a nearby tank.
The waterway is noted to be much improved but further works will be carried out as long as is deemed necessary.
Hayward hopes that the incident will be an deterrent to those engaged in vandalism.
"People need to be fully aware of what impact it can have if somebody vandalises a heating containers and tanks."
Siobhan Hawthorn, wildlife supervisor at the USPCA, has been a key part of the rescue operation.
"It's massively frustrating when these kind of incidents occur, especially when it's caused by carelessness and us humans and these poor birds have suffered because of it," she said.
"There's no reason for them to have died needlessly for that reason."
Siobhan and the team have been working tirelessly to help revive the birds which include geese, ducks and swans.
"It's been a case of getting them all bathed and treated as soon as we could because of the level of contamination they suffered," she said.
"We've given them all doses of charcoal to help combat some of the toxins that they would have ingested.
"Unfortunately not all of them got to us as quickly as we would have liked and they have ingested too much," she added.
Siobhan and the team said the incident has also placed their staff under considerable pressure "emotionally and mentally".
The centre is unsure just how long they will have to care for the remaining birds.
"We would like to think that they're over the worst of it, but you just don't know exactly how much they have potentially ingested," she explained.
"Birds are extremely good at hiding illnesses and ailments, so sometimes you don't see the symptoms until it's a little bit too late because they're just so good at hiding it.
"The majority of these birds that have come into us are actually not native species so they can't be returned until the pond is 100% fully cleaned and cleared."

title: From arm wrestling to marathons, meet the late starters shining in new sports
text:
'Never too old to start' - meet the late starters shining in new sports
Stanley Hamilton is among the most highly-decorated arm wrestlers in Northern Ireland, but what makes his success all the more remarkable is that he only got to grips with the sport in his 40s.
His rise to the top has been rapid, from absolute beginner to a world beater in less than a decade.
It is more common for people to achieve peak performance in their youth, but Stanley is far from alone in discovering a competitive edge later in life.
From marathon running to roller derby, older generations are finding new sporting passions, and sometimes unexpected talents, well beyond the age they might once have thought possible.
Old dog, new tricks? The arm wrestler
For Stanley, he had spent more than two decades playing rugby, but needed a change.
"I got to 40 with a lot of injuries. A lot of broken bones. I thought, right, I need something low impact," he said.
The 47-year-old always had a passive interest in the sport of arm wrestling over the years but decided to train competitively after hanging up his boots.
"It looks simple. You grab a person's hand and you drag them to the pad, but there's so much going on there.
"I realised after the first session I know absolutely nothing about arm wrestling.
"I trained for five months before I did my first competition, and by the end of my first year, I was British novice champion."
He has gone on to win three world championship medals, clinching bronze in his left arm and silver in his right in 2022 and another silver in 2023.
"Everybody starts somewhere, but whether you start at the bottom rung or you start three rungs up, nobody starts as a champion.
"Don't be afraid to be useless."
The marathon champion
From novice runner to Dublin Marathon triumph in just four years, Judith Storm says her remarkable achievement is proof that success can come later.
"It's never too late to start something new," the 39-year-old told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme.
Her journey into running began during the Covid-19 pandemic, turning to exercise after giving birth to triplets.
Just four years ago, she lined up for her first race.
"I didn't really do much exercise until my 30s, so I started off just riding a bike in my garage during the pandemic and then when we later moved to Derry I didn't set up the bike that time and just thought I'll just start running," she said.
Beyond her marathon success, Judith hopes her success will encourage other women, particularly those who have had children, to make time for themselves and discover the benefits of running.
"I have got up early and I have fitted in the training around the kids so it's hard work, but for anybody you know resetting your own limitations is really powerful.
"I have such a busy life and running is just the time I dedicate to me, and I do prioritise it and sometimes as woman we can feel selfish for taking an hour here or there, but I am such a more patient and better mother when I have been out on a run, and my kids can attest that I am like a battle axe if I don't."
She described running as like being in her "flow state" and encouraged others to find something they love and go out and do it.
"Especially as mothers you can sometimes juggle so much, and sometimes you have to give yourself back that time so just start, nothing is impossible."
The roller skater
When people decide to take up a new sport, they typically choose more obvious options such as running or padel.
But Bangor woman Sarah McMillan chose roller derby, a full-contact sport played on skates.
Each team has five skaters consisting of one 'jammer' and four 'blockers'.
The aim is for the jammer to score points by lapping opposing blockers, who in turn try to prevent the opposing jammer from getting past, whilst also helping their own jammer score.
Sarah got into the niche sport in her 30s and is still going strong in her 50s.
Prior to this she had dabbled in sports such as hockey and running.
"I didn't find anything that really excited me," she said.
As the sport grows, people are getting involved from a much younger age. She has played against others where she's jokingly thought "I could have been their grandmother".
However, she thinks there's an advantage to picking up a new sport later in life.
"In the same way that if you are a mature student going to university," she said.
"I think your head is in the right place and you are there because you want to be there."
She has since represented Team Ireland at two Roller Derby World Cups and is hoping to line out at next Autumn's European Roller Derby Cup.
"Give it a go. What have you got to lose? Put yourself out there and try it."
'Feeling you are good at something'
Dr Gavin Breslin, a sport and exercise psychologist at Queen's University Belfast, believes people's experience of sport at a young age can influence activities they pursue in life.
"That stems from our childhood. In terms of making decisions about what activities and behaviours to be involved in," he said.
"If you get rewarded, either verbally or non-verbally, then you're more likely to keep going with that."
But discovering an activity that you enjoy, even at a later stage in life, helps motivate people to continue.
"A key thing here is their competence or actually feeling that they're good at something," he added.
"As a result, they're keeping going with it because their basic psychological need of competence and feeling good that they can actually achieve something is being met."
description: From marathon running to roller derby, older generations are finding new sporting passions, and sometimes unexpected talents, well beyond the age they might once have thought possible. But what does it take to start from scratch as an adult?

title: Crowfield emus' dating woes leaves glut of 14 unfertilised eggs
text:
Emu's failed romance leads to massive egg dilemma
A farm has been left with more than a dozen emu eggs after a failed romance between their birds meant none of them had been fertilised.
Dexy the male emu was seemingly unimpressed romantically after he failed to fertilise any of the 14 eggs laid by his companion Eyeleen, at Cloverfield Farm in Crowfield, Suffolk, in recent weeks.
Farm co-owner Jo Saberton said Dexy had been good at helping incubate the eggs, but he perhaps did not "fancy Eyeleen enough" as no chicks emerged.
The unfertilised eggs, each equivalent to about 12 chicken eggs in volume and weight, can instead be eaten and Saberton said one could be scrambled to feed four people.
The farm bought Eyeleen four years ago and decided to bring in Dexy shortly afterwards for some company.
Eyeleen got her name after losing one of her eyes, and Dexy was named after Dexys Midnight Runners - the band behind the song Come On Eileen.
In the UK emus typically lay their eggs during the winter and it is the job of the males to incubate them.
"They get on OK, but I'm not quite sure we're ever going to have the patter of little emu feet," Saberton said.
She added: "I think he's just very young, maybe he doesn't fancy Eyeleen enough."
Saberton's husband Nick, who she runs the farm with, said perhaps it was Eyeleen's one eye that had caused Dexy to be "a bit more fussy", despite her "long legs".
Initially, they had stepped in and taken some of the eggs away to be placed in an incubator, but still no chicks arrived, making the farm owners believe Dexy had been able to fertilise them.
While the farm did nothing with the 28 emu eggs last year, Saberton said they were keen not to waste them this year.
Their grandsons had experimented with using one for boiled egg and soldiers, and it took 35 minutes to boil it.
"They gave it the thumbs up and then a friend of mine scrambled it and she sent me a picture," Saberton continued.
"We're probably going to try it [ourselves] now.
"They do look so lovely, you don't really want to break them because they look like an ornament."

title: Military vehicle from latest Spider-Man film is up for auction
text:
Vehicle from hit Spider-Man film to be auctioned
The original military vehicle used in the latest Spider-Man film and currently housed in Northamptonshire is to be auctioned.
Known on screen as DD6, the machine is featured in a major chase sequence in Spider-Man: Brand New Day, alongside the web-slinging superhero played by Tom Holland.
It is currently being kept at a military vehicle experience company based in Brackley, which has been home to other iconic motors from films including Fast and Furious 6 and Black Widow.
The vehicle will be auctioned online by Humbert & Ellis on 25 November with a guide price of between £50,000 and £70,000.
Jonathon Humbert, auctioneer, said: "This film star could prove to be one of the most collectable movie props ever."
The film, starring real-life husband and wife Tom Holland and Zendaya - set a North American record, with box office takings of $360m (£268m). It was the biggest opening weekend ever in the US and Canada.
Film production company Marvel bought the vehicle from Nick Mead who has been running Tanks A Lot in Helmdon for the last 30 years.
Originally a 1969 Alvis Stalwart 6x6 military load carrier, the vehicle was developed to carry military supplies across difficult terrain and waterways. It was known as "the Stolly".
Mead said Marvel "completely transformed" the machine into a futuristic hero strike vehicle. It included a dramatic armoured appearance, desert camouflage and studio weathering.
Other than making it legal to be driven on the road he said it is "completely the same as it was when it left the film set".
Mead said he has owned about 400 other military-style vehicles.
He said: "I do tend to chase film props. The [Spider-Man vehicle] is a pretty cool piece of kit."
Mead believes the vehicle is "likely to appear in a lot more famous films." Although he'd like it to stay in the UK, he thinks it will be used in America for film promotion.
Aside from film appearances a large number of machines have been bought from Mead's tank collection to be used in Ukraine for casualty evacuation.

title: Armagh Observatory and Planetarium: 'Rok' solid recognition for space scientist
text:
'Rok' solid recognition for Slovenian space scientist
As a child growing up in Slovenia in 1999, Dr Rok Nežič couldn't have known that an asteroid that was discovered in New Mexico that year would be named after him almost three decades later.
The Orchard County may be best known for its apples, but for Nežič the real attraction was astronomy.
He first arrived at Armagh Observatory and Planetarium (AOP) in 2015 to complete his doctorate in space and climate physics, and has remained there ever since.
More than a decade on, he is one of two AOP employees to have recently been chosen to have a celestial body named after them.
Nežič, who works at the planetarium as a tours and outreach officer, said he thought it was "so cool" when he learned that asteroids can be named after people.
Speaking to BBC News NI, Nežič said he wished he "could get there some day" and, now that he has, he described it as "a dream come true".
"I'm not sure how to believe it myself,” he admitted.
He explains that an asteroid is "a smallish rock in space" compared to planets, and that his one is named (20560) Nežič.
"That's its official name, so the number there tells you basically the order of discovery."
It is currently "sitting safely out in the asteroid belt and just going around the Sun, just like we are", he explained.
The naming process for small bodies in the solar system is governed by the International Astronomical Union. Asteroids can be named by their discoverers once their orbits are sufficiently known.
Nežič's asteroid is 10.9km across, while that belonging to his colleague Shane Kelly is 15.6km.
"They're both actually quite large as far as these asteroids that are named after people tend to be, because most of the really large ones were discovered first," Nežič said.
"So they were named a long time ago, and now we're finding smaller and smaller ones."
Nežič's asteroid was discovered by "one of the big missions", he said.
"This is an Earth-based mission in this case, which is looking for lots of asteroids, essentially, because the more we know about them, the more we know where they're going, the more we know which ones are not hitting us, including mine and Shane's."
To be considered for an asteroid namesake, someone must nominate you, and in Nežič's case, two people put his name forward.
He doesn't know who chose him for the honour - but his PhD supervisor, and a former astronomer from the observatory nominated him.
Nežič focused on comets with polarised light for his studies and years later is "still" talking about space.
The planetarium and observatory is "punching well above our weight", he said.
"Even though we're a small institution, people who work here can just focus on the research so much that we have really top researchers in the field."
The planetarium's neighbouring observatory has monitored the weather for more than than 230 years.
Shane Kelly, who is the principal meteorological observer at Armagh Observatory, was nominated by the emeritus director.
Since 1999, his role involves opening what is known as the Stevenson screen which holds sensitive thermometers, before noting down his readings for the day into the handwritten ledger.
His hand has entered far more lines of data than any of his 17 predecessors and his asteroid is called (7050) Shanekelly.
Kelly has been "doing this for 27 years", the institute's director said.
"He's probably observed the weather more than anyone else in the world, I suspect," Prof Michael Burton said.
"So this is in recognition of Shane's contribution to the observatory and to the measuring of the weather."
Kelly's asteroid was discovered in Chile in 1982.
Burton said it's "fantastic" that the two members of the team have been awarded in this way.
"There are now 29 asteroids which have some connection with the observatory and planetarium here in Armagh."
The AOP now plans on recognising their achievements with a new LED dome, which will show the asteroids and their orbits.
description: Two men from the Armagh Planetarium and Observatory have had asteroids named in their honour in recognition of their work.

title: Max Hall: Corby family praise brain cancer government meeting
text:
Brain cancer campaigners praise government meeting
A family campaigning for increased investment in brain cancer research after the death of their teenage son have said their meeting with a government official "could not have gone better".
Max Hall, 14, from Corby, was diagnosed with an incurable brain tumour last year - and died in August.
The family met James Frith, the health minister for rare diseases, at Westminster on Wednesday, to discuss commitments on annual funding for research as well as targets to ensure rare tumours received the same attention as other cancers.
Max's mother Jackie said Frith "made commitments" to take the family's questions forward.
Speaking to BBC Radio Northampton, she said: "Currently there's absolutely nothing out there for children that are diagnosed with a terminal brain tumour.
"The options are standard care which is radiotherapy and chemotherapy and after that there isn't anything, there are no trials, there's nothing in this country, you have to go outside of the UK to access that."
She said that Frith had "promised he will take this forward" and would update the family in three months' time.
In a statement, Frith said: "Our hearts go out to Max's family and friends.
"Earlier this month, the Prime Minister and Health Secretary announced new action to accelerate progress on brain cancer, including a rapid expert review, a national action plan and a dedicated national clinical lead to drive change.
"We are determined to turn that renewed focus into faster progress on research, clinical trials and new treatments for people affected by this devastating disease."

title: No homosexual offence disregards since law introduced in Northern Ireland
text:
No homosexual offence pardons since law introduced
There have been no pardons for convictions for now abolished gay sex offences in the eight years since a scheme was introduced in Northern Ireland.
Three people have applied to the pardons and disregards scheme since the laws' introduction, however their applications did not meet the relevant criteria.
Offences include gross indecency and procuring others to commit homosexual acts. The activity must have been consensual, with a person aged 17 or over and must not still be an offence.
The Department of Justice (DoJ) said a review of the scope of the scheme is taking place, with a view to making reform proposals to ministers after the next assembly elections.
The scheme was approved by the Northern Ireland Assembly in 2016 and came into force in 2018.
Posthumous pardons automatically apply to anyone convicted of offences who have since died.
While a definitive number of those convicted has not been formally established, it is estimated that hundreds can apply.
Male homosexual acts were criminalised until 1982 in Northern Ireland.
The Rainbow Project helped some of those who applied for their conviction to be quashed or disregarded.
The charity's chief executive, Scott Cuthbertson, said he is not surprised at the low uptake, but "that doesn't mean the scheme hasn't been a success".
"There's the message it sends that what happened prior to 1982 was wrong and shouldn't have happened and that the people who were convicted under legislation at that point deserve not to have that stain on their record," he said.
"When it comes to the low uptake, I would encourage anyone who has that on their record, who wants to remove it and are maybe a wee bit worried about opening up old wounds or dealing with past issues, it is worth it."
Cuthbertson also welcomed the DoJ's review.
"I think anything that can be done to make people aware of the scheme and increase the uptake of the number of people applying would be a good idea."
Jeffrey Dudgeon, a gay rights campaigner, won a landmark legal case in the European Court which ruled that the law was in breach of the human right to a private life.
He told BBC News NI that he "always knew that there wouldn't be very many people eligible for pardons given the length of time had elapsed since".
"I would say most of the people involved in that had either died or were not really interested in in resurrecting the whole matter."
He said there was a "different mood" in the preceding years before decriminalisation.
"From the late '60s until 1982, which is the period I was mostly involved in, gay liberation had happened in America and in England. The whole mood had changed from being a sort of silent minority that was pleading for decriminalisation and we'd become an organised group looking for rights.
"The big problem always was that most convictions were not exactly within the remit or ambit of the criminal law that was repealed in 1982. Which was very particular in that it was only decriminalised gay sex between men over 21 in private.
"I think a lot of the actual cases that came into the courts involved some form of sex with somebody under 21 or in public or was it with a third party present."
What is the history?
Prof Tom Hulme is a cultural historian of modern Ireland and Britain at Queen's University Belfast.
He said that the history of same sex convictions in Northern Ireland is "quite a complex one" as Victorian laws were used against gay and bisexual men prior to decriminalisation.
After the repeal in 1982, laws against acts such as sex in public places, which remain illegal today, were used disproportionately against gay and bisexual men, due to attitudes towards homosexual activity in Northern Ireland, he said.
"Far more people were arrested throughout Northern Ireland than had been in the previous hundred or so years, so there is an issue here with convictions in that the repeal scheme or the disregard scheme that is in current existence essentially does not capture many of those offences because they are still in essence illegal today.
"You have to remember that these were not people convicted as such for being homosexual or gay or bisexual but they were rather convicted for acts that had taken place in public places."
Hulme said that there needs to be a "broader public conversation about the conditions under which gay men and bisexual men were seeking sex" and the role of the police during these times.
"There is much more to learn about Northern Ireland's gay and bisexual history and that might provide some form of redress as well."
What's happening elsewhere?
In England and Wales, the scheme was initially open to men with specific convictions for homosexual offences that have since been repealed.
It was extended in June 2023 with the aim to enable more people, including women and those serving in the UK armed forces, to apply.
Since then, 19 convictions have been eligible for a disregard for the year ending March 2026, lower than the 35 convictions in the previous year.
Prior to the extended scheme, there were 522 applicants and 208 convictions were eligible for a disregard.
In Scotland, 22 people have applied to have their convictions disregarded and 16 applications have been granted since 2019.
The legislation provides an automatic pardon for any man convicted of same-sex activity between men that would be legal today.

title: Judge's Great Yarmouth exhibition shines light on roller skating
text:
Judge's exhibition shines light on roller skating
A national roller skating judge and photographer, who has captured the lives of seven artistic skaters over 10 years, hopes her exhibition can shine a spotlight on the sport - and wishes that one day it will be in the Olympics.
Debby Besford grew up in Great Yarmouth, Norfolk, which has a strong roller skating heritage, and travelled all over the country to compete.
While flicking through photo albums on a visit to her parents and reminiscing over her skating days, she decided it would be "fantastic" to do an exhibition about young skaters from the town's Retro Skating Academy.
She said it was "amazing" to see how skating had shaped their lives during the decade.
Besford said roller skating had been "very, very important for many, many years" to Great Yarmouth, with the town producing a number of champions.
She said the Victorian Winter Gardens on the seafront, which used to house a prominent rink and is undergoing restoration, was "a place that was like my creative space and my safe space as well, and to have another family of skaters and parents to support you".
Over the years she has gained various items of memorabilia, which she is also featuring in her exhibition called The Art of Roller Skating, based at the town's Time and Tide Museum until April.
Artistic roller skating is not yet recognised as an Olympic sport, which Besford said she wanted to put under the spotlight in her exhibition.
GB Skate Artistic, Britain's governing body, said not being an Olympic sport meant it struggled to gain funding, adding that it believed every nation was striving to see it one day get accepted.
Skate Norfolk runs sessions for children and adults across the county and said roller skating was much more popular than it was 10 years ago.
"We are busy, we just do not have enough volunteers to run more sessions," said a spokesperson.
Speaking about her photography, Besford said she wanted to remove the skaters from the intensity of the rink and portray them in everyday life in their bedrooms, alongside their array of medals and trophies.
She has seen them all grow from young teenagers into adulthood.
"They're all doing incredibly well, with going to university, having careers," she said.
"Their connection with the sport has very much influenced in the way that they think, and the way they believe in themselves as young adults now."

title: 'Twitchers gathered to see northern nutcracker on our gutter'
text:
'Why were 50 cameras pointing at my window?'
Looking out of your window to find "at least 50" photographers staring back at you isn't the norm for many people.
But that's what teenager Max was faced with when a rare bird settled on the guttering of the Norfolk house he was staying in.
Max had come face to face with a flock of bird fans who had travelled from far and wide to Mundesley in the hope of spotting a northern nutcracker, not seen in the UK since 1991.
The 17-year-old said: "It was mad because all the photographers that were around in the street, it looked like they were all taking photos of us."
However, he said the confusion was brief as his grandfather eventually put two and two together.
Max, from Ruislip, West London, had already read about hundreds of twitchers causing disruption to buses in Mundesley after the bird was spotted in the area.
He said the bird stayed put for five to 10 minutes, flew off and then returned to settle outside their window.
The teenager said: "I don't know much about birds myself but it wasn't a very spectacular-looking bird.
"I didn't notice it was anything special but it was amazing because it was clearly a big deal for all these other people."
Northern nutcrackers are slightly smaller than a city pigeon but much chunkier and heavier than a blackbird.
A spokesperson for the RSPB said migrations like this are "not unheard of". They said pine seed crops in Siberia have likely failed, causing many birds to venture west in search of food.
Following the descent on the village by people hoping to see the bird, avid twitcher Wayne Glossop set up a fundraiser for Mundesley Inshore Lifeboat.
He said he wanted to "give something back" to the community. It has raised almost £1,500 so far, almost tripling its target.

title: Essex man says 'my life was put on hold after crash'
text:
'Crash with speeding driver left my life on hold'
A 21-year-old man who spent four months in a critical condition after a crash with a speeding driver said his life has been put on hold.
Fletcher Rice said he now struggles with walking, jumping, running and playing his guitar, following the crash at Chipping Hill in Witham on 17 August 2025.
Essex Police said the crash on the pedestrian crossing "could easily have been fatal".
Conner Phillips, 22, of Mann Close, Witham, was driving at 53mph in a 30mph zone on the wrong side of the road when the crash happened. He admitted dangerous driving and causing serious injury by dangerous driving and was sentenced in June to two years in jail.
Before the crash, Rice had just qualified as a chef and was looking forward to going on his first holiday with friends.
However, the crash left him with serious head injuries and fractures to his pelvis, shoulder, collarbone, arm, and finger.
He now struggles to play the guitar. He said: "The whole left hand, the fingers don't work very quick so I can't play the same stuff that I could."
Rice said the crash has changed his life forever, adding: "If he didn't hit me, I'd be driving, I'd be working - I'd be normal [and] it is frustrating.
"I was just going to live my life. Now my life's been put on hold."
But he said his dad, Keith, has told him to put his energy towards getting better rather than anger towards the driver.
Following the sentencing of Phillips of Mann Close, Witham, Adam Pipe, from Essex Police said: "I want to pay tribute to the determination and resilience of the victim and his family as he tries to recover from this horrific incident.
"His [Phillips'] selfishness means the victim in this case now faces a future of extensive rehabilitation and a life that looks very different to how it did a year ago."
Rice's story is part of a campaign by Safer Essex Roads Partnership which targets young drivers, asking them to rethink their speed.
The No Respawns campaign uses gaming terminology to show the consequences of dangerous driving. The partnership has also teamed up with Essex content creators to help spread the message.
William Cubbin, manager, said: "We want to make that contrast that in computer games you do get second chances but in fact in real life there are no second chances."
He said a lot of young people do not perceive the risk associated with speeding because "there is a feeling of invulnerability when you are behind a wheel and in a car."
But he added: "There are real life-changing, life-long consequences of that speed. "

title: The homes row brewing in Basildon, the town with no local plan
text:
The homes row brewing in the town with no plan
When some senior councillors in Basildon talk about housing, one perhaps surprising name keeps getting repeated.
The Conservative cabinet member for housing said in a recent meeting that development proposals were not "Basildon homes for Basildon people – we know they're building homes for Sadiq Khan".
His reference to the London Mayor was echoed by another cabinet member in the meeting and by the borough's Reform UK group leader.
Khan has no powers over housebuilding in Basildon and targets are set by central government.
But Basildon is in the middle of a row over housing with the Labour government, with some claiming not enough infrastructure is planned and the protected green belt is threatened.
What is happening and what are the issues?
No new plan since 1998
The government wants to see 1.5 million homes built in England between 2024 and 2029.
To help plan where they will go, all local councils must have an official "local plan".
But Basildon Borough Council has not adopted a new one since 1998, a delay believed to be among the longest in England.
It has spent years trying to finalise a plan covering 2023 to 2043, with its leader blaming "changes in the administration nationally and locally".
In the introduction to the most recent draft, the borough's chief executive says the document will "manage... growth and development" in the borough, which includes the towns of Basildon, Wickford, Billericay and Pitsea.
The plan tries to identify sites for 28,000 new homes, increasing the number of homes in the borough by 34%.
Since 2015, Basildon has built an average of 422 additional homes each year, far short of its target.
In 2024-2025 that target was 1,039 but has since risen to 1,287.
Basildon borough is 63% green belt, a protection given to some areas of countryside around towns and cities.
The draft plan proposes releasing some of that to allow housebuilding, arguing it is justified by "exceptional circumstances".
What has the government said?
The government is trying to force Basildon to adopt the plan as it currently stands.
In July, Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook ordered the authority to submit its final draft by the end of the year, warning that without a plan development could happen on a "piecemeal and speculative basis".
He also noted Basildon's poor housing delivery record – in 2024-25 its performance was the fifth-worst in England – and that housing was "considerably" less affordable than the national average.
Homes cost an average of 9.66 times average annual local wages, compared to 7.63 across England.
"All of this is unlikely to improve without the prompt adoption of an up-to-date local plan," Pennycook wrote.
How did Basildon respond?
Andy Barnes, the Conservative council leader, said he was shocked by what he called the government's "authoritarian" intervention.
He said it had removed the council's ability to make further changes to the plan and warned there would be no more local decision-making.
Barnes said the current draft plan was flawed, citing concerns about infrastructure, employment land and traveller site allocations.
Last summer Basildon recorded more unauthorised Gypsy and traveller caravans than anywhere else in England.
Pennycook ordered the council to hold a public consultation on the draft plan, which it completed in September.
In its consultation response, Essex County Council raised concerns about a lack of planning for transport and education.
For Barnes, that showed the government had "forced through a consultation" and "the answer they got isn't what they wanted".
He said: "The answer is actually you can't put 28,000 homes in Basildon."
Councillors have voted to explore a legal challenge – known as a judicial review – of the minister's intervention and the housing target.
Barnes warned this could cost "millions" and he hopes other councils might join in.
Reform UK group leader Sam Journet described the draft plan as an "absolute disaster", warning it would destroy "our beautiful green spaces" and increase the borough's population by a third without adequate infrastructure.
His party was recently involved in judicial reviews that changed government plans to pause county council elections and for local government reorganisation.
"Reform UK will always back legal scrutiny," Journet added.
"You can't just bulldoze through a plan of this scale and expect no-one to challenge how it was done."
Green belt politics
Basildon is not just resisting the government's local plan intervention.
Barnes said its planning committee had "taken a fairly hard-line view" and rejected a number of housebuilding applications, many involving green belt land.
The government has tried to make it easier to develop in the green belt, introducing the concept of "grey belt" for areas that do not "serve the purpose" of the green belt and could therefore be built on.
Developers who follow "golden rules", including promising to make 50% of new homes "affordable" and boosting infrastructure, should see planning applications approved.
But Barnes said there could be a "spike in appeals", with developers challenging Basildon's rejections at the Planning Inspectorate.
Journet, deputy chair of the planning committee, said the committee was there to "scrutinise development" and that its members had a responsibility to have their say.
"If for whatever reason an application doesn't go through on that basis, then welcome to democracy," he added.
What happens next?
Basildon has asked the government to extend the deadline for submission of its local plan to the end of April 2027.
A judicial review remains an option.
Barnes said the council could also withdraw the draft local plan entirely.
The Labour group leader Gavin Callaghan recently told a meeting that planning to withdraw the plan was the "height of irresponsibility" because the minister had warned it would be "unlawful".
The council said housing delivery was a "complex issue", influenced by factors including legislation and policy, economic conditions, demand and infrastructure.
Responding to Pennycook's claim that a local plan could speed up housebuilding, a spokesperson said that this alone was no guarantee.
"Whether homes are built is largely dependent on development viability, which is in turn impacted by macro- and micro-economic conditions outside of the control of a local authority," they added.
A Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government spokesperson said: "Basildon must play their part in building the homes local people need, and we will not hesitate to step in if councils are not doing their job by putting up-to date plans in place.
"We have instructed Basildon Borough Council to progress their draft local plan at pace, and those directions remain in force."

title: Decision due on £1.5m redevelopment for Wisbech's High Street
text:
Approval of £1.5m regeneration funding recommended
Funding for a multi-million pound redevelopment project of land that has been empty for six years has been recommended for approval.
In September, Fenland District Council approved plans for flats and a commercial unit at the empty site in Wisbech's High Street, where two former council-owned, Grade II-listed buildings had been demolished in 2020.
The authority has applied for £1.5m in funding from the Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Combined Authority, which would contribute to the scheme's estimated £3.3m cost.
Documents published by the combined authority's funding committee state the bid is recommended for approval and is due to be considered at a meeting on Monday.
The approved plans include building six one-bedroom flats and commercial premises.
The scheme is expected to create three full-time equivalent jobs in the town, according to the combined authority.
It also said the scheme "responds directly to identified issues within Wisbech, including declining town centre vitality, underutilised heritage assets and reduced investor confidence".
If approved by the funding committee, the proposal would go before the combined authority board for final approval on 25 November. The funding would come from its Local Growth Fund.
Fenland District Council has also bid for £1.5m in funding from The National Lottery Heritage Fund, with the remaining costs covered by its own capital funding.

title: Rare damselfly spotted by restored chalk river near Hertford
text:
Rare damselfly spotted by restored chalk river
An endangered damselfly has been spotted in wetlands created by an "ambitious" project that restored a stretch of a rare chalk river.
The scarce blue-tailed damselfly, one of the world's earliest flying insects, was recorded alongside the River Ash near Hertford.
The 4.3-mile (7km) stretch at the Easneye Estate was restored to its original course last year.
The Herts and Middlesex Wildlife Trust said that for species facing increasing pressure, creating and restoring suitable habitats was "vital to reversing declines".
The scarce blue-tailed damselfly was recorded at two monitoring sites located close together in late summer.
A new assessment of Britain's dragonflies and damselflies highlighted growing concerns about the future of some species.
The British Dragonfly Society's Red List review reclassified the scarce blue-tailed damselfly from Near Threatened to Endangered.
It found that eight species were now classed as endangered, twice the number identified in the previous assessment in 2008.
The River Ash is one of about 260 chalk rivers in the world, and the restoration project has included the creation of new gravel beds.
The trust said brown trout were already spawning on them.
In addition, monitoring carried out before and after the restoration found an increase in river invertebrates, including mayflies and stoneflies.
Sarah Perry, rivers recovery manager at the trust said: "Natural rivers, connected floodplains and healthy wetlands support biodiversity by providing places for wildlife to feed and breed.
"They also help water move through the landscape and can contribute to resilience against both flooding and drought.
"The scarce blue-tailed damselfly sightings along the River Ash offer a hopeful example of what these efforts can achieve."

title: 'My cattle don't care I'm in Clarkson's choir' say Bucks farmer
text:
'My cattle don't care I'm in Clarkson's choir'
Richard Heady has been involved in farm life ever since he could "lift a barrel".
His day job is tending hundreds of cows on his family's Buckinghamshire farm, a role he has undertaken full-time since he was 22.
But in May, the 39-year-old's life changed when the group he is part of, Hawkstone Farmers' Choir – put together by Jeremy Clarkson to support farmers with their mental health – won Britain's Got Talent.
"It's such a great feeling, and then you come back to the everyday life and the cattle couldn't care less what I've been up to," he said.
His family runs the WF Heady and Sons farm in Newton Longville, near Milton Keynes.
"We have beef cattle, we grow all of our own food for the cattle, our silage, beans and barley; then we also have arable crops: wheat for bread, oats for porridge and muesli," he said.
Heady said there had been times when the pressures of farm life had "gotten tough" for him.
"I've had a really good support network around me – I've changed things on the farm to make it slightly easier," he said.
"I do a lot of running, which helps clear my head. The key is just talking; opening up.
"It's so nice to have these breaks off the farm, catching up with friends, singing in unison – but then you come back to earth with a bump."
After the win, the choir announced it was donating £50,000 of its £250,000 prize money to five charities supporting farming, mental health, and rural communities.
"It's a community of farmers trying to do their best for the whole farming industry and we're so lucky that we can do that in a fun and kind of buoyant way," said Heady.
"It's a really hard message to get across but if we can do it by singing and just having a good time and spreading the message I just feel so honoured and lucky that we can do that."
Heady said the choir was made possible by its director, Lizzie Dean, from Milton Keynes, who was its "heart and soul".
"She completely took a bunch of farmers who were probably in their shells a bit, scared to show vulnerability, and she just pulled that out of us and just got us acting silly and sharing our stories and opening up," he said.
He does not think they would have made it past the first round without her.
Since the win the choir has released a song and announced a tour, which needs to be juggled with working life.
"I'm going to be working on the farm, evenings, mornings, and shooting off to try and do the shows and then shooting back as soon as I can to get back and finish doing the work," said Heady.
He said he was only able to do it with "fantastic family support".
"They've all had to step up and my wife's doing far more of the children's ferrying around.
"My dad and uncle are doing more than they should be doing because I should be the younger generation, taking on most of the work.
"I just owe them so much for helping me along this journey."

title: More anger and uncertainty – so what now for local councils?
text:
More anger and uncertainty – so what now for local councils?
It has been another week when politicians and council officers across the East have shaken their heads in disbelief and probably uttered a few choice expletives as well.
The reason? Yet another delay to the plans to reform local government.
This time it involves local government reorganisation (LGR), which would see existing county, borough, district and city councils replaced by large unitary authorities.
But while LGR is on hold again, the other big local government reform – directly elected mayors – has moved another step forward.
So what is going on and when, if ever, will we see some change?
Why the delay?
Local councils are responsible for providing or overseeing more than 150 local services from social care to emptying the bins.
They matter, and so does the way they are run.
In March the government decided that Norfolk and Suffolk should each have three unitary authorities, while Essex would have five and Hertfordshire four.
But these were controversial decisions, prompting some local councils to threaten legal action and in September, days before they were to go to court, the plans were put on hold.
There was also a sparky debate going on over what local government should look like in Cambridgeshire. A decision was promised by September.
Now Local Government Minister Jim McMahon has announced that while he can give the go-ahead to five new authorities in the country, he needs longer to make a decision about the councils in the East.
"All options and proposals for those areas will remain under consideration, and I will approach them all with an open mind... It is important to allow the process to run its course and to allow full and proper consideration," he told MPs.
He has promised a decision by early 2027 and also revealed that the new councils will not come into being until 2029, a year later than previously planned.
'Nothing short of a farce'
The news was greeted with fury in Parliament.
Shadow Local Government Secretary Katie Lam MP said the situation was "nothing short of a farce".
She said: "People across the country are left without any sense of which council will be providing services in the year and years to come."
Liberal Democrat MP Pippa Heylings attacked the government's "botched handling" of the process.
"In my constituency of South Cambridgeshire, one of the fastest-growing areas in the country, businesses need certainty to invest and plan, councils need certainty to set budgets and deliver services, and council staff deserve clarity about their future," she said.
The Local Government Association said "many councils [will] remain frustrated by the situation they have been placed in. All councils affected need urgent clarity on the next steps."
McMahon insisted that the plans for LGR were "robust".
But Reform UK, which was involved in some of the legal action, was delighted.
"It was a ridiculous plan [and] fundamentally a bad decision," Peter Harris, leader of Essex County Council, told the BBC's Politics East programme.
And he now expects ministers to change their plans. "We are willing to talk to the government about making the changes necessary to make councils work better," he said.
Government MPs are insisting that LGR will still happen and stress that it's important to get the details right to avoid any further legal challenges.
They also point out that there is a new ministerial team in post following Andy Burnham's appointment as prime minister. It needs to be sure of what it's doing.
But a growing number of local politicians are sceptical and wonder, after the other delays, if ministers can ever come up with proposals that will command popular support.
"At the moment we have absolutely no idea what this government is thinking, and that's because the government isn't sure what it's thinking after two and a half years," said Jerome Mayhew, the Conservative MP for Broadland and Fakenham.
Several MPs have suggested to me that, with many opposition councillors and MPs either lukewarm about or openly hostile to the plans, and public enthusiasm seemingly lacking, will the prime minister really want to spend so much political capital getting LGR over the line in the run-up to a general election?
But devolution IS happening
The plans for combined authorities with directly elected mayors have been on and off for the last 15 years but with the former mayor of Greater Manchester now in charge, there seems to be no stopping them.
Burnham sees devolution as a way of moving money out of Whitehall to the regions where local people know best how to spend it.
Cambridgeshire and Peterborough already have a directly elected mayor and Norfolk and Suffolk, along with Essex, are due to have mayors in 2028.
Milton Keynes, Bedfordshire and Northamptonshire are likely to follow in the future.
This was very clear in the budget where the Chancellor John Healey announced that directly elected mayors would eventually be allowed to keep 100% of local business rates and a share of local income tax revenue.
There are also plans to give the combined authorities increased funding and make it easier for them to borrow money.
"These are long-term funding streams that they can use to back investment into big local infrastructure, so that more of the money that is raised locally can be invested and spent locally," he said.
The government's plans for this part of LGR are taking shape.
But the uncertainty continues with staff and councillors trying to run their existing authorities with one hand while trying to plan for the future – whatever that might be – with the other.

title: On the frontline of social care as prime minister promises reform
text:
On the frontline of social care as PM promises reform
Prime Minister Andy Burnham wants to offer access to free social care services to everyone in England and to put his plans to voters at the next general election.
He told the BBC that it would be a system in which "everyone contributes, everyone is covered" and did not rule out tax rises, acknowledging it may be "difficult or unpopular" with some.
BBC Politics East has been looking at the four key areas of care provided now, spending time with care workers and managers to find out about their experiences and what they would like from a new expanded system.
'You want to make it count'
Tsitsis Tabvuma, who is from Zimbabwe, is a senior care worker with Caremark in Cambridgeshire.
She saw three people, mainly older people with health needs, from 09:00 to 12:00 on the day we went out with her.
"When you go into a home you are the only person they see that day or that week, so you want to make it count," she said.
"If you go in and do it all in a rush it is no good. If you have to do things in a rush you cannot do what needs to be done.
"You can go into a person's home and leave them with a clean home but an empty heart because you haven't had time to have a good conversation with them."
Robert Johnstone, managing director of Caremark (Cambridge and South Cambridgeshire), said if visa schemes do not allow people like Tabvuma, it will cause a major problem for the care sector.
He said recruiting her was "expensive but it's worth it because you get quality carers that are going to be around for three to five years".
Without these schemes, Johnstone said he could see many older people missing out on the care they needed.
'You realise how lovely our residents are'
The BBC spent the night with staff at the ArmsCare home for older residents in Hunstanton, Norfolk.
Some residents wake up in the middle of the night, while others do not want to go to bed or cannot sleep.
Home manager Jasmine Sehgal said: "I heard a resident screaming. I went to the room and found him on the floor.
"We have crash mats in place especially for residents with a high risk of falling out of bed, so the bed is lower and there is a crash mat in place. He's absolutely fine."
Later, when it was a bit quieter, Sehgal said: "There are times when you want to throw in the towel and ask 'Why am I in this sector?' but then you spend a little time here and you realise how lovely our residents are.
"You realise how much they need you and that just changes your whole perspective."
'You realise it is more than just a job'
The charity HFT runs a home for 11 adults with complex needs, including disabilities and autism, in Shefford, Bedfordshire.
Support worker Prince Masvaure has been working with Ali, who is blind and cannot talk or walk.
"As time goes on, you realise it is more than just a job," said Masvaure.
"For me, working in care, I see it as more like a calling. I'm here with Ali and it's more like he is my brother.
"I need to be there for him. I need to lift him up. I need to give him a hand. I need to support him all the way."
'We try to make the job as enjoyable as possible'
Claire Davies-Sond, service manager with HFT, said it was difficult finding staff for the home.
"The pay is not great in social care. For us, we pay above the minimum wage and we try to make the job as enjoyable as possible but we still struggle [to find employees]."
Steve Veevers, HFT chief executive, said: "As someone who has worked in care for 40 years, the multitude of demand on our support workers, I think, is on parity to some areas of the NHS, such as a paramedic."
'It is hard when you've got funding restraints'
Fay Bartholomew, transition co-ordinator at the Milton Keynes offices of national charity MacIntyre, works with young people as they transition to adult care services.
"The work that I do with them in their final year is to let them look and see what is out there," she said.
"Their voices and choices matter, but it is hard when you've got funding restraints in all areas of care.
"There are limitations. Everyone is using the same pot of money and a lot of the time it can be down to the resources that are there.
"I'm also so proud of them. I don't like to let them go. We still like to check in."
Her message to the prime minister is that it would be great to see care work seen as "more as a profession" as those in the industry "strive for the very best for the individual".
'We're still ambitious'
Bruce Smith, head of No Limits for MacIntyre, said: "I think what motivates me and all our frontline staff is to really unlock the skills and passions that the young people we work with have and to see them flourish."
He said despite budget pressures, "what's important for us is we're still ambitious. We find ways to shout about the talent these young people have."
What is the government's view?
A Department of Health and Social Care spokesman said: "This government is committed to fixing adult social care and creating a National Care Service.
"Social care workers are skilled professionals who will form the backbone of the new National Care Service, so we are developing a workforce plan to support recruitment, retention and career development.
"We are also establishing the first ever Fair Pay Agreement for care workers and making over £4.6bn additional funding available for adult social care in 2028-29."

title: Democrats are used to heartbreak in Texas - will Talarico turn the tide?
text:
Democrats are used to heartbreak in Texas - could Talarico turn the tide?
The race for a US Senate seat in Texas may prove crucial in determining which party controls Congress next year – a significant prize in its own right - but for both parties it represents so much more than that.
For the Democrats, their losing streak in statewide elections now stretches back more than three decades. In the second most populous state in America, liberals have been in the wilderness for a generation.
But polls suggest their candidate, 37-year-old James Talarico, may be on the verge of breaking through and turning a Texas Senate seat blue for the first time since 1988.
That would be a dream scenario for Democrats - and a potential nightmare for Republicans.
"If the Democrats do pull it off, I think it's going to cause a lot of soul searching and a lot of psychological damage to the Republican Party in Texas and nationwide," said Brendan Steinhauser, a Texas-based Republican campaign strategist.
These dramatic stakes help explain how this Senate race has rocketed to become the most expensive in US history, with total spending reaching more than half a billion dollars.
For Talarico, it has been a remarkable rise for a candidate who in 2025 was a relatively unknown state-level Democrat.
At the Fiesta Center in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday night, the line to see the softly spoken former teacher, who studied to be a Christian minister, stretched around the building and down the wide parking lot to a busy road.
In this dusty western plains town of about 250,000, which voted overwhelmingly for President Donald Trump two years ago, a visit from a major Democratic candidate on the eve of an election was unusual.
"It's just so amazing to watch," said Aaron Gonzalez, the Democratic Party chair for Hockley County, which borders Lubbock. "This time is different."
When Talarico took the stage before an estimated 3,000 supporters – with another thousand listening on speakers outside - his pitch was a familiar one for many national Democrats this year, albeit with a Texas twist.
He railed against a conservative political establishment that he said is insensitive to the economic hardship of average Americans. He condemned the corrosive influence of big money in politics. And he promised to advance a "comprehensive anti-corruption agenda" in the Senate.
"Texans are ready for change," he said. "We are done with the extremism and the corruption. We're done with the politics of division, and we are ready for something new."
The slogan for his final two weeks of campaigning – "clear eyes, full hearts, can't lose" – is taken from Friday Night Lights, a popular early 2000s TV show about a plucky small-town Texas high school football team.
His music playlist leans heavily on twangy Texas country music. He celebrates Texas breakfast tacos, quotes legendary Texas singer-songwriter Lyle Lovett and frequently mentions that his ties to the state go back eight generations.
In the Lubbock audience, Andrew Robinson, a student from nearby Texas Tech University, liked what he heard. But the 26-year-old's optimism was tempered by an entire lifetime spent watching Democrats try, and fail, to get a toehold in the state.
"A Talarico win would mean so much," he said. "I haven't been keen on wanting to stay in Texas. And if the government were to change, it could give me a reason."
For Republicans, a Democratic win in Texas would have a very different meaning.
At roughly the same time Talarico was addressing his supporters in the Fiesta Center, Trump – alongside the Republican Party's Senate candidate Ken Paxton – was just a few miles away, in a venue twice the size.
"If you go out and vote, we're going to have a tremendous win in Texas," the president told the crowd.
Trump's visit to reliably-Republican Lubbock suggests the party is concerned about turnout even in the most conservative portions of the state. It is a worry that has been echoed by other Texas Republicans.
"Understand, we could lose Texas," Texas Senator Ted Cruz said in his podcast on Friday. "The Democrats are massively out-turning-out the Republicans."
Don Huffines, who is running for election as the state's chief financial officer, issued an even more dire warning. "Texas is the foundation of the Republican Party in America," he posted on X.
"When the foundation breaks, it all falls apart. When we lose Texas, we lose the USA."
For weeks now, party leaders have been warning that a liberal breakthrough in the Lone Star State could have dire consequences.
They fear a Talarico win would motivate more local Democrats to run for statewide and federal offices. Better quality candidates with more funding could lead to a snowball effect similar to the Democratic inroads seen in other southern states, such as Georgia, North Carolina and Virginia.
"I think that it's pretty clear that Republicans, especially candidates, consultants, operatives, and others who are active in the party, see that this is a real threat," said Steinhauser.
"The days of waving this off and saying that Texas would never turn blue are over."
For the Texas Senate race to come to the point where recent polls suggest Talarico has a slim but stable lead has required a unique confluence of events and political dynamics – a "perfect storm", in the words of Steinhauser.
"Everything that could go well for the Democrats is going well," he said, "and everything that could go badly for the Republicans is going badly."
But it is also a whirlwind that, in a significant part, has been sown over the past year by Trump himself.
The national environment for Republicans is a harsh one.
Voters are frustrated with high consumer costs, including the price of petrol, and largely blame Trump's tariff policies and the Iran war.
Political corruption has become an issue of growing concern. Democrats, independents and many Republicans in a recent Cook political report poll identified "greedy billionaires and corporations" and politicians seeking "personal gain" as the ones to blame.
Texas-specific issues have also contributed to a hostile climate for the in-power party.
Polling and recent special elections in Texas indicate that Hispanic voters – many of whom switched to Trump to help him win the White House in 2024 – have soured on the administration's immigration enforcement policies.
Hispanics make up nearly a third of the state's population - and in more than a week of early voting in Texas, they have been casting ballots in historically large numbers.
Data centre construction, which Texas Republicans had touted as a welcome investment in the state, has drawn widespread criticism, particularly in rural areas that have traditionally been solidly conservative.
Texas Governor Greg Abbott, in his own tight re-election race, recently announced a one-year moratorium on AI construction in the state – a reflection of how quickly the issue has become a political liability.
"It's bad for Republicans," one Texas political strategist, who asked to remain anonymous, told the BBC. "We're asking a whole lot of the electorate at this point for us to continue to be the guys in charge."
Then there's the baggage that Paxton, who defeated longtime incumbent Senator John Cornyn in a contentious primary campaign earlier this year, brings to the race.
The 63-year-old Republican successfully painted the 74-year-old Cornyn as too old and too out-of-touch with Texas conservatives. He received a late boost, just days before his run-off election victory over Cornyn, in the form of a Trump endorsement.
"Ken Paxton has gone through a lot, in many cases, very unfairly, but he is a Fighter, and knows how to WIN," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "Our Country needs Fighters, and also Loyalty to the Cause of Greatness."
The "a lot" the president referenced Paxton going through includes a 2015 federal indictment on charges of securities fraud – later dropped – and a 2023 impeachment by the Republican-controlled Texas House of Representatives on corruption, bribery and abuse of power charges.
The Texas Senate would later acquit Paxton after Trump intervened to pressure state Republican leaders.
All of this has meant that Paxton has more than a few critics – and enemies - in Texas, including within his own party.
Talarico, by contrast, has proven to be an effective candidate. The state legislator defeated a well-known opponent, Dallas Congresswoman Jasmine Crockett, in the Democratic primary.
Since earning the nomination, he has maintained his polling lead despite a withering onslaught of negative advertising - much of it funded by the world's richest man Elon Musk, whose SpaceX company is based in Texas.
Musk alone has funnelled more than $170m into the race. Trump's MAGA Inc. committee has chipped in $40m.
While Paxton has proven to be an ineffective fundraiser, the third-party money spent on his behalf has blanketed the airwaves in the state – spilling over into sporting events involving Texas teams that air across the nation.
They have targeted Talarico for his past comments supporting transgender people, for calling "radicalised white men" a domestic terrorism threat and for criticising the fossil fuel and beef industries – two powerful interests in the state.
Talarico has distanced himself from some of those earlier comments, arguing many were taken out of context and "missed the mark" or were "deliberately provocative" or "cringy".
Meanwhile, the Texas Democrat has proven to be a historically successful fundraiser, amassing more than $140m in donations over the course of his campaign and setting a three-month fundraising record for a Senate candidate.
The funding has allowed Talarico to hit back at Paxton, highlighting his past controversies, and defending himself from Republican attacks.
He frequently leans into his religious upbringing – as the grandson of a Southern Baptist preacher who spent time in a seminary – leavening his stump speeches with biblical references.
There is one particular passage Talarico has been partial to of late – the familiar Old Testament showdown between scrappy David and the giant Goliath.
"We are going up against our own Goliaths," he said in Lubbock. "The billionaire mega-donors, the corporate special interests, the entire Washington DC establishment. Their power is real, but so is ours."
But the power of Texas Democrats has been overestimated in the past. In 2018, Congressman Beto O'Rourke posted his own historic fundraising numbers, generated serious national attention and ultimately lost to Texas Senator Cruz by just over 2%.
Talarico's polling lead, while stable, continues to rest near the margin of error in most surveys. And last-minute Republican appeals, as well as Trump's repeated campaign visits, could spur conservatives to turn out in greater numbers on election day, erasing any Democratic early voting advantages.
Inside the tiny Democratic Party office at a Talarico rally in Amarillo on Tuesday, retired schoolteacher Terri Mills listened to the candidate's stump speech.
Despite acknowledging the decades of Democratic futility and false dawns, she said she was allowing herself to hope for a Democratic victory once again.
"I have gotten my hopes up before, you know," she said. "But I do feel that this time is a little different."

title: Reeves says UK's future should be inside the EU
text:
Reeves says UK's future should be inside the EU
Former Chancellor Rachel Reeves has argued the UK's future should be inside the EU, and that Brexit has made the country "poorer, weaker and less secure".
In her first major intervention since leaving the Treasury, Reeves said she welcomed debate around the UK's relationship with Europe.
At the last election, Labour's manifesto said a Labour government would stay outside the EU and make Brexit work.
But Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said there needs to be an honest discussion about what the future relationship looks like.
The Conservatives have said there is no desire to rerun the Brexit debate and Reform UK's Nigel Farage has said there is no mandate to pursue closer EU ties.
Labour's 2024 election manifesto ruled out a return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.
Burnham has said that any changes would require a mandate at a general election, which is next due by 2029.
In the Sunday Times, Reeves wrote: "No-one in the Treasury ever doubted where my instincts were. I do believe Britain's future lies in the European Union."
She said supporters of rejoining the EU had to "make the argument, demonstrate tangible benefits and to get the next steps right".
Reeves added that at the forthcoming UK-EU summit, she hoped for confirmation of the youth mobility scheme she has been pushing for since she was in office.
She also said she was hoping for "progress towards entry" into the Security Action for Europe (SAFE) scheme.
Announced last March, SAFE is part of an EU-wide effort to rearm after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
A defence pact agreed with the EU last May paved the way for UK-based defence companies to be part of projects funded by SAFE.
In her piece for the Sunday Times, Reeves also sought to defend her record in office.
She wrote about the need for governments to be "braver" in building big infrastructure projects and "clear eyed" about the risks and benefits AI would drive in advanced economies.
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said she "can't even believe we are reopening" the Brexit debate.
She told BBC One's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg: "This is not something that is needed in order to cut welfare, in order to spend money on defence.
"We are having yet another Westminster bubble argument about the EU when it is time for us to actually start using the opportunities, fix mistakes that have been made and go into the future."
Badenoch added: "I do not want to indulge Andy Burnham's fantasies about redoing the referendum because he doesn't have a plan for what to do today."
Burnham told Badenoch during the most recent session of Prime Minister's Questions that he was focused on "getting a better deal for Britain, that is my responsibility".
The next UK-EU summit will take place in Brussels on 20 November.
description: In her first major intervention since leaving the Treasury, Rachel Reeves says Brexit has made the UK "poorer, weaker and less secure".
