title: Shops looted as German cost-of-living protests turn violent
text:
Shops looted as German cost-of-living protests turn violent
Rioters looted shops in central Frankfurt late on Saturday as clashes erupted in German cities over the cost of living.
Besides Frankfurt - Germany's financial hub - there were incidents of violence in Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg, with police saying they used water cannon to disperse protesters who were targeting emergency workers with fireworks, stones and bottles.
Thousands joined largely peaceful demonstrations earlier in the day. They were organised by the campaign group Gen Z regelt - meaning "Gen Z takes charge" - to protest against underfunding in schools, the high cost of living, public spending cuts and military service.
The unrest in Germany follows similar youth-led mass protests in France, where more than 320,000 people also demonstrated on Saturday.
On Sunday, Germany's Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told Bild newspaper that overnight police had prevented "violence like that seen in Paris" in recent weeks and called for "harsh punishments" for rioters and looters.
Overnight, a large section of Frankfurt's main shopping street was closed off by police. A police spokesperson said many arrests were made in the city.
Authorities in Frankfurt, Munich and Berlin reported as many as 18,000 protesters, roughly half of what the organisers had estimated on their website. German media say tens of thousands protested in German cities on Saturday.
Gen Z regelt spokesperson Lina Friedrich said the demonstrations were "to fight for peace and freedom, rather than for war and coercion".
She said: "What matters most to us is better support for the health and education systems. We are against compulsory military service and we are in favour of a fairer distribution of the burden."
On Saturday night Frankfurt police said "violent riots" were occurring in the city centre and that special police units had been deployed.
The windows of several shops had been smashed and molotov cocktails were thrown at emergency services, police said.
Officials said the windows of a gun shop were smashed and that they had seized two weapons after arresting a suspect. People also broke into other shops, stealing items like trainers.
Roman Poseck, interior minister of Hesse state, of which Frankfurt is the biggest city, said that "around 100 clearly identified left-wing extremists" had infiltrated the protest in the city. He added that it was "shameful" how the protests had ended.
"We all have those images from France in our minds - looting, burning houses, burning police vehicles, and attacks on police officers... France must not be held up as a model in this regard."
Police said the situation calmed down overnight into Sunday in the city.
Similar instances took place in other German cities, following largely peaceful demonstrations.
In Cologne, police said officers were attacked near the main train station, with bottles thrown and a bicycle launched.
Cologne's police chief Johannes Hermanns said it was "deeply saddening that young people who wanted to peacefully demonstrate for their future were infiltrated today by extremists who had nothing but violence in mind".
A smaller demonstration in the evening in Berlin - following larger protests in the day - resulted in 27 police officers being injured, and up to 56 people temporarily detained, Berlin police said.
In Hamburg, people dressed in black set off fireworks and set barricades on fire, with public broadcaster NDR reporting that 120 people were arrested.
The protests in Germany took place on the same day as other large-scale demonstrations in Europe.
In France, more than 320,000 people took part in a third consecutive weekend of largely peaceful protests in cities across the country, demanding action on the high cost of living and poor public services, especially in the education sector.
Thousands of police officers were deployed across the country, and officers fired tear gas at demonstrators in some cities.
There were more than 770 arrests across France during the demonstrations on Saturday, roughly half as many as the previous week's protests, the French interior ministry said.
French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said a police officer had been injured by a molotov cocktail and French prosecutors later launched an attempted murder probe.
Police in Paris said several hundred rioters had attacked security forces with projectiles.
French protest organisers, the Gilet Jaune, or Yellow Vests, have said dozens of protesters have been seriously injured during recent demonstrations across the country, with many hurt by "grenades".
France suspended the use of one type of stun grenade while policing student protests in early October after a 15-year-old's hand was blown off, but French newspaper Le Monde has reported that police have continued to use a different model in subsequent protests.
Protests also took place in Italy, with some clashes between police and demonstrators in Rome and Turin.
In Portugal, police moved to clear a new tent camp that had been assembled after thousands marched to protest against a rental bill that they argue could worsen a housing crisis in the country, where house prices have more than doubled over the past decade.
Mostly young protesters have recently taken to the streets in a swathe of European nations: France, Belgium, Ireland, Spain, Portugal, Italy, Greece, Serbia and Albania.
While the specific demands vary from country to country, the protesters have largely focused on cost-of-living issues, such as access to housing, the quality of education and cuts to public services.
description: The protests in cities across Germany - including Berlin, Hamburg and Frankfurt - came on the same day hundreds of thousands also protested in France.

title: Second night of drone disruption at Jersey Airport
text:
Second night of drone disruption at Jersey Airport
People at Jersey Airport have said they are frustrated and angry that "unauthorised drone" activity caused more flight cancellations on Saturday, the second night in a row.
Jersey Airport said at 20:05 GMT on Saturday that it had experienced disruption "affecting inbound flights as a result of further drone activity in the vicinity of the airfield".
States of Jersey Police are investigating the incidents and appealed to anyone with information about who was responsible to come forward.
The Government of Jersey said it had been working on arrangements to reduce the risk of further disruption and to minimise passenger impact. There were no reports of disruption to Sunday evening's flights.
Jersey RFC said its team's flight home from Southampton on Saturday evening had been cancelled and it would cost the club "thousands and thousands of pounds", including unforeseen hotel costs.
Also caught in the chaos was Iselin Jones, director of Jersey's The Moorings Hotel, whose flight home from Madeira was diverted to Paris.
Pacific Basirwe was waiting for his wife and young son to fly in from London Heathrow when he heard the news.
He said: "It's annoying, this should be regulated, and the people doing those things should be prosecuted.
"It's been two days in a row now… If there is no further action, they will keep doing it, which is not good."
Insp Rob McCallum said it was believed "two or three" drones had entered the restricted airspace on Saturday evening, but they were not thought to be linked to terrorism.
Chief Minister of Jersey Senator Lyndon Farnham said operating a drone close to an airport was "not a prank or a harmless hobby".
"To those responsible, the message is clear: if you are identified, you should expect to face the full consequences of the law," he said.
'Utmost seriousness'
He continued: "The government and our operational partners are treating these incidents with the utmost seriousness.
"We are also working closely with UK authorities and specialist agencies to explore additional operational support, enhanced detection capability and counter-drone technology."
He added: "The public can be assured that all relevant agencies are working together at pace and that lessons from these incidents will be acted upon swiftly.
"Our airport is a vital lifeline for the island. We will not tolerate behaviour that jeopardises its safe operation or undermines public confidence in our transport infrastructure."
Airline Loganair, whose Southampton to Jersey flights on Friday and Saturday evening were cancelled, said it had provided overnight accommodation to all affected passengers.
It added extra aircraft were flown from Scotland on both days to "protect early morning services from Jersey and minimise disruption".
Jersey RFC said the plane the team was on, operated by another airline, taxied but was returned to the stand and stood there for a few hours before finally being cancelled at about 21:30 GMT on Saturday.
A spokesperson said: "As this was a group booking, there was no scope for rebooking given that it is half-term and sufficient flights were not available today.
"The team have had to rebook from Southampton on Monday morning. As a community club we have to work incredibly hard to fund local rugby and travel.
"Put simply this will cost thousands and thousands of pounds, including unforeseen hotel costs.
"Whilst we'll leave the authorities to investigate, the acts of a few have far impacting consequences both financial and physical. It couldn't be further from a 'bit of fun'."
Iselin Jones was flying home from Madeira on Saturday night when her plane got diverted to Paris after circling over Jersey.
"We were descending ready to land, when we were told that Jersey Airport was closed due to renewed drone activity and we most probably wouldn't be able to land and would be diverting to Paris," she explained.
"After holding for 10 to 15 minutes and circling at Jersey that is indeed what happened."
Jones said she was due to return on a rescheduled flight to Jersey at 20:00 GMT on Sunday but she and other passengers were uneasy there could be more disruption.
"Obviously, I think everybody's a little bit stressed about the fact that it's another nighttime flight," she said.
"Evening seems to be when the drones are active and we would have all preferred to be flying during daylight hours, either in the morning or at lunchtime, so we're all now trying to make the most of having an extra day in Paris.
"If we end up having the same experience that the people coming in from London had the first night of the drones, and then again yesterday, I think obviously you know it starts to feel a little bit different to that."
Richard De La Haye has been a taxi driver for more than 40 years and believes the drone activity is affecting business for drivers like him.
He said: "It's a bit of a nightmare because we're sitting here for a couple of hours really not knowing what's going to happen."
De La Haye added: "If we pull away and the flights come in then people will be stranded waiting for taxis but if they don't come in we're sat here for two hours waiting for passengers.
"It's getting silly and I don't know the answer, but it really needs to be resolved, quite honestly."

description: Jersey Airport says it experienced disruption to inbound flights on Friday and Saturday due to drone activity.

title: Neoclouds: These firms you've never heard of are feeding fears the AI bubble could burst
text:
These firms you've never heard of are feeding fears the AI bubble could burst
A once-obscure corner of the AI ecosystem finds itself in the spotlight – and investors don't all like what they see.
Names like CoreWeave and Nebius are familiar to the tech set in San Francisco and Silicon Valley.
These data centre companies, known as neocloud firms, run large warehouses packed with expensive computers, which they lease to major AI developers like Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta.
They're now the subject of one of Silicon Valley's most heated debates.
Many question whether neocloud firms are financially sound and what their recent stumbles tell us about the state of the AI economy.
Analysts at Gartner predict by 2030, 80% of neocloud firms will "cease independent operations", while Forrester's experts expect at least three of them to be imminently acquired "as finances get shaky".
On Thursday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent tried to downplay recent concerns about neocloud firms, calling them "a small component of the overall ecosystem" on CNBC.
Debt worries
Neocloud firms often finance themselves by signing long-term lease contracts with major tech customers who need quick access to computing power.
Firms can then borrow money using those contracts – plus the AI chips they purchase – as collateral, explained analyst Cory Johnson of "The Quiet Period" IPO research outfit.
He said debt is common across neocloud firms because the hardware has to be paid for up front.
Take the industry leader: CoreWeave. It's a fraction of the size of some of the Big Tech companies it serves.
But Johnson believes lenders sometimes consider the creditworthiness of CoreWeave's customers, like Microsoft or Meta, more than the company's when they lend.
"This helps explain how CoreWeave accumulated $35.1bn (£26.3bn) in debt," he said.
Some jittery investors appear to be having second thoughts.
CoreWeave stock has lost a quarter of its value over the past month, and it's not alone.
Shares in other neocloud firms like Nebius, IREN, and Applied Digital have all shed about that much if not more during the same period.
Debt investors also appear spooked, and are demanding ever-higher returns from several firms in the sector.
CoreWeave's CEO Mike Intrator has said that the market is acting "irrationally" and has expressed confidence in its business model. Some of the world's most consequential companies are queuing up for CoreWeave's infrastructure and other AI services.
Origins in crypto
Several neocloud firms have their roots in the volatile crypto mining industry, made of companies that generate cryptocurrencies, like Bitcoin.
Crypto miners use some of the same kind of physical infrastructure that is used to develop AI.
CoreWeave was founded in 2017 with a focus on mining Ethereum.
IREN, Core Scientific and Applied Digital also started in crypto mining.
Their infrastructure left them well-positioned when AI exploded in 2022 with the introduction of OpenAI's ChatGPT.
One outlier is Nebius, which was known as Yandex NV when it was part of Russia's version of Google before splitting off and changing its name in 2024.
Now, the success of these firms hinges on the fate of major AI developers and hyperscalers – even larger data centre operators which neocloud firms often count as key customers.
"There is just an enormous amount of spending getting injected into the system," said Melissa Otto, head of Visible Alpha Research at S&P Global. "It's an arms race."
And neoclouds have benefitted.
But the trade-off of their model is "greater financial risk" in the face of change, said Forrester VP and principal analyst Charlie Dai.
That includes any adjustments that their Big Tech customers might make to their spending plans.
This past week, when Microsoft and Google forecast less AI spending than Wall Street analysts had projected, shares in several neocloud firms tumbled.
Much is also riding on Anthropic and OpenAI, which are both expected to start selling shares to the public in the months ahead.
If AI proves to be a bubble – and bursts – neocloud firms "are definitely going to face collateral damage," said Bradley Tusk of Tusk Ventures.
'Guppy-level death'
The future of the neoclouds also depend on their ability to keep borrowing, which gets more expensive as interest rates rise.
In a recent social media post, Elon Musk suggested this challenge could lead more than 200 neoclouds to "see guppy-level death and consolidation", with the smallest firms being the most vulnerable.
"Some will make it through, but not many," he added.
For now, analysts at Yorkville Ives said demand for computing power still exceeds supply, adding that neoclouds are filling an important gap that larger data centre companies cannot fill.
But to some, the neocloud sector's recent wobbles are concerning.
Microsoft recently cancelled a deal with a British neocloud outfit called Nscale amid power supply issues which could last through to 2030.
Australia's Firmus just shelved plans to start selling shares to the public.
These developments come amid a public backlash against data centres and questions about how much value AI can add to worker productivity.
"There's reason to worry," said Johnson.

title: Newspaper headlines: 'PM lets down the King' and 'Kenny's secret night at Maya's'
text:
'PM lets down the King' and 'Kenny's secret night at Maya's'
Warning: Sunday's paper review contains spoilers for The Celebrity Traitors.
The Sunday Times leads with Rachel Reeves' comments on the UK rejoining the EU - noting that, in her article, the former chancellor does not offer any thoughts on a timeline, or whether a fresh referendum would be needed. The chief minister of Gibraltar is much more forthcoming: Fabian Picardo tells the Sunday Mirror he is looking forward to seeing the issue go before the British people once again, in a "very clear manifesto commitment", or a fresh public vote.
In the Sunday Telegraph, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accuses the government of making unfunded spending promises that will need to be paid for through tax rises. She says proposals including setting up a National Care Service have left a "colossal" black hole in the public finances after the budget. The Treasury tells the paper the budget met fiscal rules and set borrowing on a downward path.
"An ill-timed intervention that's triggered a fresh call for billions" is how the Mail on Sunday sees Andy Burnham's suggestion that the UK could apologise for its role in the transatlantic slave trade. An editorial in The Sunday Express accuses the prime minister of having made life harder for King Charles III during his Caribbean tour and suggests he stop "shooting from the hip" to avoid sowing international chaos. The last thing this country needs, says the Sun on Sunday, is what the paper calls a new chorus of financial demands from governments, lawyers and bleeding-heart campaigners.
The Sunday Times reports on claims that an AI programme ignored the evidence given to a landmark maternity review by women who say they were harmed by a drive for births with no medical intervention. The Amos review concluded in June that what is known as "normal birth ideology" was not widespread in maternity care in England. But the paper says there were many devastating accounts among the more than 10,000 responses which, the Times has learned, were fed into Microsoft Copilot, with NHS staff asking it to "identity themes and produce summaries". Former Health Secretary Sir Jeremy Hunt tells the paper the allegations are deeply troubling. Baroness Amos did not respond to a request for comment.
The lead story for the Sunday Mirror is an investigation into cosmetics firms up-selling surgery abroad. A surgeon is said to have tried to "flog a Brazilian buttlift" to an undercover reporter. The Mirror's editorial advises that world-class surgery comes with a world-class price and any offer of cheaper rates should be handled with care.
There is no let-up in the pressure on the Manchester United manager Michael Carrick on the back pages after his team's loss to Chelsea. The Telegraph says it was a "Halloween Horror" that puts the club on its worst run of results since 1988. For the Star, Carrick's spell at the club is now surely "deader than disco".

title: How the downfall of Serbia's Vučiċ mirrored that of Hungary's Orbán
text:
How the downfall of Serbia's Vučiċ mirrored that of Hungary's Orbán
When they met in northern Serbia last November, Serbian President Aleksandar Vučiċ and Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán could hardly have guessed they would both be out of power within a year.
Both were ousted by popular movements - Orbán fell first, in April, defeated by Péter Magyar's Tisza party. Then last Sunday a student movement less than two years old won Serbia's parliamentary elections by a landslide.
The Tisza party in Hungary and the Student List in Serbia look very different - Tisza is centred on the personality and energy of its leader, while the students in Serbia insist they have no leadership.
But the huge turnout - 79% in Hungary and 69% in Serbia, was driven by tech-savvy young people in both countries. They used AI tools to crunch numbers, identify threats to the vote, and mobilise tens of thousands of election monitors to prevent intimidation and electoral fraud by the governing parties.
Mobilisation of voters, and the role of election monitors, played a big role in the opposition victory in both countries.
Last weekend, the DE civic action group in Hungary sent 70 election monitors to Serbia, to work with students' movement representatives, visiting polling stations in the northern Serbian province of Vojvodina.
During the summer, even before the election was called, they held workshops to share their experience and methods from the Hungarian election with the Serbian students.
A key technique was to identify "infected" polling districts in advance - places where the surprisingly high number of votes for the governing party at previous elections suggested that voter intimidation or "chain voting" techniques were used.
"From around 16:00 on election day, we noticed groups of masked hooligans - Vučiċ supporters - gathering near voting stations," Péter Klemm, a student activist from Subotica, told the BBC. "So we sent mobile teams, and started filming everything."
Combined with the "stationary" monitors already in place, 20 to 30 volunteers at each threatened polling station acted as a strong deterrent, he believes, and prevented intimidation or fraud.
Orbán in Hungary, Vučiċ in Serbia, both looked invincible. Both were powerful leaders, in office for 16 and 14 years, who had taken over state institutions and established business empires overlapping the two countries.
Orban chose cheese, Vučiċ meat, when they sat down to a quick lunch of traditional burek pastries at a small, popular town centre bakery in Subotica almost a year ago.
They continued to a local winery, to talk about oil and other business deals - the planned Hungarian purchase of a controlling stake in Serbia's NIS oil company. The two nationalist leaders found much in common, in business and politics, not least their friendship with Vladimir Putin in Russia and Chinese President Xi Jinping, and their strong support for Milorad Dodik, the separatist leader of the Bosnian Serbs.
A high-speed railway between Belgrade and Budapest is being built with Chinese finance and know-how.
The parallels between the fall from power of the two men are extraordinary. Aleksandar Vučiċ admitted defeat at exactly 21:30 on Sunday evening, just as Viktor Orbán did on 12 April. Few observers expected either leader to concede peacefully.
There has been speculation this week that Vučiċ spoke to Orbán twice on Sunday night to ask his advice - once before he conceded, and again at 23:15. And that Orbán convinced his Serbian ally not to use force.
Vučiċ denies that he spoke to Orbán before he made his announcement, but acknowledges the later conversation. Viktor Orbán, contacted by the BBC, declined to comment.
An hour before polls closed in Serbia, masked and hooded vigilantes took up position in central Belgrade. During voting, similar groups were photographed at many polling stations, and blocked by election monitors.
There is another strange numerical similarity. The Student List will have 140 seats in the 250-seat Serbian parliament, the same number Péter Magyar's Tisza party won in the 199-seat Hungarian parliament.
Magyar was the only European leader to ring the students directly to congratulate them that evening - and probably the only one who had their number.
"It is always good to hear that the story of Tisza could provide an inspiration for other nations," the Hungarian prime minister told the BBC.
"The result of the Hungarian election clearly showed us that what we are doing here is right," the head of the Student List, Ilija Srdanoviċ, said on the eve of the vote.
Srdanoviċ was one of those Péter Magyar spoke to that Sunday evening.
Orbán, 63, and Vučiċ, 56, may now both face prosecution for corruption and abuse of power.
The judicial machinery in both countries is similar. Serbia's special prosecution service for organised crime, JTOK, and Hungary's brand new special prosecutors, known as NVVH, have similar powers. They could prove useful to each other.
Hungarian companies close to Orbán were also involved in the Novi Sad railway station construction project. The collapse of the station's canopy on 1 November 2024 - blamed on corruption, as well as negligence - killed 16 people, and acted as the catalyst for the Serbian student movement.
"There was a perception in Europe that the longer the Orbán and Vučiċ regimes stayed in office, the stronger they got," Áron Timar, founder of the DE civic action group in Hungary told the BBC.
"In fact they got weaker. And once society found its voice and rose up, there was no way of stopping it."
description: Defeat for Serbia's Aleksandar Vučiċ in last weekend's vote was a carbon copy of Viktor Orbán's fall in Hungary.

title: Judge dismisses Trump's lawsuit against WSJ over Epstein birthday book
text:
Judge dismisses Trump's lawsuit against Wall Street Journal over Epstein birthday book
A US judge has thrown out President Donald Trump's $10bn (£7.4bn) lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal, ruling the suit was "grasping at straws".
Trump had sued the media outlet's parent company Dow Jones and its leader Rupert Murdoch last year after it reported on a letter allegedly written by Trump to disgraced financier and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein as part of a birthday book in 2003, before Epstein was charged with sex crimes.
Trump has denied writing or signing the letter, which included suggestive language and a drawing of the outline of a woman's body.
Judge Darrin Gayles threw out the case, finding the suit runs counter to the First Amendment, which protects freedom of the press.
Gayles had already once dismissed the defamation lawsuit, which sought $20 billion in damages. Trump's team refiled the suit seeking $10 billion, and this time, the judge threw out the case "with prejudice," meaning the suit cannot be filed again.
The news outlet's story about Epstein's 50th birthday book - and the letter with Trump's name - came as the Trump administration battled intense bipartisan criticism over the summer for its handling of Epstein documents.
Trump had said the newspaper had slandered him and violated libel laws in publishing the article.
In his 20-page ruling, Gayles noted the paper's "thoughtful and detailed investigation" that led to the story and said the lawsuit was "grasping at straws" to "manufacture flaws" in their work.
The judge wrote that Trump's legal team did not prove that the defendants made defamatory statements with "actual malice", which the law requires be proven.
Actual malice is high bar to meet, as it requires proof that the defendant knew the defamatory statement was false or acted with reckless disregard for whether it was true or not.
Trump alleged that the letter obtained and released by the Journal, which features his signature at the bottom, was "fake" and that the defendants devised the story in order to defame him.
Trump's legal team had argued that because Trump denied writing the letter when contacted by the Journal, the paper should have "disregarded everything else they learned in their investigation and not published the story", Gayles wrote.
"But that is not what the actual malice standard requires and runs afoul of the First Amendment," Gayles wrote.
If that were the law, he wrote, then "any time a public figure or his team denies an accusation, journalists would be immediately blocked from publishing negative or contradictory press—a result that flies in the face of the 'American privilege to speak one's mind'".
According to the Wall Street Journal story, a letter bearing Trump's name "contained several lines of typewritten text framed by the outline of a naked woman, which appears to be hand-drawn with a heavy marker".
It reportedly contained a joking reference that "enigmas never age" and allegedly ended with the words: "A pal is a wonderful thing. Happy Birthday - and may every day be another wonderful secret".
description: Trump had sued the media outlet after it published a letter to Epstein purportedly written and signed by the president as part of a birthday book.

title: No more washing up: How Airbnb's new house rules have divided hosts and guests
text:
No more washing up: How Airbnb's new house rules have divided hosts and guests
When Lisa Clewes returned to her Welsh holiday let after a group of guests checked out, she was horrified by the mess.
Just days earlier, she had met the group in person and helped with their luggage.
But after a dinner party, the house was left "in a complete mess" with broken glasses, drinks cans on the floor, pans full of food on the table and fish guts left in the garden.
"It was really unbelievable. Had I had another booking the same day, I would have had to cancel or delay check-in," says Clewes.
She charges a cleaning fee that covers around 75% of the cost of a cleaner and asks guests to empty the fridge, put rubbish in the bins and load the dishwasher.
But Airbnb's new rules mean hosts can no longer ask guests to do jobs normally carried out by cleaners, including washing and putting away dishes, stripping beds and taking rubbish off site.
The updated guidelines, which apply to bookings made globally from 20 November, state that hosts can now set seven standard house rules and add other "reasonable" requests.
Clewes says it typically takes cleaners four hours to turn around her three-bedroom property. She fears guests leaving more mess could mean hiring extra cleaners and increasing costs – expenses that may ultimately be passed on to her guests.
The changes have come as a relief to guests like Jessica Newhook, who says she has been faced with lengthy checkout lists, often on top of hefty cleaning fees.
She booked an Airbnb in Florida for a family reunion of 11 guests and says they had to "leave the property move-in ready for the cleaners", despite paying a $250 (£187) cleaning fee.
Newhook says the host told them to wash and fold towels, clean the bedding and kitchen, and sweep and mop the floors. She was also warned by the host that their behaviour needed to improve or they could be told to leave, because they had left chairs blocking bins.
"We had rules about everything and it was not relaxing at all."
While Newhook likes the home comforts of staying in an Airbnb, she says the combination of relentless rules and rising cleaning fees has taken away much of its appeal.
"It is getting to the point where a hotel is cheaper and I know what to expect."
Krissi Foskett, 46, from Glasgow, runs a national cleaning company and regularly stays in Airbnb properties so "can see the issue from both sides".
During a recent stay in Stafford, she paid a £35 cleaning fee but was still asked to strip the beds, put on a wash, empty bins and carry rubbish down a long track to a recycling area.
"I don't particularly mind doing those things, but it did make me question what exactly I was paying the additional cleaning fee for," she says.
For Foskett, there is a difference between being a considerate guest – "putting your dirty dishes in the dishwasher" – and being "expected to prepare the property for the next guests".
Through her cleaning business, she has also seen the other extreme, with teams arriving to find broken furniture, vomit and pet urine.
While she sympathises with hosts facing tight turnarounds and rising cleaning costs, these should not be passed on to guests, she says.
"If you're running an Airbnb as a business, professional cleaning is a cost of doing business."
Anthony Marsh, who co-owns a cabin retreat in North Yorkshire with his husband, used to list five of their 12 properties on Airbnb, but says the new rules have prompted him to reduce this number to just two.
His concern with the changes is that "Airbnb has effectively given guests permission to come and leave properties a tip, and a host can't do anything about it".
He believes asking guests to wash their pots and put out the bins is hardly unreasonable and, with a small cleaning team and tight turnaround times, he worries extra mess could leave properties unready for the next arrivals.
"It's common sense and common decency," he says.
His company does not charge a cleaning fee, and Marsh says most guests are respectful. But fees are more common than not. Some 63.2% of Airbnb listings charge a cleaning fee, with an average cost of £55 according to data from AirROI.
Laura Lewis runs a directory that helps holiday-let owners market their properties and connect with potential guests.
Many of her clients also list on Airbnb and she says most are unhappy with the new rules, arguing that asking guests to wash up is a matter of basic respect.
"Some people say it's factored into the cleaning fee, but I wouldn't leave a holiday let with all the washing-up to do. It's not the right thing," she says.
The announcement has added to growing frustration among owners following increases in Airbnb's commission rates last year. Many are investing in their own websites and social media to attract direct bookings and avoid platform fees.
Lewis has taken the same approach with the three treehouses on her farm – most of her bookings are already direct and she now plans to remove her listings from Airbnb altogether.
Not all hosts are concerned about the changes, however. Matt Porsz, who hosts and manages other Airbnb properties full-time, believes the update will improve the guest experience without changing how most people behave.
Guests at his property in south-west London are asked only to lock up and return the keys. "People sometimes strip the beds or do things without me asking, and that's nice for my cleaners, but I don't expect it."
Porsz doubts the changes will lead to guests leaving properties in a worse state, pointing to Airbnb's mutual review system.
"If I put a big chore list, I wouldn't expect a five-star review and vice versa – if a guest leaves the place in a state, you're not going to give them a good review."
He believes the system encourages both sides to behave reasonably, and that most guests will continue to treat properties with respect.
"Airbnb is trying to cut out the silly stuff because it's not a good guest experience."
Update 1 November - this article has been updated to remove a photograph of a contributor after they confirmed AI had been used in the image.
description: Airbnb hosts must stop asking guests to wash-up or take out bins under rules coming into force in November.

title: Rahul Gandhi: India's opposition rallies against voter roll revision exercise
text:
India's opposition holds mega rally seeking election chief's resignation
Tens of thousands gathered in Delhi for a rally demanding the resignation of India's chief election commissioner over a controversial revision of voter lists.
Organised by the opposition INDIA bloc and led by Rahul Gandhi's Congress party, the protest drew many of the alliance's most prominent leaders in a show of strength against Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government.
Protesters waved flags and chanted "Save the vote, save the country" and "Vote thief, give up power".
It was the latest in a series of protests over electoral roll revision that the opposition says has removed eligible voters to benefit the Bharatiya Janata Party. The BJP and the Election Commission deny the allegations.
The crowds gathered at Ramlila Maidan, a sprawling ground in central Delhi known for hosting major political and cultural events. Some protesters sang and danced to patriotic Bollywood songs, while others waited beneath a large canopy in the colours of the Indian flag to hear opposition leaders speak.
Gandhi and several senior opposition leaders arrived at the venue in an open jeep, travelling through crowds of cheering supporters.
The event was also attended by Congress leaders Sonia Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge, alongside leaders of regional parties such as Mamata Banerjee, Akhilesh Yadav, Mehbooba Mufti, Supriya Sule and Tejashwi Yadav.
Addressing the crowds, Rahul Gandhi said those gathered had sent a message to Modi, Home Minister Amit Shah and Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
"This is not the voice of a single political party or of politicians. It is the voice of India's youth, women, farmers and workers," he said.
"We will not allow democracy to be destroyed in India. We will not allow the constitution to be destroyed."
Other opposition leaders echoed Gandhi's criticism of the Election Commission. Congress president Kharge said the alliance would continue its campaign until Kumar resigned, while Banerjee pledged to keep fighting against what she described as threats to democracy.
Speaking to reporters in Delhi on Sunday, senior BJP leader and federal minister JP Nadda accused the opposition of trying to create unrest and destabilise the government under the guise of defending democracy.
He described the rally as a "calculated conspiracy to plunge the nation into anarchy - in the name of democracy".
At the centre of the dispute is an exercise known as the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), which has resulted in more than 130 million names being removed from India's draft electoral rolls.
The Election Commission says the exercise is intended to remove duplicate registrations and the names of people who have died, moved away or are otherwise ineligible to vote. It says eligible voters who have been wrongly excluded can seek to have their names restored.
But opposition parties allege that the process is removing legitimate voters and could benefit the governing BJP in future elections.
The controversy deepened in September when The Indian Express newspaper reported that Kumar had made key decisions about the revision despite repeated objections from the two other election commissioners.
The poll panel said differences of opinion were normal in any institution and did not affect its functioning.
Sunday's rally followed weeks of protests over the voter-list revision, including demonstrations by student groups and the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP).
Last month, Gandhi led tens of thousands on a march from central Delhi's Connaught Place to the Supreme Court, demanding Kumar's resignation.
The CJP also backed Sunday's rally but chose not to participate. Its founder Abhijeet Dipke said the group wanted to maintain its independence from established political parties.
The event took place under strict conditions imposed by Delhi Police. According to local media reports, organisers were required to end the gathering by 5pm, install CCTV cameras at the venue and ensure that protesters did not march beyond the designated grounds.
The restrictions came against a backdrop of tensions over the policing of demonstrations in the capital. On 10 October, several leaders of the CJP were detained during protests against Kumar, while BBC reporters witnessed police dragging demonstrators away and beating some with batons.
At Ramlila Maidan, however, the atmosphere was largely peaceful, with people of different ages and professions turning out to express their concerns about the integrity of India's elections.
"We don't even know if this is a people's mandate or a stolen mandate," Isha, a development sector professional from Delhi, told the BBC.
Deepro Guha, a lawyer from Delhi, said he was concerned about the way the revision had been carried out.
"It's important because voting is the basis of democracy. If people's names are removed without any explanation, there is a problem," he said.
On Saturday, opposition leaders also staged a symbolic impeachment of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, accusing him of undermining the electoral process.
The proceedings were purely symbolic and had no legal standing. Under Indian law, the chief election commissioner can only be removed through a formal parliamentary process.
But the move was another show of unity by the INDIA bloc, an alliance of opposition parties formed in 2023 to to take on Modi's BJP.
Modi did not directly comment on the mock impeachment, but at public rallies on Friday and Saturday he accused opposition parties of trying to create chaos and undermining the dignity of the constitution.
description: Thousands gathered in the heart of delhi, calling for the chief election commissioner to step down.

title: Celebrity Traitors: Why the real winners are Maya Jama, King Kenny and Miranda Hart
text:
Who are the real winners of Celebrity Traitors?
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from The Celebrity Traitors final
In some ways, all the players on The Celebrity Traitors can be seen as winners.
They all got to appear on a hugely popular TV show, rubbing shoulders with other stars and gaining new fans along the way.
But there are certain celebrities, such as Miranda Hart, King Kenny, Maya Jama and Joanne McNally, who have been tipped by industry experts as getting the biggest career boost after the show.
Sebastian "Bash" Croft - who won the game, alongside Romesh Ranganathan - could also now be in line for greater roles.
We've taken a look at the breakout stars of the series and what might lie ahead for them.
Miranda Hart
After a spell of ill-health, the show has done wonders for bringing Miranda Hart back into the public eye.
There was that incredible “Little Mix Big Mix” viral dance moment, but Hart also displayed a level of vulnerability which stood out in a show where the stars don't really talk about their personal lives.
When her friend Joe Lycett was banished, her tearful reaction to his exit provided a rare poignant moment.
"Connection and laughter and joy are bigger than this game - and to meet someone and just play and laugh, it's all us humans need, you know?" she said.
When she was murdered, she also demonstrated genuine emotion in her response. "Ultimately, in my little personal story, this has been quite extraordinary," she said.
For culture journalist Natalie Jamieson, Hart's openness and relatability made her the "standout" star from this year's series.
And it could also lead to us seeing more of Hart on the small screen. According to The Sun, the BBC is looking to bring back her self-titled sitcom after her stint on Celebrity Traitors led to fresh interest in the show.
The BBC declined to comment on the possible return of Hart’s show.
But she’s not the only one who won hearts by showing real warmth.
The same could be said for Romesh Ranganathan - who, in a departure from his usual cynical, deadpan stand-up persona, seemed really to care about his fellow cast members. Jerry Hall also won viewers over with her charming eccentricity.
And then there’s James Acaster, who showed genuine vulnerability as he struggled to come to terms with being a traitor.
Social media users seemed split after his bombshell confession to being a traitor, with some totally exasperated and others saying they respected him for going out on his own terms.
Either way, he's definitely got the nation talking.
King Kenny
When it comes to celebrities who are most likely to see the biggest career boost, most experts say Kenny is King.
Going into the castle, the 29-year-old was best known to younger fans as a member of the popular British YouTube collective Beta Squad.
But Kenny will have been "the least familiar name to a mainstream audience," says showbiz journalist Nikki Onafuye.
That all changed as he was recruited as a traitor, bringing much-needed energy to the turret - and he made it all the way through to Friday night’s tense final.
Having shown he can hold his own alongside established broadcasters, actors and comedians, big things could now be in store for Kenny.
"He 100% has just been minted as a mainstream star now," said Marina Hyde, on The Rest is Entertainment podcast.
“The next steps could be panel shows, presenting roles, reality competitions or entertainment formats,” adds TV reporter Siobhan Synnot.
Maya Jama
Fellow traitor Maya Jama also sailed all the way to the final with her cool-as-a-cucumber persona making her a traitor to be reckoned with.
Despite being banished in dramatic fashion, she could now be in line to receive £1m per deal, according to a report in The Times earlier this week.
What Celebrity Traitors has done for Jama is allow her to reveal more of her personality than on Love Island, says Onafuye.
But TV reporter Synnot thinks between the two, Kenny has more to gain because he has introduced himself to millions of new viewers - whereas Jama was already one of Britain's best-known TV presenters before Celebrity Traitors.
"Maya's gain is subtler: she can emerge looking less like the presenter of Love Island and more like a genuinely versatile television star," she says.
Joanne McNally
Of all the comedians in the castle, Joanne McNally was initially the least well known, says Caroline Frost, TV editor at Radio Times.
But she flourished on the show, lasting right up to Thursday's semi-final.
"And she's taken her own path, ignoring the herd and making her own voting decisions, sometimes chaotically, but always with charm, wit and good humour,” says Frost.
The Irish comedian's podcast was already popular before the show.
But after her stint as the joker of the pack, bigger things could now lie in store for her.
Just a few days ago, it was announced that her stand-up tour has been extended into 2027, "due to phenomenal demand".
And her agents will be "fielding calls" for her to bring her star power to other shows, adds Frost.
Culture journalist Jamieson says some of the other female contestants - such as Sharon Rooney, Leigh-Anne Pinnock and Myha'la - also stood out for showing their wit and wisdom, which could serve them well in the outside world.
Things got a bit awkward in one of the episodes, when Sharon disagreed with some of the cast on a challenge, with some social media users saying she was acting in a "childish" way.
But others argued it was a classic case of women being drowned out by men.
"There's been a subtlety in the smartness of women on display here, alongside the frustration of not always being listened to in the game," says Jamieson.
Sebastian 'Bash' Croft
In the end, it was faithful duo Romesh Ranganathan and Sebastian ‘Bash’ Croft who emerged victorious.
Comedian Ranganathan was already a huge star, but the show has introduced Croft, 24, to a much wider audience.
He’s had previous acting roles in Game of Thrones and Heartstopper, but Traitors allowed him to show his own personality, "which as we've seen has endeared him both to other players and the huge watching audience", says Frost.
He is also building his career as a pop star, and he's had a strong presence on social media during the series, posting videos of his tracks.
His debut EP comes out later in November, perfect timing to capitalise on his Traitors win.
And what's in store for the others...
What's clear is that the true victors aren't necessarily the ones who get their hands on the prize pot.
Arguably, what matters most is the amount of screen time you get - and what you do with it.
On that note, spare a thought for those who left the show early, such as Amol Rajan, Julie Hesmondhalgh and Hannah Fry.
But all made an impact in their own way and, as Synnot points out, they get "a nice anecdote" for future interviews.
And what of James Blunt, who stole hearts with his military approach to the challenges and eccentric Top Gun-style outfits - and who came so close to winning the whole show?
Maybe he's the mystery man in contention for the new James B(ond) - although his hapless theories could mean he'll be in line to be the new Johnny English instead.
description: Certain stars have been tipped by industry experts as getting the biggest career boost after the show.
